article_title: Too Good For Violence (TGFV) (Character Education)
citation: What Works Clearinghouse. (2006). WWC Intervention Report: Too Good for Violence. U.S. Department of Education. https://www.mendezfoundation.org
title: Scripted lessons combining role-playing, cooperative learning games, small group activities, and classroom discussion
description: The program's lesson design pattern pairs fully scripted lessons with active, participatory methods. As the report describes, "All lessons are scripted and engage students through role-playing and cooperative learning games, small group activities, and classr oom discussions." Cooperative learning activities, role-playing, and skill building methods reinforce positive behaviors and skills and encourage students to apply them in other contexts. Lessons run 30-60 minutes in elementary school and 30-45 minutes in middle school.
requirements: Scripted lessons are intended to be taught by trained teachers or Mendez Foundation instructors.
target_learners: elementary school students (K-5)
middle school students (6-8)
examples: Lessons include peaceful conflict resolution strategies and prosocial skill development in goal setting, decisionmaking, anger and stress management, communication, and peer resistance.
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse. (2006). WWC Intervention Report: Too Good for Violence. U.S. Department of Education. https://www.mendezfoundation.org

article_title: Read Well® (English Language Learners)
citation: Read Well®. (2010). WWC Intervention Report. U.S. Department of Education, What Works Clearinghouse. http://store.cambiumlearning.com/resource.aspx?page=ProgramOverview&site=sw&parentId=019005451
title: Scaffold early reading instruction by modeling, then gradually decreasing teacher support toward independent performance
description: Read Well® is based on "the tenets of scaffolded instruction, in which teachers begin by presenting models and gradually decreasing their support by providing guided practice before students are asked to complete the skill or strategy independently". A concrete instantiation is shared reading of new text in which the teacher reads the difficult or irregular words; as student skills and motivation increase, the amount of teacher-read text decreases and the student gains greater independence. The program also lets pacing depend on each participant's level of mastery.
requirements: Teacher materials and guided practice structures that allow support to be faded as student skills increase
constraints: The report describes this as the program's design tenet; the reviewed evidence does not isolate scaffolding as the causal ingredient
target_learners: kindergarten and first-grade students
English language learners
target_learning_goals: independent application of skills and strategies
examples: Student and teacher read new text aloud with the teacher reading the difficult or irregular words, and the amount of teacher-read text decreases as student skills increase
key_sources: Read Well®. (2010). WWC Intervention Report. U.S. Department of Education, What Works Clearinghouse. http://store.cambiumlearning.com/resource.aspx?page=ProgramOverview&site=sw&parentId=019005451

article_title: Once Early-Reading Program
citation: Once Early-Reading Program: Evidence Rating Summary. (2025). https://once.org
title: Pair scripted tutoring delivered by non-specialist staff with weekly coaching based on session recordings and real-time progress data
description: The Once model makes non-specialist delivery viable by combining scripted, laptop-delivered lessons with a structured coaching loop: tutors receive weekly 30-minute coaching sessions from a consistent coach who reviews session recordings and provides targeted feedback, and a real-time data portal lets tutors, coaches, and administrators monitor student progress. This allows "staff without specialized reading instruction backgrounds to deliver sequenced lessons with fidelity". The article presents this staffing and supervision structure as integral to implementation.
requirements: A two-day, in-person training focused on the Science of Reading, the Once delivery method and model, and the Once technology, with ample time allocated for hands-on practice.
Weekly 30-minute coaching sessions from a consistent coach, plus laptop and internet access with a front-facing camera for session recording.
constraints: Coaching and data monitoring are described as components of the Once program specifically; the article does not report separate effects for the coaching component.
target_learners: PreK through first grade students receiving supplemental literacy tutoring
target_learning_goals: Early literacy skills delivered with fidelity by staff without specialized reading instruction backgrounds
examples: Tutors receive weekly 30-minute coaching sessions from a consistent Once coach who reviews session recordings and provides targeted feedback; a real-time data portal allows tutors, coaches, and administrators to monitor student progress.
key_sources: Once Early-Reading Program: Evidence Rating Summary. (2025). https://evidenceforessa.org/program/once-early-reading-program/

article_title: Galaxy Math
citation: Galaxy Math. (2013). Program description, Evidence for ESSA. https://www.evidenceforessa.org
title: Scripted one-to-one tutoring with fixed dosage and paraprofessional tutors
description: Galaxy Math operationalizes tutoring as a scripted, fixed-dosage, one-to-one delivery model: "The program is scripted, and tutors are expected to follow the scripts without reading them or memorizing them." Sessions are "30-minute sessions 3 times a week for 16 weeks" delivered by paraprofessionals, standardizing implementation across tutors.
requirements: Tutors follow scripts without reading or memorizing them
2-day initial workshop plus weekly coordinator meetings
constraints: Designed for at-risk first graders in early arithmetic
target_learners: at-risk first graders
target_learning_goals: addition and subtraction understanding and proficiency
examples: Paraprofessionals delivered 30-minute sessions three times weekly over 16 weeks in the Nashville study
key_sources: Galaxy Math. (2013). Program description, Evidence for ESSA. https://evidenceforessa.org/program/galaxy-math/

article_title: Challenges in Adolescent Reading Intervention: Evidence from a Randomized Control Trial
citation: Naihobe Gonzalez, Sophie MacIntyre, Pilar Beccar-Varela. (2018). Challenges in Adolescent Reading Intervention: Evidence from a Randomized Control Trial. Working Paper 62. Oakland, CA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Schedule adolescent reading interventions so students do not miss grade-level content
description: This principle holds that pull-out intervention arrangements for adolescent struggling readers should be designed so that students do not sacrifice access to grade-level coursework. The Oakland LLI trial found that "Students who were pulled out of other classes to receive LLI were particularly negatively affected, possibly as a result of missing grade-level content." Scheduling is therefore a design lever, not just a logistical detail.
requirements: Intervention scheduling must account for which classes students would otherwise attend
constraints: The article frames the missing-content explanation as possible, not established
target_learners: struggling adolescent readers in secondary grades
target_learning_goals: mastery of grade-level English language arts/literacy standards
examples: In the Oakland trial, some students were pulled out of other classes to receive LLI, and this subgroup showed particularly negative outcomes
key_sources: Naihobe Gonzalez, Sophie MacIntyre, Pilar Beccar-Varela. (2018). Challenges in Adolescent Reading Intervention: Evidence from a Randomized Control Trial. Working Paper 62. Oakland, CA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/challenges-in-adolescent-reading-intervention-evidence-from-a-randomized-control-trial

article_title: Do Typical RCTs of Education Interventions Have Sufficient Statistical Power for Linking Impacts on Teacher Practice and Student Achievement Outcomes?
citation: Schochet, Peter Z. (2009). Do Typical RCTs of Education Interventions Have Sufficient Statistical Power for Linking Impacts on Teacher Practice and Student Achievement Outcomes? (NCEE 2009-4065). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ncee.ed.gov
title: Size RCT data collection for teacher practice mediators according to the power needed for mediator-achievement analyses
description: Because teacher practice mediators are costly to obtain through classroom observations, videotaping, and coded protocols, the report argues power results "may have design implications for the scope of the data collection effort for obtaining costly teacher practice mediators." If power is low, mediator analyses reduce to a heuristic qualitative linking of outcomes. Designers should therefore decide the scope of mediator data collection in light of the school sample needed for precise mediator-achievement estimates.
requirements: Sufficient study schools (about 150 to 200 under OLS assumptions) to power mediator-achievement association tests
Reliable mediator measures, since measurement error further reduces power
constraints: For typical RCTs with 60 schools, power is likely to be limited, especially for IV methods
target_learners: elementary school students in low performing schools
target_learning_goals: identifying teacher practice pathways through which interventions improve student achievement
examples: The report's simulated power analysis computes the number of schools required to detect mediator effects explaining 5, 10, and 20 percent of classroom-effect variation at different power levels
key_sources: Schochet, Peter Z. (2009). Do Typical RCTs of Education Interventions Have Sufficient Statistical Power for Linking Impacts on Teacher Practice and Student Achievement Outcomes? (NCEE 2009-4065). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/do-typical-rcts-of-education-interventions-have-sufficient-statistical-power-for-linking-impacts-on-teacher-practice-and-student-achievement-outcomes

article_title: Nudging Parents to Choose Better Schools: The Importance of School Choice Architecture
citation: Steven Glazerman, Ira Nichols-Barrer, Jon Valant, Jesse Chandler, Alyson Burnett. (2018). Nudging Parents to Choose Better Schools: The Importance of School Choice Architecture. Working Paper 65. Washington, DC: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/nudging-parents-to-choose-better-schools-the-importance-of-school-choice-architecture
title: Design the architecture of school choice interfaces to nudge parents toward better-informed choices
description: The article's central design principle is that the architecture of school choice — how school information is presented in chooser interfaces — shapes parents' decisions. It argues that "simple design choices, such as  setting the default sort order to academic performance instead of distance from home, could induce parents to choose academically higher performing schools," so interface defaults and information presentation should be treated as policy-relevant design levers.
requirements: An online chooser interface whose information presentation and defaults can be configured
constraints: Evidence comes from a factorial experiment with low-income parents choosing schools; effects on other populations are not established in the supplied text
target_learners: Low-income parents choosing schools for their children
examples: The study tested five presentation design factors, including default sort order, in an online school chooser tool
key_sources: Steven Glazerman, Ira Nichols-Barrer, Jon Valant, Jesse Chandler, Alyson Burnett. (2018). Nudging Parents to Choose Better Schools: The Importance of School Choice Architecture. Working Paper 65. Washington, DC: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/nudging-parents-to-choose-better-schools-the-importance-of-school-choice-architecture

article_title: Improving Chicago's Schools
citation: Luppescu, S., Hart, H., Jennings, S., & Dean, M. (2003). Torvalds Improving Chicago's Schools: 2003 Survey Report. Consortium on Chicago School Research. http://www.consortium-chicago.org
title: School survey profiles comparing a school to demographically similar schools and system trends over time
description: The report's display format charts a school's score on each measure across five survey years alongside two reference trends. It "compares your school both to other schools that are demographically similar to yours, and to the Chicago public school system as a whole," with a gray box marking the middle two-thirds of schools and a star locating the school's standing. Time-trend data show whether reform efforts are improving, and trend bands distinguish somewhat from substantially above- or below-average reports.
requirements: Multiple years of survey participation to display trends; at least seven respondents per measure for a valid school reading
constraints: Star placement carries unavoidable imprecision, so small differences between the school and reference lines should not be over-read; a school's own data may be missing for some years
target_learners: school leadership teams, principals, teachers, and Local School Councils
examples: The illustrative Program Coherence display charts 1994-2003 trends with the school's line, a schools-like-yours dashed line, and the systemwide solid line
key_sources: Luppescu, S., Hart, H., Jennings, S., & Dean, M. (2003). Torvalds Improving Chicago's Schools: 2003 Survey Report. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/improving-chicagos-schools-torvalds

article_title: Charting Reform in Asbury School
citation: Sebring, P. A., Bryk, A. S., Luppescu, S., & Thum, Y. M. (1995). Charting Reform in Asbury High School: Results of Student and Teacher Surveys. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://ccsr.uchicago.edu
title: School report pattern: summary profiles plus detailed scale distributions with quartile benchmarks
description: Each school report has two parts: Part I gives five profile graphs summarizing each essential support, allowing a school to compare itself with all participating schools and alerting it to possible strengths and weaknesses; Part II details how students and teachers responded to each contributing scale. Each scale section shows item endorsement percentages, an interpretation table mapping scale scores to qualitative descriptions, and bar charts comparing the school's score distribution with top- and bottom-quartile schools.
requirements: A separate guide on how to read the report and familiarity with the Self-Analysis Guide are recommended before beginning the analysis.
constraints: The report is intended to assist schools in assessing strengths and weaknesses and improvement efforts, not to prescribe actions.
target_learners: school staff and Local School Council members conducting self-analysis
examples: The LSC Contribution section reports that in bottom-quartile schools about 35 percent of teachers see a limited contribution and 40 percent no contribution, while in top-quartile schools a little over half judge the LSC has made significant contributions.
key_sources: Sebring, P. A., Bryk, A. S., Luppescu, S., & Thum, Y. M. (1995). Charting Reform in Asbury High School: Results of Student and Teacher Surveys. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/charting-reform-asbury-school-results-student-and-teacher-surveys

article_title: Charting Reform in Prairie School
citation: Sebring, P. A., Bryk, A. S., Luppescu, S., & Thum, Y. M. (1995). Charting Reform in Prairie School: Results of Student and Teacher Surveys. Consortium on Chicago School Research.
title: School report pattern: summary profiles plus detailed scale distributions benchmarked against similar and quartile schools
description: The report follows a two-part design: Part I gives five profile graphs, one per essential support, offering a quick comparison of the school with all participating schools and with similar schools matched on IGAP scores and school size; Part II details each scale with item-level endorsement percentages, an interpretation table for scale scores, and distributions comparing the school with top and bottom quartile schools. This design is intended to alert schools to possible strengths and weaknesses and guide deeper examination.
requirements: Comparison groups of schools similar with respect to IGAP scores and school size, and sufficient respondent counts per scale
constraints: The report advises reading a separate guide on how to read the report and the Self-Analysis Guide before beginning analysis
target_learners: school staff and Local School Council members conducting school self-analysis
target_learning_goals: diagnosing school strengths and weaknesses to guide improvement efforts
examples: The report suggests staff study Part I summary profiles while assigning Part II subsections such as Parent Community Partnerships to smaller groups with specialized interest.
key_sources: Sebring, P. A., Bryk, A. S., Luppescu, S., & Thum, Y. M. (1995). Charting Reform in Prairie School: Results of Student and Teacher Surveys. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/charting-reform-prairie-school-results-student-and-teacher-surveys

article_title: A cessation of measurement: Identifying test taker disengagement using response time
citation: Wise, S., & Kuhfeld, M. (2020). A cessation of measurement: Identifying test taker disengagement using response time. In M. Margolis, & R. Feinberg (Eds.), Integrating Timing Considerations to Improve Testing Practices, Routledge. https://www.routledge.com/
title: Decisions to include or exclude rapid guesses during scoring should hinge on the intended purpose of the measurement
description: The chapter recommends that the choice about how to treat rapid guesses in scoring be driven by the test's purpose. As it states, "the choice to include/exclude rapid guesses during scoring hinges primarily on whether measurement is intended to indicate as accurately as possible what the test taker knows and can do or if it represents an achievement hurdle that is considered the test taker's responsibility to clear." When the goal is accurate indication of achievement, disengaged responses should be managed during scoring rather than counted as evidence of low ability.
requirements: A clear decision about whether the test is intended to indicate achievement accurately or to serve as an achievement hurdle the test taker is responsible for clearing
target_learners: test takers on large-scale and interim assessments
examples: The chapter frames scoring decisions for rapid guesses around this purpose distinction rather than prescribing a single uniform rule
key_sources: Wise, S., & Kuhfeld, M. (2020). A cessation of measurement: Identifying test taker disengagement using response time. In M. Margolis, & R. Feinberg (Eds.), Integrating Timing Considerations to Improve Testing Practices, Routledge. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/a-cessation-of-measurement-identifying-test-taker-disengagement-using-response-time-book/

article_title: Effort analysis: Individual score validation of achievement test data
citation: Steven Wise. (2015). Effort analysis: Individual score validation of achievement test data. Applied Measurement in Education, 28(3), 237–252. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/effort-analysis-individual-score-validation-of-achievement-test-data/
title: Trust in an achievement score requires that the test event not be unduly influenced by construct-irrelevant factors
description: This principle states a validity precondition for achievement testing: users can trust that a score "accurately reflects what that student knows and can do" only if the test event is not unduly influenced by construct-irrelevant factors that could distort it. The article uses this premise to justify screening individual scores for distortion from low test-taking motivation before drawing inferences about achievement.
requirements: Score users must be able to assume the test event was not unduly influenced by construct-irrelevant factors before trusting the score for achievement inferences
constraints: Test-taking motivation is presented as one such construct-irrelevant factor, not the only possible one
target_learners: K-12 students taking achievement tests
target_learning_goals: Valid inference about what a student knows and can do from test scores
examples: The article's abstract presents this trust assumption as the foundation for its argument that non-effortful test taking must be detected
key_sources: Steven Wise. (2015). Effort analysis: Individual score validation of achievement test data. Applied Measurement in Education, 28(3), 237–252. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/effort-analysis-individual-score-validation-of-achievement-test-data/

article_title: Are achievement gap estimates biased by differential student test effort? Putting an important policy metric to the test.
citation: James Soland. (2018). Are achievement gap estimates biased by differential student test effort? Putting an important policy metric to the test. Teachers College Record, 120(12), 1-26. https://www.tcrecord.org
title: Interpret test scores as achievement only to the extent that students are willing and able to demonstrate what they have learned
description: Because low test effort biases observed test scores downward and effort differs by subgroup, score-based comparisons such as achievement gaps reflect achievement only conditionally on student engagement. The article states that "test scores reflect achievement only to the extent that students are willing and able to demonstrate what they have learned," reminding users of policy metrics to consider effort when interpreting subgroup score differences.
requirements: Test interpretation should account for, or at least consider, measures of student test effort such as rapid guessing.
constraints: The bias introduced into achievement gap estimates by differential test effort is hard to quantify.
target_learners: K-12 students in subgroup comparisons used for policy and accountability
target_learning_goals: Valid interpretation of achievement gap estimates and subgroup score differences
examples: The study conditioned achievement gap estimates on measures of rapid guessing to test the sensitivity of gap conclusions to differential effort.
key_sources: James Soland. (2018). Are achievement gap estimates biased by differential student test effort? Putting an important policy metric to the test. Teachers College Record, 120(12), 1-26. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/are-achievement-gap-estimates-biased-by-differential-student-test-effort-putting-an-important-policy-metric-to-the-test/

article_title: Introducing Blended Learning in Low-Tech Settings: Lessons from Haiti
citation: Digital Promise (2021). Introducing Blended Learning in Low-Tech Settings: Lessons from Haiti. https://digitalpromise.org/initiative/global-education/haiti
title: Scale blended learning deeply before scaling broadly by investing in communities and tools
description: The article recommends to "Focus on depth over breadth and build a lasting and catalytic impact by investing in communities and tools." This principle directs implementers to concentrate resources on fewer communities, engaging them "throughout the process of planning, implementation, and improvement," rather than expanding coverage quickly.
requirements: Sustained engagement with pilot communities across planning, implementation, and improvement
target_learners: Rural primary school students in low-tech settings
target_learning_goals: Sustainable adoption of blended learning practices
examples: The pilot focuses on 12 rural schools and recruits and trains staff from the schools' rural zones
key_sources: Digital Promise (2021). Introducing Blended Learning in Low-Tech Settings: Lessons from Haiti. https://digitalpromise.org/initiative/global-education/haiti

article_title: Reducing Behavior Problems in the Elementary School Classroom
citation: Epstein, M., Atkins, M., Cullinan, D., Kutash, K., and Weaver, R. (2008). Reducing Behavior Problems in the Elementary School Classroom: A Practice Guide (NCEE #2008-012). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/publications/practiceguides
title: Assess whether schoolwide behavior problems warrant adopting schoolwide strategies or programs, and if so, implement ones shown to reduce negative and foster positive interactions
description: A teacher may be more successful creating a positive classroom behavioral environment when schoolwide efforts also exist. Classroom teachers, in coordination with administrators, grade-level teams, and special educators, should involve a school improvement team, collect information on behavioral hot spots throughout the school, monitor implementation and outcomes with efficient data collection, and, if warranted, "adopt a packaged intervention program that fits well with identi-fied behavior problem(s) and the school context". This recommendation carries a moderate evidence rating.
requirements: Address schoolwide behavior issues by involving a school improvement team
Collect information on the hot spots throughout the school, including frequency and timing of particular schoolwide behavior problems
Monitor implementation and outcomes using an efficient method of data collection and allow ample time for the program to work
constraints: Changes in practices, structures, or programs within schools are unlikely to be implemented, sustained, or effective in the long term without concerted attention to enhancing the fundamental relationships within schools
target_learners: All students in U.S. elementary schools (K-5)
target_learning_goals: Reducing negative and fostering positive social interactions schoolwide
examples: Just as teachers document classroom behavior contexts, school leadership teams can map the behavioral territory of the school and use the information to develop prevention strategies and select schoolwide programs.
key_sources: Epstein, M., Atkins, M., Cullinan, D., Kutash, K., and Weaver, R. (2008). Reducing Behavior Problems in the Elementary School Classroom: A Practice Guide (NCEE #2008-012). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/4

article_title: Teaching Academic Content and Literacy to English Learners in Elementary and Middle School
citation: Baker, S., Geva, E., Kieffer, M. J., Lesaux, N., Linan-Thompson, S., Morris, J., Proctor, C. P., & Russell, R. (2014). Teaching Academic Content and Literacy to English Learners in Elementary and Middle School. What Works Clearinghouse Practice Guide. https://www.whatworks.ed.gov
title: Provide scaffolded small-group instruction with frequent practice and review of newly learned skills across varied contexts over several lessons
description: Small-group intervention for struggling students should be scaffolded so that students get "frequent opportunities for students to practice and review newly learned skills and concepts in various contexts over several lessons to ensure retention." The guide also advises that for students struggling with basic foundational reading skills, time should go not only to those skills but also to vocabulary development and listening and reading comprehension strategies, illustrated with a teacher think-aloud modeling inferential comprehension of a Rosa Parks text.
requirements: Use assessment information to identify students with persistent struggles and design intervention content targeting identified needs
constraints: One-size-fits-all interventions are unlikely to meet diverse needs of English learners who struggle; keep a portfolio of intervention options
When a majority of English learners struggle with a grade-level comprehension skill, teach it in core classroom instruction rather than delegating it to Tier 2
target_learners: English learners in K-8 identified via assessments as struggling with language and literacy development
target_learning_goals: Foundational reading skills, vocabulary development, listening and reading comprehension
examples: A teacher think-aloud on a Rosa Parks text models drawing inferences from textual clues to describe a character
key_sources: Baker, S., Geva, E., Kieffer, M. J., Lesaux, N., Linan-Thompson, S., Morris, J., Proctor, C. P., & Russell, R. (2014). Teaching Academic Content and Literacy to English Learners in Elementary and Middle School. What Works Clearinghouse Practice Guide. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/19

article_title: Lift Every Voice in Tech: Co-designed Recommendations to Support Black Workers and Learners Seeking to Enter and Advance in Technology Industry Career Pathways
citation: Bria Carter, Britney Jacobs, Zohal Shah, Chioma Aso-Hernandez. (2024). Lift Every Voice in Tech: Co-Designed Recommendations to Support Black Workers and Learners Seeking to Enter and Advance in Technology Industry Career Pathways. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Social Cognitive Career Theory and Cultural Historical Activity Theory framework for navigating tech career pathways
description: The report grounds its inquiry in Social Cognitive Career Theory (SCCT), examining how "socialcognitive factors (e.g., learner variability and learning experiences) and contextual affordances" shape self-efficacy, persistence, and perceived barriers in career development. It layers on Cultural Historical Activity Theory (CHAT) to analyze relationships between Black tech workers and learners and their contextual environment, using an activity triangle identifying mediators such as tools, rules, community, division of labor, and the object or activity goal.
requirements: Application requires examining lived experiences to identify factors salient for self-efficacy, persistence, and perceived barriers
constraints: The framework is applied specifically to Black workers and learners in technology career pathways in the U.S.
target_learners: Black workers and learners in non-four-year-degree technology career pathways
target_learning_goals: Academic and career development in technology career pathways
examples: The report used the framework to structure interview and survey questions across six pathway aspects: awareness and exploration, education and training, recruitment and hiring, career entry, career advancement, and career retention.
key_sources: Bria Carter, Britney Jacobs, Zohal Shah, Chioma Aso-Hernandez. (2024). Lift Every Voice in Tech: Co-Designed Recommendations to Support Black Workers and Learners Seeking to Enter and Advance in Technology Industry Career Pathways. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/5dcf2bc8-f40c-4942-96a4-c4a5bda965e3

article_title: Sacramento County Office of Education: Transforming Schools into Centers of Wellness
citation: Sacramento County Office of Education: Transforming Schools Into Centers of Wellness. (2024). WestEd. https://www.centersofwellness.scoe.net/our-work#collectiveimpact
title: SCOE centralized school-based mental health services through an FQHC-eligible Medi-Cal billing model
description: SCOE hires clinicians and places them in schools under the Sacramento County Health Center, a Federally Qualified Healthcare Center eligible for Medi-Cal billing. The brief states these clinicians "provide clinical mental health services (Tier 3) to students and support Tier 1 and Tier 2 prevention and early intervention programs and services at school sites." SCOE also manages Medi-Cal billing centrally, which the brief says removes administrative burden from schools and allows centralized data tracking such as numbers of students served.
requirements: Clinicians must be placed under an FQHC-eligible health center for Medi-Cal billing to function
constraints: Described for Sacramento County schools under SCOE's purview
target_learners: K-12 students in Sacramento County schools
target_learning_goals: Access to school-based clinical mental health services and prevention supports
examples: SCOE manages Medi-Cal billing centrally and tracks data such as numbers of students served
key_sources: Sacramento County Office of Education: Transforming Schools Into Centers of Wellness. (2024). WestEd. https://www.centersofwellness.scoe.net/our-work#collectiveimpact

article_title: Sacramento County Office of Education: Transforming Schools into Centers of Wellness
citation: Sacramento County Office of Education: Transforming Schools Into Centers of Wellness. (2024). WestEd. https://www.centersofwellness.scoe.net/our-work#collectiveimpact
title: Coordination of Services Teams (COST) link students to mental health supports within a multi-tiered system of supports
description: COST is SCOE's coordination mechanism linking students in Sacramento County schools to mental health supports within a multi-tiered system of supports (MTSS). The brief states that "Rather than relying on direct referrals to clinicians, COST coordinates referrals using systematic and proactive approaches (e.g., universal screening data)." This is intended to ensure students' needs are met through appropriate channels, for example avoiding inappropriate referral to therapy when a classroom-based issue is present.
requirements: Universal screening data to drive proactive referral coordination
constraints: Operates within SCOE's multi-tiered system of supports in Sacramento County schools
target_learners: K-12 students in Sacramento County schools
target_learning_goals: Appropriate matching of students to mental health supports and services
examples: COST uses universal screening data rather than direct clinician referrals to coordinate support
key_sources: Sacramento County Office of Education: Transforming Schools Into Centers of Wellness. (2024). WestEd. https://www.centersofwellness.scoe.net/our-work#collectiveimpact

article_title: Sacramento County Office of Education: Transforming Schools into Centers of Wellness
citation: Sacramento County Office of Education: Transforming Schools Into Centers of Wellness. (2024). WestEd. https://www.centersofwellness.scoe.net/our-work#collectiveimpact
title: SCOE mental health career pathway employing peer specialists, graduate clinical interns, and associate clinicians
description: To address a shortage of available mental health clinicians, SCOE built a career pathway using peer specialists, graduate clinical interns, and associate clinicians in paid positions. The brief states these roles "provide career support while establishing a professional pathway for school-based mental health service providers." Internships for undergraduate and graduate students are available, and associate clinicians with graduate degrees can earn clinical hours while employed full-time. Recent partnerships also nurtured the School Based Mental Health and Wellness Path, one of SCOE's Career Pipeline Paths.
requirements: Paid positions for peer specialists, interns, and associate clinicians to sustain the pipeline
constraints: Designed to address the clinician shortage in SCOE's region
target_learners: Undergraduate and graduate students and aspiring school-based mental health professionals
target_learning_goals: Building a professional pathway into school-based mental health careers
examples: Associate clinicians with graduate degrees earn clinical hours while employed full-time
key_sources: Sacramento County Office of Education: Transforming Schools Into Centers of Wellness. (2024). WestEd. https://www.centersofwellness.scoe.net/our-work#collectiveimpact

article_title: Sacramento County Office of Education: Transforming Schools into Centers of Wellness
citation: Sacramento County Office of Education: Transforming Schools Into Centers of Wellness. (2024). WestEd. https://www.centersofwellness.scoe.net/our-work#collectiveimpact
title: Collective impact model aligning health and education systems for school-community mental health
description: SCOE leaders organize their county-wide mental health work through a collective impact model that aligns health and education systems. Partners include the County Department of Health Services, regional Medi-Cal plans, all districts and schools under SCOE's purview, and student, family, and community partnerships. The brief states the organizations are "committed to learning together and aligning and integrating their activities" to achieve population and systems-level change. Core values of relationships, collaboration, and equitable access to care shape the work, alongside a commitment to diversity, equity, inclusion, and belonging.
requirements: Cross-sector partners committed to learning together and aligning and integrating their activities
constraints: Applied to Sacramento County school communities under SCOE's purview
target_learners: Students in Sacramento County school communities
target_learning_goals: Population and systems-level change in school-community mental health support
examples: Partners include the County Department of Health Services, regional Medi-Cal plans, and all SCOE districts and schools

article_title: Accelerate Success for English Learners: Students Work beyond the Edge of Their Current Abilities with Formative Assessment
citation: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate Success for English Learners: Students Work Beyond the Edge of Their Current Abilities With Formative Assessment. WestEd, Region 15 Comprehensive Center. https://www.wested.org/
title: Matching scaffolding practices to formative assessment evidence
description: The brief presents a table pairing scaffolding practices with the formative assessment evidence that would indicate their need — for example, visual aids when students struggle to connect word meanings to spelling, graphic organizers when students need help getting started, sentence stems when small-group discussion is challenging, modeling with think-alouds, structured partner work, whiteboard responses, story retells, and home-language translations. The pattern is that "these scaffolds and related contexts demonstrate the instructional adjustments teachers can make in response to evidence of learning."
requirements: Evidence of student learning that makes the need for a particular scaffold visible and audible
constraints: Practices are keyed to specific evidence conditions rather than applied uniformly to all students
target_learners: English learners across proficiency levels in elementary and secondary classrooms
target_learning_goals: Comprehension of complex content, participation in disciplinary discussion, and language development
examples: The brief suggests visual aids such as pictures of different mammals along with the written word mammal

article_title: Early Literacy Performance in Massachusetts: Results of Ongoing Analysis of Literacy Screening Assessments (2023/24 Data)
citation: Lemke, M., Faulkner-Bond, M., LeBeau, B., Soo Ping Chow, A., & Quesen, S. (2025). Early literacy performance in Massachusetts: Results of ongoing analysis of literacy screening assessments (2023/24 data). WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Screening assessment risk benchmarks are set by three distinct methods (predictive, judgment-based, normative), so there is no common definition of risk across assessments
description: The report organizes how approved Massachusetts screening assessments define their significant-risk cut scores into three approaches: predictive analysis against an external criterion, judgment-based standard setting, and normative percentile cutoffs. It states that "The most common approach across screening assessments is a predictive approach that establishes a risk cut score by using an external criterion," while Star uses the 25th national percentile and i-Ready uses judgment-based standard setting. Because cut scores are derived differently, the report concludes "there is no truly common definition of risk across screening assessments," which complicates cross-assessment and cross-school trend analysis.
requirements: Interpreting risk categories requires knowing which benchmark-setting method each assessment's publisher used, as compiled in the report's Table 2 from technical documentation and publisher communication.
constraints: The report states the lack of a common definition of risk can create challenges for schools, districts, and the state, including inconsistent identification of mobile students and potentially conflicting information for parents.
target_learners: Kindergarten through grade 3 students in Massachusetts public schools
target_learning_goals: Early identification of students at risk of reading difficulty
examples: Table 2 classifies Acadience, DIBELS 8th Edition, MAP Reading Fluency, mCLASS, EarlyBird, and FastBridge as predictive; i-Ready as judgment-based; and Star Early Literacy and Star Reading as normative (below 25th national percentile).

article_title: Learner Variability Is the Rule, Not the Exception
citation: Pape, B. (2018). Learner Variability Is the Rule, Not the Exception. Digital Promise Global. https://lvp.digitalpromiseglobal.org/
title: The science of the individual: pathways and context principles for understanding learner variability
description: Drawing on Todd Rose and colleagues, the paper presents the science of the individual as a framework resting on two notions: the object of interest is the individual, not the statistical average, and human individuals are remarkably variable. It depends on pathways (multiple routes exist to learn to read, so non-mainstream progress is not necessarily delay) and on the context principle, which holds that behavior results from an interaction between traits and situation.
requirements: Addressing the needs of the individual requires abandoning statistical-average thinking and attending to both pathways and context
constraints: The paper attributes this framework to Rose and colleagues rather than testing it; it is presented as a research-based account
target_learners: all learners, including children progressing on alternative reading pathways
target_learning_goals: understanding depth and breadth of learner variability to inform classroom learning
examples: Initial thought heralded a single progression for developing strong reading skills; current research shows multiple pathways exist, so children progressing differently may not have delays
key_sources: Pape, B. (2018). Learner Variability Is the Rule, Not the Exception. Digital Promise Global. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/b7b14506-0b46-4279-9f9e-675c694b06a6

article_title: Strengthening Policies and Practices for the Initial Classification of English Learners: Insights from a National Working Session
citation: H. Gary Cook & Robert Linquanti. (2015). Issues and options associated with initially classifying English learners (ELs). Council of Chief State School Officers. https://www.ccsso.org
title: The initial classification screener should align to state ELP standards and strongly predict performance on the annual ELP summative assessment
description: The report proposes a two-step validation process: first, an alignment study (or a test-blueprint comparison) establishing proportionately comparable match, depth, and breadth of coverage between the screener and state ELP standards; second, a formal study of the predictive relationship between classifications from the initial assessment and the annual summative assessment, examined through correlation and/or regression analyses. Moderate to low associations would suggest the assessments measure different aspects of English language proficiency.
requirements: The predictive study should administer both assessments to already confirmed ELs within a few days, so that instruction during the interval does not measurably change proficiency
constraints: For brief screener instruments the alignment will not be as extensive as with the annual summative assessment, though coverage should be proportionately comparable
target_learners: Potential English learners undergoing initial classification
target_learning_goals: Consistent, defensible English learner classification decisions
examples: The report suggests giving the initial classification assessment and, a few days later, the annual summative ELP assessment to the same confirmed ELs and checking score and proficiency-category relationships
key_sources: H. Gary Cook & Robert Linquanti. (2015). Issues and options associated with initially classifying English learners (ELs). Council of Chief State School Officers. https://www.ccsso.org

article_title: Using Assessment Data to Guide Math Course Placement of California Middle School Students
citation: Chun-Wei Huang, Jason Snipes, Neal Finkelstein, WestEd. (2016). Using assessment data to guide math course placement of California middle school students. SREE Spring 2016 Conference. https://www.sree.org
title: Use continuous scale scores and immediately available diagnostic assessments rather than proficiency status alone to guide grade 8 algebra I placement
description: The article recommends that districts making grade 8 algebra I placement decisions move beyond the binary proficiency indicator on the grade 6 math CST and rely on scale scores identifying students with at least a 50 percent chance of success, supplemented by immediately available diagnostics. It states that "immediately available, easily administered assessments such as MDTP scores are potentially effective tools for making placement decisions," since CST results are not available until August or later.
requirements: Access to continuous scale scores from prior math assessments, and a diagnostic test such as the MDTP that can be administered online with results available immediately after completion
constraints: Grade 7 CST data are not typically available in time for initial placement decisions
Simply scoring at the proficient level (a scale score of 350) is not enough to give a student a greater than 50 percent chance of achieving proficiency
target_learners: Grade 8 middle school students being placed into algebra I
target_learning_goals: Accurate identification of students likely to achieve proficiency in grade 8 algebra I
examples: SVRA districts participating in the study had agreed under a 2010 memorandum of understanding to use multiple criteria including course performance, teacher recommendations, diagnostic tests, and CST performance for placement

article_title: The Racial School-Climate Gap
citation: Voight, A. (2013). The Racial School-Climate Gap. A report from the Region IX Equity Assistance Center at WestEd. San Francisco: WestEd. http://cal-schls.wested.org
title: School climate as a four-theme construct associated with achievement and a candidate lever for reducing racial achievement gaps
description: The article treats school climate as "a broad term used to describe the school environment" with "no consensus definition" but several recurring themes: "(a) order, safety, and discipline; (b) teaching and learning supports; (c) social relationships; and (d) school connectedness." It uses this construct to organize six WestEd studies showing climate perceptions vary by race, and proposes a three-step logic linking climate to achievement: climate is associated with achievement, climate experiences vary by race, and reducing racial climate disparities would reduce achievement disparities.
requirements: Regular assessment and monitoring of school climate as perceived by different racial/ethnic student groups, e.g., using the Cal-SCHLS system
constraints: The studies provide empirical support for the first two points of the logic; proving that reducing climate disparities reduces achievement disparities "necessitates further research"
target_learners: K-12 students in California public schools, grades 7, 9, and 11 in the studies cited
target_learning_goals: Reducing racial achievement gaps through improved school climate and equity in students' school experiences
examples: WestEd researchers analyzed Cal-SCHLS student and staff data collected biennially in nearly two thirds of California public schools from 2004 to 2010

article_title: Five Misconceptions about School Shootings
citation: Langman, P., Petrosino, A., & Persson, H. (2018). Five misconceptions about school shootings. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.wested.org/resources/five-misconceptions-about-school-shootings/
title: Langman's three-category typology of school shooters: psychopathic, psychotic, and traumatized
description: The brief presents a typology in which, although no single psychological profile fits all school shooters, perpetrators "tend to fall into one of three categories: psychopathic, psychotic, or traumatized." Psychopathic shooters are narcissistic and lack empathy; psychotic shooters show symptoms such as hallucinations and delusions; traumatized shooters come from severely dysfunctional families with abuse, substance abuse, or criminal behavior. The brief uses the typology to organize case examples while cautioning it does not by itself explain shootings.
requirements: Used as a classification framework for perpetrators, not as a standalone causal explanation of attacks
constraints: The brief states the typology "does not — by itself — explain school shootings"; most people in these categories or with mental illness do not commit mass murders
target_learners: Educators
School safety personnel
Reporters and the public
target_learning_goals: Understanding the psychological diversity of school shooters to counter the single mental-illness stereotype
examples: The brief classifies one Columbine killer as psychopathic, the Thurston High School killer as psychotic with auditory hallucinations and paranoid delusions, and a Bethel, Alaska shooter as traumatized based on family abuse history

article_title: What Do We Know about the Effects of School-Based Law Enforcement on School Safety?
citation: Stern, A., & Petrosino, A. (2018). What do we know about the effects of school-based law enforcement on school safety? San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.wested.org/resources/effects-of-school-based-law-enforcement-on-school-safety
title: Two common types of school-based law enforcement strategies: school resource officers and school district police
description: The brief organizes school-based law enforcement into two common U.S. strategies. The most common is the school resource officer (SRO), where a school or district partners with the local police department so municipal police devote time to a presence on school property. The alternative is school district police, where districts establish their own sworn police departments, as large urban districts like Miami-Dade County Public Schools do. Officers' roles vary by school and district policy, including coordinating security, monitoring and responding to criminal activity, building relationships, and referring students to external services.
requirements: Personnel must be sworn officers who carry firearms, have arrest powers, and carry a police department badge
constraints: The brief excludes security guards, who are not an extension of law enforcement, and officers who only teach prevention curricula such as D.A.R.E. or G.R.E.A.T.
target_learners: K-12 students, including at the elementary school level
examples: The brief cites Miami-Dade County Public Schools as an example of a large urban district with its own sworn police responsible for school grounds

article_title: Reimagining School Safety: A Guide for Schools and Communities
citation: Trout, L., Pate, C., Wu, K., & McKenna, J. (2022). Reimagining school safety: A guide for schools and communities. WestEd. https://wested.org
title: School safety as a complex, adaptive system on the simple–complicated–complex continuum
description: Adapting Glouberman and Zimmerman, the guide places problems on a continuum from simple to complex and locates school safety at the complex end: "Complex problems or systems are based on relationships and their properties of self-organization, interconnections, and evolution (“adaptive”) (e.g., school safety)." Because safety is inherently adaptive and nonlinear, it cannot be achieved by linear steps, top-down policies, or experts alone. The guide recommends systems thinking and an engineering or systems design approach that iterates as conditions evolve, rather than the linear determine-intervene-evaluate method traditionally used in education.
requirements: Educators must engage in formal and informal processes of emergence with their community, observing how properties and behaviors emerge as parts interact.
constraints: The guide states complicated challenges have a time and place, such as determining truancy policies or lockdown procedures.
target_learners: educators
school leaders
district administrators
target_learning_goals: understanding school safety as a complex adaptive system
examples: The guide offers a sticky-note exercise in which participants brainstorm ten or more leverage points for a school safety issue and map the individuals and groups most affected.
key_sources: Trout, L., Pate, C., Wu, K., & McKenna, J. (2022). Reimagining school safety: A guide for schools and communities. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED628885

citation: Voight, A., Austin, G., and Hanson, T. (2013). A climate for academic success: How school climate distinguishes schools that are beating the achievement odds (Full Report). San Francisco: WestEd. https://www.WestEd.org/
title: School Climate Index framework of five recurring climate dimensions
description: The report organizes school climate, a term with "no consensus definition," around five recurring themes identified in prior reviews: order, safety, and discipline; academic supports; personal and social relationships; school facilities; and school connectedness. Operationally it uses the California Healthy Kids Survey to build a School Climate Index combining two domains — supports and engagement, and low violence, victimization, and substance use — plus a truancy indicator, rescaled to a mean of 300 and SD of 50.

constraints: The report notes school climate "has no consensus definition" and the term has become something of a catchall for school-improvement targets

examples: The study computed SCI scores for roughly two thirds of California public middle and high schools that administered the CHKS in 2008-09 or 2009-10

CBEDS truancy data

article_title: If You Listen, We Will Stay: Why Teachers of Color Leave and How to Disrupt Teacher Turnover
citation: Davis Dixon, Ashley Griffin, and Mark Teoh. (2019). If You Listen, We Will Stay: Why Teachers of Color Leave and How to Disrupt Teacher Turnover. The Education Trust & Teach Plus. https://edtrust.org
title: Build a schoolwide family with formal and informal mentorship, pairing novice teachers of color thoughtfully with veterans
description: Case-study schools foster strong relationships among teachers, students, and administrators so teachers of color feel they belong; principals schedule team-building, off-site PD, and informal rapport-building time. Formal mentorship assigns new staff a veteran teacher, and pairings must be strategic: when teachers "experience bias, stereotyping, and racism, it requires a partner teacher who can help with those problems because they have experienced them first hand."
requirements: Mentor pairings must be chosen thoughtfully, including shared content areas and shared lived experience, with required check-ins.
constraints: One principal cautioned a familial culture can become "a dysfunctional family that often has led to complacency and comfortability," so professionalism boundaries must be maintained.
target_learners: Novice and veteran K-12 teachers of color
examples: New hires received two and a half days of onboarding on school culture and were assigned veteran teachers as resources, with a required number of check-ins.

article_title: Cultivating Math Mindsets: Teaching Practices That Enable Equitable Classroom Learning
citation: Price, H., & Fitz, J. (2026). Cultivating math mindsets: Teaching practices that enable equitable classroom learning. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/810.406
title: Support math teachers with collaboration time, sustained professional learning, and coaching focused on contextual needs
description: The report identifies organizational practices that enable teachers to improve math classroom conditions: allocating school-day time for collaborative learning such as professional learning communities, shared planning, and peer observation, which can build teachers' efficacy and confidence; enabling access to well-designed professional learning, "particularly when these opportunities align with school goals and involve sustained engagement over an extended period of time"; and providing coaching or expert support focused on teachers' contextual needs. At the school level, teachers valued in-classroom support staff and structured collaboration norms set by leaders.
requirements: Staffing capacity and resources allocated to support organizational priorities
constraints: Findings reflect the supports identified by teachers in three California districts serving majority students of color and students from low-income families
target_learners: middle school math students
examples: Teachers from schools with strong PLC collaboration and on-site math coaches described these as key supports; leaders' norms around collaboration time guided improvement-focused conversations between teachers.

article_title: AgentSchool: An LLM-Powered Multi-Agent Simulation for Education
citation: Yulei Ye, Wenhao Li, Zhong Wen, Yunshu Huang, Yichen Hu, Zifan Wei, Yige Wang, Xinyu Xie, Haoxuan Yang, Yanjun Huang, Ruijia Li, Hong Qian, Yu Song, Bo Jiang, Bingdong Li, Lijun Li, Bo Zhang, Pinlong Cai, Xingcheng Xu, Shuangye Chen, Xia Hu, Liang He, Aimin Zhou, Jingjing Qu, Jing Shao, Xiangfeng Wang. (2026). AgentSchool: An LLM-Powered Multi-Agent Simulation for Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30144
title: Configurable scenery generator instantiating formal and informal learning fields
description: The scenery generator instantiates scenarios as parameterized learning fields with spatial structure, participant roles, resources, communication channels, schedules, norms, and evaluation expectations. The paper states that "scenery is not a decorative background. It is a parameterized object that constrains observation, action, and interpretation." Predefined templates (traditional, open small-group, online) carry default interaction-graph priors; informal scenery models recess conversation and peer gossip with weaker institutional scripts; an evolutionary pipeline is planned for counterfactual scenario generation.

informal scenes tracking topic formation, joining, withdrawal, emotional tone, and relationship change

article_title: AI-peer integrated feedback in second language writing classes: exploring students' engagement and writing performance
citation: Liu W (2026) AI-peer integrated feedback in second language writing classes: exploring students' engagement and writing performance. Front. Psychol. 17:1871951. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1871951
title: Sociocultural Theory framing of AI-peer integrated feedback as layered scaffolding within the Zone of Proximal Development
description: The study frames AI-peer integrated feedback through Vygotsky's Sociocultural Theory, whose core constructs are the Zone of Proximal Development, mediation, and scaffolding. ZPD is "the gap between students' independent writing ability and the higher level of writing performance they can attain with tailored external support". The intervention operationalizes scaffolding as sequentially layered support: AI-mediated individualized feedback on key writing dimensions first, then peer-driven social mediation in which learners elaborate on and negotiate revision suggestions. Mediation positions feedback, whether from peers or AI, as a mechanism steering learners toward enhanced performance.
requirements: Feedback must be matched to learners' developmental potential within their ZPD
AI feedback precedes peer feedback so peer mediation can elaborate on AI suggestions
constraints: The framework was examined specifically in EFL argumentative writing among Chinese English majors at B2 proficiency
target_learners: tertiary EFL students
English majors in advanced writing courses
examples: The experimental group received AI feedback on four rubric dimensions via standardized prompts, then engaged in 30-minute rubric-based peer evaluation followed by 15-minute small-group discussion across five biweekly writing tasks

Analysis used VOSviewer for keyword co-occurrence and research theme evolution analysis.

article_title: When Saying No Makes Better Videos: Designing Dual Gatekeeping for Pedagogically Grounded AI Content Creation
citation: Yearim Kim, Injun Baek, and Nojun Kwak. 2026. When Saying No Makes Better Videos: Designing Dual Gatekeeping for Pedagogically Grounded AI Content Creation. In Proceedings of Understanding and Engaging Critical Resistance to AI in Education (CHI '26 Workshop). ACM, New York, NY, USA. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19812
title: Place pedagogical friction at the script stage, where textual revision is efficient and rendered errors are nearly impossible to correct
description: The article argues productive friction should be strategically embedded upstream: "Textual revisions are computationally and laboriously efficient, whereas pedagogical errors baked into a rendered visual narrative are nearly impossible to correct post-synthesis." Placing the human checkpoint at the intermediate script stage makes pedagogical critique economically viable while keeping the system advisory and preserving the educator's authority to say no based on curricular context. The authors also state productive friction is most effective when theoretically grounded and hybridized across human and computational agents.
requirements: A structured review cycle with AI reviewer feedback organized by principle, repeatable until the educator is satisfied with the script
constraints: The article notes the long-term viability of iterative review in daily classroom preparation remains unknown and a threshold where productive friction transitions into friction fatigue must be identified
target_learners: educators creating instructional video content
target_learning_goals: pedagogical quality of AI-generated instructional video scripts
examples: In PedaCo's Layer 1, an AI reviewer prompted with CTML principles produces feedback organized by principle, identifying potential violations rather than definitive judgments, and the educator decides what to accept, revise, or regenerate
key_sources: Yearim Kim, Injun Baek, and Nojun Kwak. 2026. When Saying No Makes Better Videos: Designing Dual Gatekeeping for Pedagogically Grounded AI Content Creation. article_title: AI as Teammate: Rethinking Task Distribution in Medical Training
citation: Tsim, F., Gutoreva, A., Weiss, A., & Dubosh, N. (2026). AI as Teammate: Rethinking Task Distribution in Medical Training. Correspondence: fenditsim@gmail.com
title: SCAN: a four-subzone task-allocation framework extending Vygotsky's ZPD with metacognition for human-AI task distribution
description: SCAN is a human-centric decision-making framework organizing clinical tasks along four subzones—Substitute, Complement, Aid, and Non-Negotiable—defined by two dimensions: the degree to which AI can appropriately assume cognitive responsibility and the developmental consequences for the learner. The article states that "SCAN is a human-centric, decision-making framework for systematic task allocation between a learner, human experts, and AI." It extends Vygotsky's ZPD by adding a 'known to AI' circle to the zones of actual and potential development, and operates through task identification, processing, and evaluation.
requirements: Adequate learner metacognition: without it, task classification collapses because learners cannot reliably assign tasks to correct subzones
constraints: Developed for cognitively demanding professional domains; the article presents it as a conjectural, testable framework rather than an empirically validated one
target_learners: Medical students and residents in clinical training
target_learning_goals: Metacognitive task classification and AI engagement
examples: Figure 1 locates S between 'unknown to learner' and 'known to AI', C between 'known to learner' and 'known to AI', A at the overlap of all three circles, and N as the original ZPD

citation: Serpil, H., & Mor, M. K. (2026). Bounded reliance: A source credibility perspective on EFL students' engagement with AI-generated writing feedback. Journal of Language Pedagogy and Linguistics, 1(1), 1-27. https://doi.org/10.0.20.161/zenodo.22828386
title: Source Credibility Theory as a lens for evaluating algorithmic feedback providers
description: Source Credibility Theory holds that message effectiveness depends on perceived source credibility across three dimensions: expertise (knowledge and competence), trustworthiness (honesty, dependability, lack of bias), and goodwill (caring and responsiveness to the recipient). The article applies this lens to AI-generated writing feedback, arguing that "learners apply to an algorithmic provider the same multidimensional source judgments the theory was developed to explain for human communicators." It uses the three dimensions to organize its thematic analysis of student interviews.
requirements: Learners must have sustained direct experience with the feedback source before evaluating its credibility
constraints: The study examined perceptions in one undergraduate translation-studies writing course, not causal effects of credibility on learning outcomes
target_learners: undergraduate EFL students in higher education
target_learning_goals: evaluating and selectively using AI-generated feedback in academic writing revision
examples: The study coded interview themes abductively against the three SCT dimensions (expertise, trustworthiness, goodwill) in a 15-week GROK-supported writing course
key_sources: Serpil, H., & Mor, M. K. (2026). Bounded reliance: A source credibility perspective on EFL students' engagement with AI-generated writing feedback. Journal of Language Pedagogy and Linguistics, 1(1), 1-27. https://doi.org/10.0.20.161/zenodo.22828386

article_title: Bots and Blocks: Presenting a Project-Based Approach for Robotics Education
citation: Tobias Geger, Dominique Briechle and Andreas Rausch. (2026). Bots and Blocks: Presenting a project-based approach for robotics education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.14529
title: Schools: interactive lecture-demonstration-exercise sessions embedded in the project timeline
description: Schools are the article's format for teaching base qualifications within the project. "Each school covers a different topic and always begins with a short lecture of around sixty minutes." After a live demonstration by a supervisor, students work on a matching exercise with instructor support, then present, reflect on and discuss results in the plenum, with critical parts addressed explicitly. Some schools are followed by tasks that feed the next session or an intermediate exam. In the robotics project, schools covered ROS/ROS2 and object detection with YOLO.
requirements: A supervisor who gives a live demonstration of a minimal working example
Exercises matched to the demonstrated concepts and plenum discussion of student results
constraints: School time is front-loaded: the first two weeks are reserved for schools, and school time decreases from weeks three to six as project work takes over
target_learners: undergraduate project-team students in a robotics-focused computer science course
target_learning_goals: base qualifications such as ROS programming, node and interface creation, and object detection with YOLO
examples: The ROS school used a TurtleBot minimal working example; students reproduced and adapted it, then developed their own ROS nodes, packages, messages, services and launch files
key_sources: Tobias Geger, Dominique Briechle and Andreas Rausch. (2026). Bots and Blocks: Presenting a project-based approach for robotics education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.14529

article_title: Confidence Estimation in Automatic Short Answer Grading with LLMs
citation: Longwei Cong, Sonja Hahn, Sebastian Gombert, Leon Camus, Hendrik Drachsler, and Ulf Kroehne. (2026). Confidence Estimation in Automatic Short Answer Grading with LLMs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.00200
title: SciEntsBank Test_UD evaluation split for confidence estimation in ASAG
description: SciEntsBank is described as "a widely used benchmark dataset for ASAG containing nearly 11,000 student responses to 197 science questions across 15 domains". The study uses the Test_UD split with 4,562 responses (1,917 correct, 2,645 incorrect), treating correct responses as positive and grouping all remaining labels as incorrect. The split was further divided into a 10% calibration subset and a 90% held-out test subset via stratified sampling. Its diverse error types make it suitable for studying confidence estimation.
requirements: Human-annotated labels reflecting semantic correctness of student answers
constraints: Binary correct/incorrect grouping collapses the dataset's finer label distinctions
target_learners: students answering science short-answer questions
target_learning_goals: automated assessment of semantic correctness of constructed science responses
examples: Used to evaluate ROC/ARC selective prediction and reliability diagrams for five confidence estimation methods
key_sources: Longwei Cong, Sonja Hahn, Sebastian Gombert, Leon Camus, Hendrik Drachsler, and Ulf Kroehne. (2026). Confidence Estimation in Automatic Short Answer Grading with LLMs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.00200

article_title: Concept Catalyst: Exploring Scrutable Interfaces to Structure K-12 Teacher Interactions with Generative AI
citation: Gennie Mansi, Sunni Newton, Roxanne Moore, Meltem Alemdar, Mark Riedl. (2026). Concept Catalyst: Exploring Scrutable Interfaces to Structure K-12 Teacher Interactions with Generative AI. https://ceismc.gatech.edu
title: Scrutable interfaces for generative AI: manipulable knowledge representations that let users shape outputs without understanding the model
description: Scrutable interfaces use a knowledge representation, such as a concept map, to structure users' interactions with an underlying AI model. Critically, scrutable systems "don’t require users to understand how the underlying AI model works to change the AI system output"; instead the representation supports metacognitive self-monitoring, reflection, and planning. This article broadens the concept in two ways: extending scrutable systems from students to teachers as users, and applying them to black-box generative AI models, where the interface lets users "understand, reflect on, and directly edit the inputs to the GPT model to achieve their desired outcomes".
requirements: A knowledge representation (e.g., a concept map) that users can create, edit, and iterate on, which feeds the AI's inputs
An underlying AI model whose outputs change in response to the representation, so users need not understand the model's internals
constraints: Concept Catalyst does not allow teachers to scrutinize the inner workings of the GPT model; scrutability is limited to editing inputs
Prior scrutable systems targeted students, not teachers, so this extension is exploratory
target_learners: K-12 engineering teachers
target_learning_goals: Reflective practice in curriculum and scaffold design
Effective structuring of generative AI interactions
examples: Concept Catalyst links a teacher-built concept map to a pre-written ChatGPT prompt template; as teachers reflect and edit the map, they alter the selected concepts and thereby the generated scaffolds
key_sources: Gennie Mansi, Sunni Newton, Roxanne Moore, Meltem Alemdar, Mark Riedl. (2026). Concept Catalyst: Exploring Scrutable Interfaces to Structure K-12 Teacher Interactions with Generative AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30590

article_title: Concept Catalyst: Exploring Scrutable Interfaces to Structure K-12 Teacher Interactions with Generative AI
citation: Gennie Mansi, Sunni Newton, Roxanne Moore, Meltem Alemdar, Mark Riedl. (2026). Concept Catalyst: Exploring Scrutable Interfaces to Structure K-12 Teacher Interactions with Generative AI. https://ceismc.gatech.edu
title: Designers should weigh a scrutable interface against an explainable one based on users' social needs and the AI's technical capabilities
description: Rather than defaulting to AI explanations—descriptions of an underlying model—to help users change AI systems, the article argues "designers need to consider when a scrutable interface may better bridge a sociotechnical gap than an explainable one". A scrutable knowledge representation can engage higher-order metacognitive skills alongside AI use, supporting user outcomes beyond better AI outputs, such as teachers reflecting on practice and deepening engagement with the Engineering Design Process.
requirements: A manipulable knowledge representation aligned with users' existing practices that drives the AI's inputs
constraints: The article's evidence is an exploratory case study with 10 teachers using a mock-up on a single design challenge; the authors note a broader sample and teachers' own projects are needed
target_learners: K-12 teachers using generative AI tools
target_learning_goals: Reflective and metacognitive engagement during AI-supported content creation
examples: Concept Catalyst engaged teachers in the abstract thought process of the EDP through its concept map, and teachers shifted from initial AI hesitancy to wanting student-facing versions
key_sources: Gennie Mansi, Sunni Newton, Roxanne Moore, Meltem Alemdar, Mark Riedl. (2026). Concept Catalyst: Exploring Scrutable Interfaces to Structure K-12 Teacher Interactions with Generative AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30590

article_title: Associations Between Generative AI–Based Pronunciation Feedback and Willingness to Communicate in English: The Mediating Role of English Pronunciation Self-Efficacy
citation: Lu Y, Yang Y, Cui T, Yang Z, Cai Y and Jing B (2026) Associations between generative AI–based pronunciation feedback and willingness to communicate in English: the mediating role of English pronunciation self-efficacy. Front. Psychol. 17:1918980. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1918980
title: Social Cognitive Theory account of GenAI feedback as environmental influence shaping pronunciation self-efficacy and communicative readiness
description: The study applies Bandura's Social Cognitive Theory, in which "human functioning results from reciprocal interactions among environmental influences, personal factors, and behavior". GenAI-based pronunciation feedback is conceptualized as a technology-mediated environmental influence, English pronunciation self-efficacy as a domain-specific personal belief, and WTC as behavioral readiness. The article argues GenAI feedback may activate self-efficacy sources by allowing repeated practice, observation of improvement, comparison with model pronunciations, and immediate individualized corrective guidance in a private, low-pressure environment.
requirements: Learners must perceive the GenAI feedback as useful, accurate, and supportive for the self-efficacy pathway to operate as described
constraints: The cross-sectional design precludes conclusions about directionality, feedback mechanisms, or developmental trajectories, as the authors state
target_learners: Chinese university EFL learners
examples: The study operationalized the three SCT components as survey constructs and tested the mediation model with CB-SEM on 1,701 responses
