Front. Psychol. 17:1918980. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1918980

article_title: Thoughtless Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence and College Students' Self-Directed Learning: A Multi-Group SEM Analysis of Gender Differences
citation: Hui Zhao & Huijuan Gu. (2026). Thoughtless use of generative artificial intelligence and college students’ self-directed learning: a multi-group SEM analysis of gender differences. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-54337-y
title: Extended Social Cognitive Theory framework positioning thoughtless GenAI use within triadic reciprocal determinism
description: The study adopts Social Cognitive Theory—personal factors, behavior, and environment in triadic reciprocal determinism—as its core analytical framework and extends it by inserting TUGA as a behavioral element interacting with SE and MOV and the GenAI environment. The article states that "the present study incorporates the TUGA into the SCT framework to examine the role of this behavior within the triadic interaction system." It argues classical SCT's static view of environment lags behind dynamic, autonomous GenAI features and that SCT needs extension for gender-differentiated pathways.
requirements: Applicable to technology-mediated learning environments where the technology exhibits dynamic, autonomous, and interactive characteristics
constraints: The authors state SCT's traditional framework conceptualizes environment statically and lacks systematic theoretical support for explaining gender-differentiated pathways in GenAI contexts
target_learners: undergraduate students
examples: The study operationalized the framework in a PLS-SEM with TUGA, SE, MOV, and SDL measured by adapted scales and tested with multi-group analysis by gender
key_sources: Hui Zhao & Huijuan Gu. (2026). Thoughtless use of generative artificial intelligence and college students’ self-directed learning: a multi-group SEM analysis of gender differences. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-54337-y

article_title: A Guided Inquiry Approach to Students Co-Designing Generative AI Course Policies
citation: Hingle, A., & Johri, A. (2025). A Guided Inquiry Approach to Students Co-Designing Generative AI Course Policies. https://www.google.com/search?q=A+Guided+Inquiry+Approach+to+Students+Co-Designing+Generative+AI+Course+Policies
title: Scaffold co-design activities so student input moves from surface-level consultation toward substantive participation in governance
description: The article recommends that policy co-design activities be designed so students genuinely articulate values and negotiate trade-offs rather than merely being consulted. From the student voice literature, the authors conclude that "co-design activities may benefit from additional scaffolding that supports students in moving from surface-level input toward what Hart (1992) describes as 'substantive' participation." Students in the study expressed desire to shape GenAI policy while signaling uncertainty about how to contribute meaningfully, and the authors caution against arrangements where student input is solicited but does not substantively shape outcomes.
requirements: Communication between instructor, administrative, and student roles in policy formation
Scaffolding that supports students in articulating values and negotiating trade-offs
constraints: The authors caution against arrangements in which student input is solicited but does not substantively shape outcomes
target_learners: undergraduate students as primary stakeholders in course policy
target_learning_goals: genuine participation in educational governance decisions
examples: Participants in the study wanted a say in developing and revising course policies, viewing this as essential for building trust between the institution, instructors, and students

article_title: Programming Intelligent Tutoring Systems
citation: Alina Deriyeva, Jesper Dannath, and Benjamin Paaßen. (2025). SCRIPT: Implementing an Intelligent Tutoring System for Programming in a German University Context. Artificial Intelligence in Education (Springer). https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-99261-2_16
title: SCRIPT: an adaptable Python programming ITS serving as both teaching and research platform
description: SCRIPT (Step-based Coding for Research and Intelligent Programming Tutoring) is a web-based ITS supporting advanced undergraduates learning Python for data science and machine learning. The article states it "functions both as a teaching and as a research tool by enabling to record fine-grained, keystroke-level data" and is "easily adaptable to novel learner models and pedagogical models as well as randomized experiments." It was offered as voluntary exam preparation for an Introduction to Data Mining course and has supported prior learner-model and feedback research. Source code is released on a GitLab repository, though the system is still in alpha stage.
requirements: Hosted in Docker containers on the university's own server infrastructure to meet regulatory requirements
Teachers must be able to upload new course material to adapt the system to different Python courses
constraints: The system is still in the alpha stage; the authors "can not yet recommend the system for deployment but only for research use"
At present the ITS is only used in a narrow, short-term setting (Python introduction and exam preparation)
target_learners: Advanced undergraduate (third year) and early postgraduate (first year) computer science students
target_learning_goals: Python programming for data science and machine learning
examples: Offered as voluntary exam preparation for the Introduction to Data Mining course with tasks across eight subdomains such as probability theory, clustering, and deep models
key_sources: Alina Deriyeva, Jesper Dannath, and Benjamin Paaßen. (2025). SCRIPT: Implementing an Intelligent Tutoring System for Programming in a German University Context. Artificial Intelligence in Education (Springer). https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-99261-2_16

article_title: Programming Intelligent Tutoring Systems
citation: Alina Deriyeva, Jesper Dannath, and Benjamin Paaßen. (2025). SCRIPT: Implementing an Intelligent Tutoring System for Programming in a German University Context. Artificial Intelligence in Education (Springer). https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-99261-2_16
title: Four-model ITS architecture with inner and outer loop pedagogical model
description: SCRIPT adopts the standard four-models ITS approach: "a Pedagogical Model, a Learner Model, a Domain Model, and a User Interface." The pedagogical model follows VanLehn's inner/outer loop differentiation: "The outer loop is responsible for task selection and the inner loop is responsible for generating feedback to steps inside programming tasks." The domain model holds tasks, a competency model (Q-matrix), and difficulty information; the learner model derives competency states from UI actions via a knowledge tracing algorithm. Models are designed to be easily replaceable and can be randomly assigned for A/B-testing.
requirements: A knowledge tracing algorithm to derive learner competency from UI actions
Task-to-skill relations and task difficulty information from the domain model for outer-loop task selection
constraints: Only part of the features described in the outer and inner loop schemas are implemented; the system is in alpha stage
target_learners: Advanced undergraduate and early postgraduate computer science students
target_learning_goals: Python programming and data science skills
examples: Figure 3 shows the outer loop information flow from curriculum information through task selection; Figure 4 shows the inner loop hint generation flow

article_title: Generative AI in Design Thinking Pedagogy: Enhancing Creativity, Critical Thinking, and Ethical Reasoning in Higher Education
citation: Rana, V., Verhoeven, B., & Sharma, M. (2025). Generative AI in Design Thinking Pedagogy: Enhancing Creativity, Critical Thinking, and Ethical Reasoning in Higher Education. Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice, 22(4). https://doi.org/10.53761/tjse2f36
title: Integrate generative AI into design thinking pedagogy with explicit scaffolding so it augments rather than replaces student judgment
description: This principle holds that generative AI tools should be woven into design thinking coursework with pedagogical scaffolding that channels student use toward critical evaluation. The study's central finding is that "GenAI, when pedagogically scaffolded, augments rather than replaces human judgment," and that students moved from scepticism to strategic adoption. Scaffolding should therefore target bias detection, source validation, and authorship awareness rather than mere tool access.
requirements: Structured pedagogical scaffolding around GenAI use, including activities that develop bias detection and source validation strategies.
constraints: Evidence comes from a single 12-week undergraduate course; the article does not report outcomes for unscaffolded GenAI use.
target_learners: undergraduate students in higher education
examples: Students used ChatGPT and DALL·E across Design Thinking's five stages in a 12-week course, with reflections showing evolution from scepticism to strategic adoption.
key_sources: Rana, V., Verhoeven, B., & Sharma, M. (2025). Generative AI in Design Thinking Pedagogy: Enhancing Creativity, Critical Thinking, and Ethical Reasoning in Higher Education. Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice, 22(4). https://doi.org/10.53761/tjse2f36

article_title: School network reorganization under educational and spatial constraints using classical and quantum optimization
citation: Alessia Ciacco, Luigi Di Puglia Pugliese, Francesca Guerriero. (2026). School network reorganization under educational and spatial constraints using classical and quantum optimization. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05427
title: Synthetic benchmark instance generator for school aggregation problems
description: Because no public benchmark existed, the article developed a structured random instance generator producing synthetic yet realistic regional school networks. It reproduces hierarchical settlement geography (provincial capitals, large, medium, and small municipalities), heterogeneous school types and educational tracks, and differentiated territorial criticality levels. Four instance sizes were considered with n in {250,500,750,1000}, spanning medium-scale to large-scale regional planning scenarios, with schools clustered around municipality centers via bivariate Gaussian sampling.
requirements: Real-world demographic data to calibrate instance sizes and territorial structures
constraints: Instances are synthetic and abstract; the article notes limitations of the tested benchmark instances for quantum evaluation
target_learners: school-age students in synthetic regional networks
target_learning_goals: evaluating scalability of school dimensioning optimization models
examples: The generator assigns schools in small municipalities exclusively to the CI category, reflecting concentration of essential educational services in peripheral areas
key_sources: Alessia Ciacco, Luigi Di Puglia Pugliese, Francesca Guerriero. (2026). School network reorganization under educational and spatial constraints using classical and quantum optimization. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05427

article_title: From Student Risk Prediction to SC2R: Semantics-Constrained Counterfactual Recourse for Educational Decision Support
citation: Ngoc Luyen Le, Marie-Hélène Abel, Bertrand Laforge. (2026). From Student Risk Prediction to SC2R: Semantics-Constrained Counterfactual Recourse for Educational Decision Support. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17618
title: SC2R: a semantics-constrained counterfactual recourse framework for educational decision support
description: SC2R is a three-component pipeline for educational decision support: a predictive component estimating next-assessment success, an integer-programming recourse component generating candidate intervention plans over a discrete action space, and a semantic validation layer using SHACL. Plans are represented as RDF graphs and are "retained only if it satisfies the semantic feasibility condition" S(Gπ) = 1. The framework treats recourse as a constrained decision-support problem rather than geometric perturbation in feature space, turning counterfactual recourse into a machine-checkable process.
requirements: A calibrated predictive model operating on predicted probabilities rather than hard class labels
Candidate plans encoded as RDF graphs using the intervention vocabulary so SHACL validation can check them
constraints: The evaluation is offline, model-based, and observational; the authors state it does not establish that following a generated plan would improve student outcomes
target_learners: students in digital learning environments at risk of failing an upcoming assessment
target_learning_goals: next-assessment pass/fail outcomes and actionable intervention planning
examples: On OULAD, snapshots at d-14 and d-7 feed a calibrated logistic regression, an IP solver generates plans, and SHACL validation filters them before evaluation
key_sources: Ngoc Luyen Le, Marie-Hélène Abel, Bertrand Laforge. (2026). From Student Risk Prediction to SC2R: Semantics-Constrained Counterfactual Recourse for Educational Decision Support. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17618

article_title: Is Solving Better Than Evaluating GenAI Solutions?
citation: Ethan Dickey, Marios Mertzanidis, Alexandros Psomas. (2026). Is Solving Better Than Evaluating GenAI Solutions? https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27586v1
title: Incorporate structured GenAI-evaluation activities into algorithms coursework without expecting automatic learning gains; scaffold evaluation beyond simple error diagnosis
description: The article's design recommendation is that GenAI-evaluation tasks can be incorporated into algorithms coursework safely, since "GenAI-evaluation activities can be incorporated into algorithms coursework without broad performance losses". However, meaningful gains require deliberate scaffolding: the authors recommend future assignments "push students beyond simple diagnosis" by asking students to identify the first invalid step, construct counterexamples, propose corrected algorithms or invariants, and explain why the corrected solution works. Pedagogical value depends more on scaffolding than on exposure to AI output itself.
requirements: Deliberate scaffolding that pushes students beyond simple error diagnosis, such as identifying the first invalid step, constructing counterexamples, and proposing corrected solutions
constraints: In this implementation, evaluation tasks produced no measurable summative or transfer gains over direct solving
target_learners: undergraduate students in junior-level algorithms courses
target_learning_goals: algorithm design, proof of correctness, runtime analysis, and transfer of abstract algorithmic reasoning
examples: The study asked evaluating students to grade a ChatGPT-4o solution, distinguishing minor bugs (e.g., calculation errors) from major bugs (wrong algorithm, invalid recurrence, missing invariant, flawed proof step), and found most students did not change study habits
key_sources: Ethan Dickey, Marios Mertzanidis, Alexandros Psomas. (2026). Is Solving Better Than Evaluating GenAI Solutions? https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27586

article_title: From Substitution to Scaffolding: Breaking the Self-Reinforcing Harm Cycle of AI in Education (and Beyond)
citation: Lucile Favero, Juan Antonio Pérez-Ortiz, Tanja Käser, Nuria Oliver. (2026). From Substitution to Scaffolding: Breaking the Self-Reinforcing Harm Cycle of AI in Education (and Beyond). arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17451
title: Scaffold, do not substitute: AI should support effort rather than replace it
description: The paper's unifying design principle: AI systems that mediate human thinking should preserve and manage cognitive friction — withholding immediate answers, prompting recall, asking questions, surfacing uncertainty — instead of delivering pre-digested solutions that bypass effort. As the authors put it, "The principle that emerges,scaffold, do not substitute, defines a challenge for the AI ecosystem as a whole." It extends beyond education to any system that mediates human cognition, which can either weaken human capabilities through substitution or strengthen them through scaffolding.
requirements: Systems must be able to decide when to withhold an answer, ask a question, surface uncertainty, or present alternative perspectives; builders must treat scaffolding as a first-class capability
constraints: The principle is derived from a small, homogeneous exploratory essay cohort and from argument rather than controlled testing; the authors make no claims of statistical generalizability
target_learners: learners across educational settings
AI system builders
educators and policymakers
examples: Students requested an AI that does not provide solutions so they must find the correct answer themselves, and valued one that asks fundamental questions students must explain and answer
key_sources: Lucile Favero, Juan Antonio Pérez-Ortiz, Tanja Käser, Nuria Oliver. (2026). From Substitution to Scaffolding: Breaking the Self-Reinforcing Harm Cycle of AI in Education (and Beyond). arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17451

article_title: Teacher feedback vs. AI-assisted peer feedback in L2 writing: A quasi-experimental study in a Chinese university
citation: Tang J, Li P, Luo R (2026) Teacher feedback VS AI-assisted peer feedback in L2 writing: A quasi-experimental study in a Chinese University. PLoS One 21(6): e0345976. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0345976
title: Sociocultural account of feedback as scaffolding aligned to the Zone of Proximal Development
description: The article applies Vygotsky's Sociocultural Theory, specifically scaffolding and the Zone of Proximal Development, to L2 writing feedback: feedback is "an external scaffold whose value depends on its precise alignment with the learner's cognitive potential within the ZPD and its gradual withdrawal at appropriate moments". Within this account, teacher feedback acts as expert-provided dynamic scaffolding with authority and context sensitivity, while AI-assisted peer feedback acts as technology-mediated collaborative scaffolding offering real-time, standardized support. The study uses this framework to interpret its quasi-experimental comparison and to motivate a hybrid model.
requirements: Feedback must align with the learner's current ZPD and withdraw gradually to build independent task completion
constraints: The authors note the traditional SCT binary classifies technical tools only as static auxiliary intermediaries, leaving AI's scaffolding attributes inadequately theorized
target_learners: Second-language writing learners in higher education
examples: The 8-week quasi-experiment interpreted teacher feedback's dynamic focus shift and AI-assisted peer feedback's stable learning-curve effect through this framework
key_sources: Tang J, Li P, Luo R (2026) Teacher feedback VS AI-assisted peer feedback in L2 writing: A quasi-experimental study in a Chinese University. PLoS One 21(6): e0345976. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0345976

article_title: Trust calibration and perceived developmental gains in university students' collaboration with generative AI: an exploratory sequential mixed methods study
citation: Fan Bu and Wei Li (2026). Trust calibration and perceived developmental gains in university students' collaboration with generative AI: an exploratory sequential mixed methods study. Front. Psychol. 17:1861072. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1861072
title: Design GenAI-supported learning around contextual guidance, calibrated trust, and active regulation rather than expecting benefits from use frequency alone
description: The article's findings indicate that developmental benefits of student-GenAI collaboration depend on an instructional environment that frames appropriate use and on students' active management of the interaction. The authors conclude that benefits "are better understood as theory consistent structural relationships shaped by contextual guidance, calibrated trust, and active regulation rather than as automatic consequences of frequent AI use". Educational design should therefore provide boundary cues, process-oriented assessment, and norms that support task-sensitive trust judgments and enacted regulation.
requirements: An instructional environment providing teacher guidance, assessment design, peer modeling, and institutional norms surrounding GenAI use
constraints: Findings are cross-sectional self-report; the outcome is perceived transfer gains rather than objectively demonstrated competence, so the principle rests on subjective outcome measures
target_learners: university undergraduates using GenAI in coursework
target_learning_goals: perceived transfer of evaluative judgment and strategies across tasks
examples: Study 1 participants described instructor boundary cues such as an instructor saying AI can help with brainstorming while the final argument and evidence must remain the student's own, and peer norms normalizing verification
key_sources: Fan Bu and Wei Li (2026). Trust calibration and perceived developmental gains in university students' collaboration with generative AI: an exploratory sequential mixed methods study. Front. Psychol. 17:1861072. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1861072

article_title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence Anxiety and Attitudes Toward Artificial Intelligence in University Students' Job Finding Anxiety
citation: Üstün, A. G., & Danacıoğlu, N. (2026). The Role of Artificial Intelligence Anxiety and Attitudes Toward Artificial Intelligence in University Students’ Job Finding Anxiety. Participatory Educational Research, 13(2), 143-164. https://doi.org/10.17275/per.26.23.13.2
title: Social Cognitive Career Theory and Technology Acceptance Model as framework for AI-related career anxiety
description: The study interprets its findings within two frameworks. Social Cognitive Career Theory (Lent et al., 1994) is described as explaining career development through self-efficacy, outcome expectations, and goal setting, so that concerns and negative attitudes toward AI can shape students' perceptions of their future careers. The Technology Acceptance Model (Davis, 1989) explains technology acceptance through "perceived usefulness and ease of use", linking attitudes and intentions toward technology to anxiety. Together they frame AI-related emotional responses as influences on career planning and sectoral expectations.
requirements: The framework assumes career expectations are shaped by environmental factors, self-efficacy, personal experiences, and cognitive-emotional processes, as the article states within SCCT.
target_learners: university students approaching graduation
target_learning_goals: career planning and preparedness for labor market entry under technological transformation
examples: The authors interpret the moderate AI anxiety–job finding anxiety correlation as SCCT-consistent and the negative-attitudes link as TAM-consistent.
key_sources: Üstün, A. G., & Danacıoğlu, N. (2026). The Role of Artificial Intelligence Anxiety and Attitudes Toward Artificial Intelligence in University Students’ Job Finding Anxiety. Participatory Educational Research, 13(2), 143-164. https://doi.org/10.17275/per.26.23.13.2

article_title: A Multidimensional Analysis of AI Literacy Determinants: External Resources, Digital Skills, and Psychological Profile Among University Students
citation: Chow Tak Sang, To Ken, Lam Bess Yin Hung, Lau Kung Wong. (2026). A Multidimensional Analysis of AI Literacy Determinants: External Resources, Digital Skills, and Psychological Profile Among University Students. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16081448
title: Social cognitive theory as an integrative framework mapping external, experiential, and psychological determinants of AI literacy
description: The article grounds its three-block predictor model in Bandura's social cognitive theory, whose "central proposition ... is triadic reciprocal determinism", holding that functioning arises from continuous interaction of environmental, personal, and behavioural determinants. Perceived resources and teacher support map to environmental determinants (instructional scaffolding), prior digital competence to enactive mastery experience, and innovativeness, anxiety, and growth mindset to the dispositional, affective, and cognitive facets of personal determinants. The framework is additionally read through the multi-level digital divide perspective, connecting findings to equity in AI education.
requirements: All three determinant domains must be measured concurrently for incremental contributions to be interpretable, since incremental value is relational rather than intrinsic to a predictor
constraints: The article notes the framework's equity implication — that equalising access alone will not equalise outcomes if learner-level determinants carry weight — rests on cross-sectional correlational evidence
target_learners: undergraduate university students
target_learning_goals: responsible and effective engagement with generative AI
examples: The study's hierarchical regression entered covariates, external resources, digital competence, and psychological variables in four steps mirroring the framework's blocks
key_sources: Chow Tak Sang, To Ken, Lam Bess Yin Hung, Lau Kung Wong. (2026). A Multidimensional Analysis of AI Literacy Determinants: External Resources, Digital Skills, and Psychological Profile Among University Students. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16081448

article_title: Generative AI, Cognitive Offloading, and Learner Agency in Higher Education: A Scoping Review
citation: Wang Guanhua, Wang Wenna, Yang Daozhou, Ren Jifan. (2026). Generative AI, Cognitive Offloading, and Learner Agency in Higher Education: A Scoping Review. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071150
title: Embed GenAI pedagogically as scaffolded, augmentation-oriented support rather than replacement-oriented direct-answer use
description: The review's central pedagogical principle is that GenAI's educational value depends less on the technology than on how it is embedded. Scaffolded designs that provide hints, prompts, feedback, and intermediate guidance keep learners as active interpreters who inspect, revise, and justify reasoning, whereas direct-answer designs invite passive acceptance of output. The review reports that "scaffolded use is more beneficial than direct-answer use in the studies that directly compared or discussed these designs."
requirements: Learning designs must preserve reflection, evaluation, and responsibility; learners need guidance on how to use GenAI
constraints: The review notes benefits are rarely automatic and depend on learners remaining cognitively and metacognitively involved
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: maintaining learner agency during AI-supported tasks
reflective and evaluative engagement with AI support
examples: Studies of guidance-based, Socratic, and scaffolded GenAI designs reviewed in Section 4.5, in which learners remained active interpreters when AI provided hints and intermediate guidance rather than final answers
key_sources: Wang Guanhua, Wang Wenna, Yang Daozhou, Ren Jifan. (2026). Generative AI, Cognitive Offloading, and Learner Agency in Higher Education: A Scoping Review. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071150

article_title: Observer Perceptions of GenAI Use and Interpersonal Trust: The Roles of Warmth, Competence, and AI Literacy
citation: Zhang Zhen, Geng Jiaying, Qi Chunhui. (2026). Observer Perceptions of GenAI Use and Interpersonal Trust: The Roles of Warmth, Competence, and AI Literacy. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071221
title: Stereotype Content Model account of observers' evaluations of GenAI users along warmth and competence dimensions
description: The article applies the Stereotype Content Model (Fiske et al., 2002) to the human–AI–human triad, in which observers judge a GenAI user along two fundamental dimensions before adjusting trust. As the article states, "SCM posits that individuals judge others along two fundamental dimensions of social perception: warmth (e.g., friendliness, sincerity, morality) and competence (e.g., intelligence, ambition, efficiency)". In this study the framework explains why GenAI use reduces trust: use lowers perceived warmth and competence, which in turn lower interpersonal trust. It is combined with social cognitive theory to motivate perceived AI literacy as a contextual moderator.
requirements: Observers must form person perceptions of a specific target user, operationalized here via a recall method and peer-rating scales
constraints: The article tests the framework in a cross-sectional, recall-based peer-evaluation context among Chinese university students; causal inferences are precluded by the design
target_learners: university students evaluating peers
target_learning_goals: understanding social evaluation of AI users in academic collaboration
examples: Participants recalled a specific classmate who had used AI and rated the target's warmth, competence, AI literacy, and trustworthiness on adapted scales
key_sources: Zhang Zhen, Geng Jiaying, Qi Chunhui. (2026). Observer Perceptions of GenAI Use and Interpersonal Trust: The Roles of Warmth, Competence, and AI Literacy. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071221

article_title: Mapping the Scaffolding of Metacognition and Learning by AI Tools in STEM Classrooms: A Bibliometric-Systematic Review
citation: Tsakeni, Maria, Stephen C. Nwafor, Moeketsi Mosia, and Felix O. Egara. 2025. Mapping the Scaffolding of Metacognition and Learning by AI Tools in STEM Classrooms: A Bibliometric–Systematic Review Approach (2005–2025). Journal of Intelligence 13: 148. https://doi.org/10.3390/jintelligence13110148
title: Scaffolding versus sharing metacognition: a distinction between AI-supported and AI-distributed metacognitive regulation
description: The review distinguishes two ways AI can be involved in learners' metacognition. Scaffolding "treats metacognition as a human capacity that can be supported and extended through prompts, feedback, or adaptive interventions, thereby allowing learners to retain agency and responsibility." Sharing, by contrast, "distributes metacognitive functions between human and AI agents, where AI may compensate for weak regulation." The review positions AI primarily as a scaffolding tool while noting sharing must be critically evaluated because it risks substitution of learner strategy development.
requirements: AI involvement must be designed so learners retain agency and responsibility for their regulation
constraints: Sharing risks limiting learners' opportunities to develop independent strategies if applied uncritically
target_learners: STEM students in secondary and tertiary education
target_learning_goals: metacognitive planning, monitoring, and evaluation of learning
examples: The review's 24-study synthesis coded 23 studies as human-centred scaffolding orientations and one (Walker et al. 2025) as posthumanist sharing of regulation
key_sources: Tsakeni, Maria, Stephen C. Nwafor, Moeketsi Mosia, and Felix O. Egara. 2025. Mapping the Scaffolding of Metacognition and Learning by AI Tools in STEM Classrooms: A Bibliometric–Systematic Review Approach (2005–2025). Journal of Intelligence 13: 148. https://doi.org/10.3390/jintelligence13110148

article_title: Motivated numeracy and enlightened self-government
citation: DAN M. KAHAN, ELLEN PETERS, ERICA CANTRELL DAWSON and PAUL SLOVIC. (2017). Motivated numeracy and enlightened self-government. Behavioural Public Policy, Volume 1, Issue 1. https://doi.org/10.1017/bpp.2016.2
title: Science comprehension thesis (SCT)
description: SCT is the rival account the article tested. It "identifies defects in the public's knowledge and reasoning capacities as the source of such controversies" over societal risks. The thesis predicts that individuals with greater science comprehension — here operationalized as numeracy, "a measure of the ability and disposition to make use of quantitative information" — should interpret contested data more accurately and thus be less polarized. The experiment disconfirmed this prediction: polarization was greatest among the most numerate subjects.
requirements: A population measurable on knowledge and reasoning capacities (here numeracy) so that comprehension deficits can be related to risk controversy.
constraints: The article reports that this thesis was not supported in its experiment: polarization increased rather than abated among the highest-numeracy subjects.
target_learners: general public members interpreting decision-relevant science
target_learning_goals: accurate causal inference from empirical data
examples: The article used the skin rash framing to show numeracy helps when data are uncharged, isolating what SCT cannot explain about charged data.
key_sources: DAN M. KAHAN, ELLEN PETERS, ERICA CANTRELL DAWSON and PAUL SLOVIC. (2017). Motivated numeracy and enlightened self-government. Behavioural Public Policy, Volume 1, Issue 1. https://doi.org/10.1017/bpp.2016.2

article_title: Altering School Climate through School-Wide Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports
citation: Bradshaw, C. P., Koth, C. W., Thornton, L. A., & Leaf, P. J. (2009). Altering School Climate through School-Wide Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports: Findings from a Group-Randomized Effectiveness Trial. Prevention Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11121-008-0114-9
title: School organizational health as a multidimensional climate construct shaped by whole-school prevention models
description: The article treats school organizational health as a staff-reported, multidimensional property of schools, naming overall organizational health plus the dimensions resource influence, staff affiliation, academic emphasis, collegial leadership, and institutional integrity. It positions this construct as responsive to school-wide prevention models: the trial showed PBIS altered these staff-reported dimensions over 5 years. The construct is further framed as a contextual characteristic that may mediate intervention effects on student performance, making organizational climate a target and mechanism for school-wide intervention design.
requirements: Measurement via staff reports analyzed with longitudinal multilevel models to separate individual and school levels
constraints: The article's evidence comes from elementary schools in a 5-year trial; generalization to other levels is not tested here
target_learners: elementary school staff
school administrators
target_learning_goals: improve school climate and organizational functioning
support implementation of school-wide behavior interventions
examples: Longitudinal multilevel analyses of 2,596 staff across 37 elementary schools over the 5-year trial
key_sources: Bradshaw, C. P., Koth, C. W., Thornton, L. A., & Leaf, P. J. (2009). Altering School Climate through School-Wide Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports: Findings from a Group-Randomized Effectiveness Trial. Prevention Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11121-008-0114-9

article_title: Review of the effects of citizenship education
citation: E. Geboers, F. Geijsel, W. Admiraal, G. ten Dam. (2013). Review of the effects of citizenship education. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2012.02.001
title: Schools should provide citizenship education because they can play a significant role in students' citizenship development
description: The review proceeds from the premise that "schools can play a significant role in the citizenship development of students," and notes that in most contemporary modern societies schools are obligated to provide citizenship education. The review's findings on effective forms — an open democratic classroom climate and a formal curriculum with citizenship projects and courses — indicate which implementations of this obligation appear promising for secondary schools.
requirements: Schools must be positioned to offer either an open democratic classroom climate or a formal curriculum including citizenship projects and courses.
constraints: The effectiveness of different forms of citizenship education is still unclear according to the review.
target_learners: secondary school students
examples: The review identifies classroom-climate approaches and formal curricula with citizenship projects and courses as the forms appearing effective in the 2003-2009 literature.
key_sources: E. Geboers, F. Geijsel, W. Admiraal, G. ten Dam. (2013). Review of the effects of citizenship education. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2012.02.001

article_title: Language and the Performance of English-Language Learners in Math Word Problems
citation: Maria Martiniello. (2008). Language and the Performance of English-Language Learners in Math Word Problems. Harvard Educational Review. https://doi.org/10.17763/haer.78.2.70783570r1111t32
title: Scrutinize the appropriateness of inferences about ELLs' math knowledge drawn from linguistically complex test items
description: The article argues that score-based inferences about English-language learners' mathematics knowledge deserve scrutiny when test items are linguistically complex. As the abstract puts it, "Through both DIF statistics and the voices of children, the article scrutinizes the appropriateness of inferences about ELLs' math knowledge based on linguistically complex test items." The principle combines statistical item analysis with qualitative learner evidence to evaluate whether an item measures math or language.
requirements: DIF statistics identifying differentially functioning items, plus qualitative evidence such as think-aloud transcripts
constraints: Applied to fourth-grade math word problems on the MCAS assessment
target_learners: English-language learners in elementary mathematics
target_learning_goals: Valid assessment of mathematics knowledge independent of English linguistic complexity
examples: The study combined DIF statistics on 2003 MCAS fourth-grade math items with children's think-aloud transcripts to question score interpretations for ELLs
key_sources: Maria Martiniello. (2008). Language and the Performance of English-Language Learners in Math Word Problems. Harvard Educational Review. https://doi.org/10.17763/haer.78.2.70783570r1111t32

article_title: Assimilating complex information
citation: Pollock, Edwina Jane. (2000). Assimilating Complex Information. PhD thesis, School of Education, University of New South Wales. https://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/17813
title: Schema construction as the mechanism underlying the isolated-interacting elements effect
description: The thesis proposes that schema construction is the mechanism underlying the success of the isolated-interacting elements instructional method. The first, isolated-elements phase is designed to allow learners to build component schemas without overwhelming working memory, and the second, interacting-elements phase then integrates them. The thesis states that evidence was provided in support of this proposal, linking the instructional sequence to the cognitive architecture in which schemas reduce working-memory load by storing organised knowledge in long term memory.
requirements: Instruction sequenced so that component schemas can be constructed before interacting elements are presented
constraints: The mechanism claim is supported within the five experiments of this thesis on complex technical material; the supplied text reports no test beyond these domains
target_learners: Novice and more experienced learners of complex technical information
target_learning_goals: Schema construction and understanding of complex, element-interactive material
examples: The thesis's experiments measured whether the isolated-then-interacting sequence produced better understanding, interpreted via schema construction
key_sources: Pollock, Edwina Jane. (2000). Assimilating Complex Information. PhD thesis, School of Education, University of New South Wales. https://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/17813

article_title: Assimilating complex information
citation: Pollock, Edwina Jane. (2000). Assimilating Complex Information. PhD thesis, School of Education, University of New South Wales. https://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/17813
title: Schemas reduce working memory load by incorporating interacting elements as single units
description: Within the thesis's account of cognitive architecture, human cognition circumvents the severely limited capacity of working memory by constructing schemas that organise elements of information categorically and store them in long term memory. Schemas shift the burden of storage to long term memory, and interacting elements that would otherwise overwhelm working memory can be incorporated in a schema that acts as a single element and imposes a minimal working memory load. This account underpins the thesis's rationale for reducing element interactivity during early instruction.
requirements: Prior knowledge organised into schemas stored in long term memory
constraints: The account is presented as the thesis's theoretical framing of memory and schema research, not as a new empirical result of the five experiments
target_learners: All learners processing complex, element-interactive information
target_learning_goals: Comprehension and learning of complex material within working memory limits
examples: The thesis illustrates the account with algebraic schemas: a/b = c can be transformed into a = cb and both equations processed easily in working memory by anyone competent at elementary algebra
key_sources: Pollock, Edwina Jane. (2000). Assimilating Complex Information. PhD thesis, School of Education, University of New South Wales. https://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/17813

article_title: Mindfulness-based interventions in schoolsâ€”a systematic review and meta-analysis
citation: Charlotte Zenner, Solveig Herrnleben-Kurz and Harald Walach. (2014). Mindfulness-based interventions in schools—a systematic review and meta-analysis. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.00603
title: Common components of school-based mindfulness intervention programs
description: The review catalogued the components of the 24 school-based mindfulness programs. All programs used breath awareness, described as "the traditional essential exercise," and most combined multiple components including working with thoughts and emotions, psycho-education, awareness of senses and daily-life practices, and group discussion. Programs drew on mindfulness theory (100%), often linked to MBSR, MBCT, DBT, and ACT, and two thirds used manualized programs such as MindfulSchools or Learning to BREATHE.
requirements: Programs need well defined goals, explicit guidelines, training, and quality control described for evaluation, per Weare and Nind as cited by the review
constraints: Many manualized programs lacked sufficient guidance material for implementation, and only two had an enduring presence of more than five years
target_learners: pupils and students from grade 1 to 12
target_learning_goals: cultivating mindfulness, attentional and emotional self-regulation, and stress resilience
examples: Interventions varied from 4 to 24 weeks (median 8), typically 45 min once a week, totaling 160 to 3700 min of practice with a median of 420 min
key_sources: Charlotte Zenner, Solveig Herrnleben-Kurz and Harald Walach. (2014). Mindfulness-based interventions in schools—a systematic review and meta-analysis. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.00603

article_title: Scaffolding Self-regulated Learning and Metacognition – Implications for the Design of Computer-based Scaffolds
citation: Azevedo, R., Hadwin, A.F. (2005). Scaffolding Self-regulated Learning and Metacognition – Implications for the Design of Computer-based Scaffolds. Instr Sci 33, 367–379 (2005). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-005-1272-9
title: Designing computer-based scaffolds to support self-regulated learning and metacognition in educational contexts
description: The article's title frames an organizing account in which scaffolding is applied to learners' self-regulated learning and metacognition, and in which this framing carries "Implications for the Design of Computer-based Scaffolds". The piece introduces a collection of work on how scaffolds — human, software-based, and embedded in hypermedia and other learning environments — can support students in regulating their own learning. Only the title, citation metadata, and reference list were accessible, so the framework is recorded at the level of its stated focus.
requirements: Computer-based scaffolds must be designed with learners' self-regulated learning and metacognition as explicit targets of support, per the article's stated focus.
constraints: Only the title, citation metadata, and reference list of the article were accessible; the substantive argument of the editorial was not available for extraction.
target_learners: Students learning with computer-based and hypermedia learning environments
key_sources: Azevedo, R., Hadwin, A.F. (2005). Scaffolding Self-regulated Learning and Metacognition – Implications for the Design of Computer-based Scaffolds. Instr Sci 33, 367–379 (2005). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-005-1272-9

article_title: A Review of Research in Revising Instructional Text
citation: Mary H. Sawyer. (1991). A Review of Research in Revising Instructional Text. Journal of Reading Behavior. https://doi.org/10.1080/10862969109547744
title: The scenario principle: revising text around human agents, actions, and instantiated contexts based on readers' verbal protocols
description: The scenario principle is a revision framework from the Document Design Project in which text information is "reorganized the information around human agents and their actions" and instantiated with concrete contexts and examples that fill slots in abstract frameworks. It was derived from readers' think-aloud protocols showing that experienced readers radically restructure difficult text into scenarios, and it yielded revision guidelines such as itemizing, turning labels into questions, and scenario-like translations.
requirements: Access to readers' verbal protocols or think-alouds to identify how the target audience actually makes sense of the text
constraints: Developed and validated for functional documents such as regulations, contracts, and insurance policies; the review notes Flower et al. did not test how the scenario principles might best be applied to revising instructional writing
target_learners: Adult readers of public and functional documents, including Medicaid recipients who were typically poor, old, and not well educated
target_learning_goals: Comprehending and correctly using difficult procedural and regulatory text, such as Medicaid forms and insurance policies
examples: Revised headings such as "Who is an eligible student borrower?" replacing "Personal Liability; Occurrence; Social Disadvantage", and the poodle-loss illustration instantiating the insurance concept of Broader Coverage
key_sources: Mary H. Sawyer. (1991). A Review of Research in Revising Instructional Text. Journal of Reading Behavior. https://doi.org/10.1080/10862969109547744

article_title: Scientific Habits of Mind in Virtual Worlds
citation: Constance Steinkuehler, Sean Duncan. (2008). Scientific Habits of Mind in Virtual Worlds. J Sci Educ Technol. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10956-008-9120-8
title: Three-group coding framework for scientific habits of mind in informal game forums
description: The article develops a set of 18 codes (following Chi 1997) based on AAAS benchmarks for scientific literacy, Chinn and Malhotra's framework for evaluating inquiry tasks, and Kuhn's epistemological framework. The codes address "Scientific discursive practices (including social knowledge construction), systems- and model-based reasoning, and tacit epistemologies", applied by four raters with 92% four-way interrater reliability on roughly 10% of the corpus. It deliberately omits content-specific science understanding because the investigated world "makes no claims of correspondence with the natural one".
requirements: Raters with substantial participant-observer experience in the game context; a second WoW-specific content code set coded by two raters with 93% two-way reliability
constraints: Omits content-knowledge aspects of scientific understanding, justified by the study's focus on scientific practices rather than content in a simulated world
target_learners: Informal learners in online game communities
Adolescent and adult game forum participants
target_learning_goals: Scientific habits of mind: argumentation, systems and model-based reasoning, evaluative epistemology
examples: Applied to a random sample of 1,984 posts across 85 threads of the official WoW priest forum, yielding the reported proportions of social knowledge construction, systems-based reasoning, and evaluative epistemology
key_sources: Constance Steinkuehler, Sean Duncan. (2008). Scientific Habits of Mind in Virtual Worlds. J Sci Educ Technol. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10956-008-9120-8

article_title: Adolescents With Chronic Medical Conditions and High School Completion: The Importance of Perceived School Belonging
citation: Kirkpatrick, Kathryn M. (2020). Adolescents With Chronic Medical Conditions and High School Completion: The Importance of Perceived School Belonging. Continuity in Education, 1(1), 50–63. https://doi.org/10.5334/cie.5
title: School belonging as a basic need with identifiable school-level promotive components
description: The article frames belonging as "a basic human need, important for optimal functioning", with school as the primary community outside the family for adolescents. It identifies school environments promoting connectedness as those with "high academic standards, high levels of teacher support, a community where relationships between students and adults are caring and respectful, and safety". It further reports three critical school-level components identified in prior work: high academic expectations coupled with support for learning, positive and respectful student-adult relationships, and physical and emotional safety.
requirements: School environments must offer supportive relationships, structure, and safety for belonging to develop as described
constraints: The three-component list is attributed to prior sources (Blum, 2005; Klem & Connell, 2004; Wingspread, 2004), not tested in this study
target_learners: adolescents in grades 7–12
students with chronic medical conditions
target_learning_goals: academic attainment and high school completion
social and behavioral success at school
examples: The study measured belonging with a five-item Wave I scale covering closeness, part of school, happiness at school, fair teachers, and feeling safe (α = .76)
key_sources: Kirkpatrick, Kathryn M. (2020). Adolescents With Chronic Medical Conditions and High School Completion: The Importance of Perceived School Belonging. Continuity in Education, 1(1), 50–63. https://doi.org/10.5334/cie.5

article_title: School Readiness and Self-Regulation: A Developmental Psychobiological Approach
citation: Blair, Clancy & Raver, C. Cybele. (2015). School Readiness and Self-Regulation: A Developmental Psychobiological Approach. Annual Review of Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-psych-010814-015221
title: School readiness is best understood through the construct of self-regulation, spanning attention, emotion, and stress regulation
description: The article proposes a unifying framework in which school readiness is understood as the development of self-regulation, including attention focusing, emotion and stress-response regulation, reflection, and positive social interaction. It argues these attributes are interrelated with cognitive abilities, primarily executive functions, and provide the proximal mechanisms through which children acquire knowledge in classroom interactions. The framework unites biological and behavioral levels of analysis shaped by developmental context.
requirements: Research and practice must treat social-emotional and cognitive aspects of readiness as interrelated rather than separate influences
constraints: The framework concerns young children approaching school entry, particularly around age 6
target_learners: young children entering kindergarten and early elementary grades
examples: A nationally representative sample of kindergarten teachers endorsed readiness as being able to pay attention, follow directions, and regulate emotion rather than strictly academic skills
key_sources: Blair, Clancy & Raver, C. Cybele. (2015). School Readiness and Self-Regulation: A Developmental Psychobiological Approach. Annual Review of Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-psych-010814-015221

article_title: Community violence exposure and adolescents’ school engagement and academic achievement over time.
citation: Borofsky Larissa A., Kellerman Ilana, Baucom Brian, Oliver Pamella H., Margolin Gayla. (2013). Community Violence Exposure and Adolescents' School Engagement and Academic Achievement Over Time. Psychology of Violence. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0034121
title: School engagement as a multifaceted construct with emotional, behavioral, and cognitive components
description: The article adopts a conception of school engagement, drawing on Fredricks and colleagues, as a multifaceted construct reflecting adolescents' day-to-day connection to school. It is "typically conceptualized as having emotional (e.g., enjoying being at school), behavioral (e.g., helping out at school), and cognitive (e.g., feeling interested in school) components". The authors operationalized it with a seven-item self-report measure mapping onto these three facets and treat engagement as more amenable to immediate intervention than achievement.
requirements: Measurement capturing emotional, behavioral, and cognitive facets of adolescents' connection to school
constraints: The article notes there is no one definition of school engagement
target_learners: Adolescents
target_learning_goals: Connection and engagement with the school environment
examples: The study's seven-item measure asked, for example, how much students feel happy at school, help keep their school clean, and feel interested in what is going on at school.
key_sources: Borofsky Larissa A., Kellerman Ilana, Baucom Brian, Oliver Pamella H., Margolin Gayla. (2013). Community Violence Exposure and Adolescents' School Engagement and Academic Achievement Over Time. Psychology of Violence. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0034121

article_title: Learning to think together: Creativity, interdisciplinary collaboration and epistemic control
citation: Gardiner Paul. (2020). Learning to think together: Creativity, interdisciplinary collaboration and epistemic control. Thinking Skills and Creativity. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tsc.2020.100749
title: Scaffold creative collaboration by developing epistemic awareness, humility and empathy before expecting epistemic control
description: The article recommends that educators scaffold and structure creative and collaborative learning by moving students through the framework's stages: understanding their own way of knowing, recognising its limits ("Epistemic humility is the understanding that what you know and how you know it, your way of knowing, is not the whole story"), and valuing other disciplines' games and forms. Only then do students reach epistemic control, mobilising a range of ways of knowing for complex problems. Without scaffolds, interdisciplinary discussion risks being adversarial at worst and parallel at best.
requirements: Educators must maintain a safe learning environment where discomfort is intellectual rather than personal or social, balancing epistemic agency and epistemic safety
constraints: The article states educators must be prepared to allow students to sit in discomfort and ambiguity, and that epistemic empathy requires knowledge of other ways of knowing, not just goodwill
target_learners: upper secondary, undergraduate and postgraduate students
target_learning_goals: willingness to work with ambiguity and integrate disciplinary perspectives
examples: The article argues learning that does not encourage working with ambiguity and collaboration will not prepare students for interdisciplinary teams they will graduate into
key_sources: Gardiner Paul. (2020). Learning to think together: Creativity, interdisciplinary collaboration and epistemic control. Thinking Skills and Creativity. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tsc.2020.100749

article_title: Building on Prior Knowledge: Schema-dependent Encoding Processes Relate to Academic Performance
citation: van Kesteren, M. T. R., Rijpkema, M., Ruiter, D. J., Morris, R. G. M., & Fernández, G. (2014). Building on Prior Knowledge: Schema-dependent Encoding Processes Relate to Academic Performance. Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience, 26(10), 2250–2261. https://doi.org/10.1162/jocn_a_00630
title: Schema-dependent MTL–mPFC balance account of conceptual encoding
description: The article proposes that a pre-existing schema shifts the balance of encoding processing between the medial prefrontal cortex and the medial temporal lobe. On this account, "mPFC serves to assimilate new information into a schema by activating (or retrieving) the schema enabling integration of novel information, whereas MTL detects mismatches with a schema and serves to bind directly different parts of the memory trace into a specific episodic memory." Schema-related encoding thus shows enhanced mPFC activity and reduced mPFC–hippocampal coupling, while schema-unrelated encoding shows enhanced MTL activity and coupling. The account extends prior consolidation-shift findings by showing the balance shift is already present at encoding.
requirements: A pre-existing conceptual schema activated by related prior knowledge
constraints: The study tested memory only after 24 hr and cannot dissociate encoding from consolidation effects
Selection and abstraction subprocesses of schema-related learning, presumably in posterior perceptual regions, were not tapped
target_learners: second-year university undergraduates
target_learning_goals: acquisition and retention of new conceptual disciplinary knowledge
examples: Participants encoded curriculum-embedded factual sentences related or unrelated to their first-year discipline knowledge while brain activity and connectivity were measured with fMRI
key_sources: van Kesteren, M. T. R., Rijpkema, M., Ruiter, D. J., Morris, R. G. M., & Fernández, G. (2014). Building on Prior Knowledge: Schema-dependent Encoding Processes Relate to Academic Performance. Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience, 26(10), 2250–2261. https://doi.org/10.1162/jocn_a_00630

article_title: The influence of self-efficacy beliefs for student parents attending university
citation: Tricia M. van Rhijn & Donna S. Lero. (2014). The influence of self-efficacy beliefs for student parents attending university. International Journal of Lifelong Education. http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/02601370.2014.884178
title: School-family balance as a domain-general efficacy construct adapted from work-family balance
description: School-family balance is defined as an individual's perceived ability to manage both school and family role responsibilities, adapted from the work-family balance literature. The article states it is "grounded in an individual's lived experience of the work-family interface and moves beyond individual experiences of conflict and enrichment between roles," emphasizing "an individual's perceived ability to meet the demands of their multiple roles." The construct was measured with six items adapted from Carlson et al.'s Work-Family Balance Scale, with work-related wording changed to school-related, and demonstrated adequate internal reliability (α = .93) and factorial validity in this population.
requirements: Adaptation of validated work-family balance measure with domain-appropriate wording changes
constraints: Developed and validated specifically with student parents; generalizability to other populations not established in this study
target_learners: student parents attending university
target_learning_goals: managing school and family role responsibilities simultaneously
examples: Measured with six items rated on a 5-point Likert scale; sample item: "I am able to negotiate and accomplish what is expected of me at school and in my family"
key_sources: Tricia M. van Rhijn & Donna S. Lero. (2014). The influence of self-efficacy beliefs for student parents attending university. International Journal of Lifelong Education. http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/02601370.2014.884178

article_title: Sleep, School Performance, and a School-Based Intervention among School-Aged Children: A Sleep Series Study in China
citation: Li Shenghui, Arguelles Lester, Jiang Fan, Chen Wenjuan, Jin Xingming, Yan Chonghuai, Tian Ying, Hong Xiumei, Qian Ceng, Zhang Jun, Wang Xiaobin, Shen Xiaoming. (2013). Sleep, School Performance, and a School-Based Intervention among School-Aged Children: A Sleep Series Study in China. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0067928
title: Regulate school schedules (later start times) as a lever for children's sleep health
description: The article argues that school schedule, particularly early school start time, is a modifiable policy target for improving children's sleep: "school schedule could be considered as a target for sleep intervention." In its trial, delaying start time by 30 or 60 minutes in primary schools increased sleep duration (15.6 and 22.8 minutes) and reduced daytime sleepiness relative to control schools. The principle treats schedule regulation as a school-level, system-level intervention rather than an individual behavior-change program.
requirements: Schools must share a common start time that can be shifted, with academic and nonacademic activities correspondingly regulated (finishing time moved in the trial).
Comparison groups with similar sleep duration, sleepiness, schedule, socioeconomic background, and achievement are needed to evaluate the change.
constraints: The article states the intervention trial "is not a rigorous randomized control trial at the individual level, and as such, attribution of improved sleep to the regulation of school schedule alone should be prudent."
Gains were modest: only a minority reached the recommended 10 or more hours and about half still reported daytime sleepiness after the change.
target_learners: School-aged children in primary school (fourth and fifth grades in the trial)
target_learning_goals: Sufficient sleep duration and reduced daytime sleepiness as foundations for attention, learning motivation, and academic achievement
examples: Six Shanghai primary schools were randomly assigned (two schools each) to control, 30-minute delay, or 60-minute delay of the 7:30am start time, with finishing time correspondingly moved, and sleep was surveyed before and two years after.
key_sources: Li Shenghui, Arguelles Lester, Jiang Fan, Chen Wenjuan, Jin Xingming, Yan Chonghuai, Tian Ying, Hong Xiumei, Qian Ceng, Zhang Jun, Wang Xiaobin, Shen Xiaoming. (2013). article_title: Socio-Cognitive Scaffolding with Computer-Supported Collaboration Scripts: a Meta-Analysis
citation: Freydis Vogel & Christof Wecker & Ingo Kollar & Frank Fischer. (2016). Socio-Cognitive Scaffolding with Computer-Supported Collaboration Scripts: a Meta-Analysis. Educ Psychol Rev (2017) 29:477–511. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-016-9361-7
title: Script theory of guidance (SToG): internal scripts with four components and external CSCL scaffolds on three hierarchical levels
description: The meta-analysis builds on the script theory of guidance (Fischer, Kollar, Stegmann, and Wecker 2013), in which "collaboration skills can be regarded as 'internal scripts'" that guide understanding and acting in similar situations. Internal scripts comprise four partially hierarchically ordered components: play, scene, scriptlet, and role. External CSCL scripts support learners who lack appropriate internal scripts by prompting cognitive operations, sequencing activities, and distributing them among roles, with scaffolds on play, scene, and scriptlet levels.
requirements: Learners lacking appropriate internal scripts are supported by external CSCL scripts that prompt, sequence, and distribute collaborative activities
constraints: The article notes learners may gradually acquire internal scripts through repeated scripted participation and possible fading of the script
target_learners: Learners collaborating in computer-supported settings whose collaboration skills are not yet fully developed
target_learning_goals: Collaboration skills such as argumentation and peer feedback
examples: The article cites Stegmann et al. (2007), where a CSCL script structuring online discussions improved domain-specific knowledge application, and Rummel et al. (2009), where scripts improved physicians' and psychotherapists' collaboration skills.

article_title: Good for learning, bad for motivation? A meta-analysis on the effects of computer-supported collaboration scripts
citation: Radkowitsch, A., Vogel, F., & Fischer, F. (2020). Good for learning, bad for motivation? A meta-analysis on the effects of computer-supported collaboration scripts. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 15, 5–47. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09316-4
title: Script theory of guidance: internal collaboration scripts and the optimal external scripting level principle
description: The article's explanatory framework holds that collaborative learners' failure to engage in high-level collaborative processes indicates a lack of "internal collaboration scripts" — flexible cognitive structures of knowledge about collaborative practices, grounded in dynamic memory theory. External CSCL scripts scaffold collaboration by affording specific activities in a likely sequence and distributing roles, compensating for dysfunctional internal scripts. Fischer et al. identify four hierarchical script components — play, scene, scriptlet, and role — and propose the optimal external scripting level principle: learners benefit most from external scripts addressing the hierarchical level whose subordinate components learners do not yet have available.
requirements: External scripts must fit learners' prior knowledge and skills, i.e., the internal script components they have available
constraints: A CSCL script could lead to overscripting if it addresses internal script components on a level the learners are already able to activate, potentially reducing autonomy and motivation
target_learners: K-12 learners
higher education learners
professional development participants
key_sources: Radkowitsch, A., Vogel, F., & Fischer, F. (2020). Good for learning, bad for motivation? A meta-analysis on the effects of computer-supported collaboration scripts. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 15, 5–47. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09316-4

article_title: Good for learning, bad for motivation? A meta-analysis on the effects of computer-supported collaboration scripts
citation: Radkowitsch, A., Vogel, F., & Fischer, F. (2020). Good for learning, bad for motivation? A meta-analysis on the effects of computer-supported collaboration scripts. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 15, 5–47. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09316-4
title: Design CSCL scripts to scaffold specific collaborative activities (negotiation, information sharing, coordination) rather than treating transactivity as a single undifferentiated target
description: The article argues that because transactivity encompasses many specific collaborative activities, effectiveness research should and design can target the three social activities of Liu et al.'s collaborative problem-solving framework: sharing ideas or information, negotiating, and coordinating problem solving. CSCL scripts can prompt each activity specifically, and the meta-analysis codes scripts by which activities they scaffold to explain their effects on domain learning and collaboration skills.
requirements: Scripts must prompt activities that address learning partners, targeting the collaborative process of at least two learners
constraints: Coordination skills effects could not be estimated due to a small number of studies; synergistic or differentiated scaffolding is hard to achieve according to the authors
target_learners: K-12 learners
higher education learners
professional development participants
examples: The meta-analysis categorized each included CSCL script by whether it prompted negotiation, information sharing, or coordination, and by the number and combination of activities prompted

article_title: Socio-Cognitive Scaffolding with Computer-Supported Collaboration Scripts: a Meta-Analysis
citation: Freydis Vogel, Christof Wecker, Ingo Kollar, Frank Fischer. (2016). Socio-Cognitive Scaffolding with Computer-Supported Collaboration Scripts: a Meta-Analysis. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-016-9361-7
title: Script theory of guidance (SToG): internal scripts with four components scaffolded by external CSCL scripts on three levels
description: The meta-analysis builds on the script theory of guidance (Fischer, Kollar, Stegmann, and Wecker 2013), in which collaboration skills are regarded as internal scripts that, once consolidated, guide understanding and acting in similar situations. Internal scripts consist of four partially hierarchically ordered components: play, scene, scriptlet, and role components. External CSCL scripts support learners who lack appropriate internal scripts by prompting cognitive operations, sequencing activities, and distributing them among roles, with scaffolds addressable at the play, scene, and scriptlet levels. The article uses SToG to derive its moderator hypotheses about transactivity and script level.
requirements: Learners must be able to adapt and reconfigure internal script components in new collaborative situations for the scaffolding to modify the internal script
constraints: The article notes learners often cannot spontaneously engage in beneficial collaborative activities because they lack appropriate internal scripts, which is the condition external scripts address
target_learners: learners in computer-supported collaborative learning settings across domains such as computer science, economics, life sciences, educational science, medicine, and psychology
target_learning_goals: collaboration skills such as argumentation and peer feedback skills
examples: The article describes how a learner with an internal script for collaborative reading including asking thought-provoking questions might reconfigure script components for a collaborative problem-solving situation

article_title: Prospects for Scientific Visualization as an Educational Technology
citation: Douglas N. Gordin, Roy D. Pea. (1995). Prospects for Scientific Visualization as an Educational Technology. The Journal of the Learning Sciences, 4(3), pp.249-279. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190593
title: Scientific visualization as an important new inscriptional system for science and education
description: The article presents a sociological account of science in which scientific visualization functions as an inscriptional system: a medium through which scientific practices are conducted and communicated. It argues this account "portrays scientific visualization as an important new inscriptional system," and extends the view to education, where visualization can serve inquiry-driven learning and connect schooling to authentic scientific practice.
requirements: Learners and teachers must be able to engage with visualization tools as participants in scientific inscriptional practices, not merely as viewers of displays
constraints: The account is framed for science education contexts where visualization tools and supporting infrastructure are available
target_learners: secondary and undergraduate science students
target_learning_goals: understanding of scientific practices through visualization
examples: The article grounds the inscriptional-system account in examples of visualization use in science and in three educational projects

article_title: The mechanics of CSCL macro scripts
citation: Pierre Dillenbourg, Fabrice Hong. (2008). The mechanics of CSCL macro scripts. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://hal.science/hal-00692019
title: Script mechanics as data-structure transformations between phases
description: The article accounts for how script components relate to one another computationally: "These mechanisms are encompassed in the transformation of data structures (social structure, resources structure and products structure) between script phases". Designing a script thus means specifying how the social grouping, the available resources, and the expected products are reconfigured from one phase to the next.
requirements: Script phases between which the three data structures can be transformed
target_learners: students participating in scripted collaborative learning sequences
target_learning_goals: structured collaborative learning interactions across script phases
examples: The article describes how this pedagogical design model is translated into computational structures in three illustrated scripts

article_title: Teacher support in computer-supported lab work: bridging the gap between lab experiments and students’ conceptual understanding
citation: Anniken Furberg. (2016). Teacher support in computer-supported lab work: bridging the gap between lab experiments and students' conceptual understanding. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-016-9229-3
title: SCY-Lab forensic mission digital learning environment with designated support tools
description: SCY-Lab is a digital learning environment from the SCY project containing tools supporting conceptual understanding and inquiry skills. Its forensic mission is "a highly structured environment featuring designated digital support tools" where most tools are text editors with "directive questions or sentence openers". In this study three tools scaffolded annotation of DNA profiles, writing conclusions, and producing an official forensic report, alongside information resources such as a forensics handbook and DNA animations.
requirements: Students work in supported group-based activities with designated tools per task
A teacher available for help-seeking during tool use
constraints: Was used here with one upper secondary class in a genetics/forensics project; the study examines it in a naturalistic intervention setting
target_learners: Upper secondary school students aged 16-17 in science
target_learning_goals: Understanding scientific concepts and procedures of DNA analysis and gel electrophoresis
Analysing, concluding and reporting lab experiment findings
examples: Students uploaded gels to a drawing/annotation tool, used a text-editing tool with three topical sentence openers for conclusions, and wrote an official report addressed to a fictive general attorney

article_title: Forming social systems by coupling minds at different levels of cognition: Design, tools, and research methods
citation: Cress, U., Stahl, G., Rose, C., Law, N., & Ludvigsen, S. (2018). Forming social systems by coupling minds at different levels of cognition: Design, tools, and research methods. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 13, 235–240. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9284-z
title: Use scripts and awareness visualizations as coupling mechanisms because they force consideration of partners' actions and perspectives
description: The editorial presents collaboration scripts and visualizations as primary tools for coupling individual minds at different processing levels. It states that 'The high efficacy of scripts as coupling means is not surprising, as they force the individuals to consider the actions and perspectives of their partners', while visualization is a more implicit support that fosters awareness. Across the issue, scripts appear at the cognitive, metacognitive, and activity levels, and visualizations also serve researchers as analysis tools.
requirements: Scripts must prescribe actions such as sharing, copying, or discussing ideas so that individuals consider their partners' actions and perspectives
constraints: The editorial notes the Wikipedia-style script practiced in the wild is not informed by any theoretical consideration about collaboration
target_learners: collaboratively learning students, including middle school science students and wiki writers
examples: The idea manager's private and shared baskets, Hadwin et al.'s awareness visualization of planning perceptions, and the deliberation-first wiki alternative script

article_title: Bringing maker practices to school: tracing discursive and materially mediated aspects of student teams’ collaborative making processes
citation: Riikonen, S., Seitamaa-Hakkarainen, P., & Hakkarainen, K. (2020). Bringing maker practices to school: tracing discursive and materially mediated aspects of student teams' collaborative making processes. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09330-6
title: Collaborative making project pattern: multi-material, digitally enhanced, holistic, thematically anchored
description: Drawing on craft (sloyd) tradition, the authors characterize school-based collaborative making projects as "1) multi-material, including both soft (e.g., textile) and hard (e.g., metals) materials; 2) digitally enhanced (integrating digital devices and applications); 3) holistic in terms of including all stages of creation from design ideation to experimentation, and from fabrication to evaluation of the final productions." The fourth feature anchors projects on integrative thematic studies orchestrated by teacher teams from multiple subject domains. The pattern was enacted in Finnish craft lessons extended with digital fabrication instruments such as 3D CAD, robotics, e-textiles and GoGo Boards.
requirements: school makerspaces expanding craft classrooms with digital fabrication instruments
teacher teams representing multiple subject domains
constraints: embedded in Finnish basic education's compulsory weekly craft lessons through seventh grade
target_learners: seventh-grade students (aged 13–14)
examples: Five teams invented artifacts such as a smart three-wheeled bike, a mobile gaming grip, an environment-responsive sports outfit, a warming insole, and a plant-care system.
