article_title: Integrating collaboration scripts, group awareness, and self-regulation in computer-supported collaborative learning
citation: Lenka Schnaubert · Freydis Vogel. (2022). Integrating collaboration scripts, group awareness, and self-regulation in computer-supported collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2022) 17:1–10. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09367-9
title: Script theory of guidance: four hierarchical components of internal collaboration scripts
description: The article presents collaboration scripts as learners' activated cognitive schemata guiding behavior in social learning situations. It reports that "The script theory of guidance distinguishes four script components that are related in a sequenced and hierarchical way": scriptlets (single activities), scenes (sets of scriptlets in sequential order), plays (the overarching goal comprising all scenes), and roles (how scriptlets are assigned to individuals). External collaboration scripts scaffold learners toward an ideal internal script.
requirements: Learners activate internal scripts based on their interpretation of a social situation and its perceived goals; to be functional, scripts must integrate activities supportive of knowledge and skill acquisition through collaboration
constraints: Learners may struggle to autonomously activate the most appropriate functional internal script in a given situation
target_learners: collaborative learners in CSCL settings
target_learning_goals: collaborative learning skills and knowledge acquisition through collaboration
examples: External collaboration scripts are offered as socio-cognitive scaffolding consisting of a sequence of prompts reflecting play, scene, and scriptlet components

article_title: Comparing the effects of a collaboration script and collaborative reflection on promoting knowledge about good collaboration and effective interaction
citation: Sebastian Strauß, Isis Tunnigkeit, Julia Eberle, Arlind Avdullahu, Nikol Rummel. (2025). Comparing the effects of a collaboration script and collaborative reflection on promoting knowledge about good collaboration and effective interaction. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09430-7
title: Script theory of guidance: collaboration knowledge resides in internal collaboration scripts that external scripts can reshape
description: The article's explanatory account holds that knowledge about collaboration is encoded in internal collaboration scripts, analogous to cognitive scripts for everyday situations, comprising knowledge and expectations about situation structure, phases, roles, and goal-directed actions. When learners lack effective internal scripts, "external collaboration scripts" provide scaffolds that prescribe beneficial interactions or inhibit undesired patterns. Through repeated guided practice, learners build internal script components; the internalized script "is not a direct replication of the external" but a reconfigured internal representation.
requirements: Learners must actively process the script's action sequences and enact the scripted actions to benefit
constraints: Overscripting: a detailed external script may cause process losses for learners with well-developed internal scripts (expertise-reversal effect); overly vague scripts offer insufficient guidance for learners with low prior knowledge
Concerns that scripts limit learner autonomy and hamper natural interaction are discussed
target_learners: university students collaborating in small groups
examples: The study's script condition embedded a four-phase external script in the video-conference margin with prompts, colored phase bars, progress bars, and audio signals for phase changes

article_title: Accomplishing collaboration at scale: How professionals jointly frame problems on Stack Overflow
citation: Alena Seredko. (2025). Accomplishing collaboration at scale: How professionals jointly frame problems on Stack Overflow. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09451-w
title: Qualitative reconceptualization of scale as a local practical concern of participation fluidity
description: The article reconceptualizes scale from a quantitative property (user numbers, content volume) into a qualitative one: "the defining condition of scale is not simply large numbers of users but rather the open-ended, asynchronous and fluid nature of participation". Even interactions among few participants are shaped by the expectation that future, unknown contributors must understand what is going on, making scale a local concern that shapes how intelligibility is accomplished. This framework motivates the study's sequential analysis of turn design.
requirements: A platform record of durable traces (posts, comments, edits) on which participants and analysts can rely, since "durable traces such as comments and edits maintain joint work as publicly accessible over prolonged periods"
constraints: Developed from ethnomethodological analysis of a small number of Python-tagged threads; the article contrasts it with macro-level quantitative approaches rather than testing it statistically
target_learners: professionals in knowledge-intensive domains
software developers
target_learning_goals: understanding how collaboration is accomplished in large-scale online communities
examples: The study applies the framework by asking how users design turns presupposing any present or future user may read them

article_title: Data to decision-making: how elementary students use their Community and Citizen Science project to reimagine their school campus
citation: Erin Bridges Bird · Heidi L. Ballard · Margaret Harte. (2023). Data to decision-making: how elementary students use their Community and Citizen Science project to reimagine their school campus. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09612-6
title: Instructional design pattern: a school-based CCS project enacting the full data lifecycle with youth-led decisions
description: The study's program design builds on the CCS education framework and aligns its phases with the data lifecycle: developing expertise through bird-identification lessons; defining research questions in the after-school Ornithology Club (50 min weekly); designing an observation protocol with student-chosen tools; interpreting and evaluating data; making decisions and taking action, funded by a school-garden grant for a Bird Sanctuary; submitting data to eBird and presenting to audiences; and evaluating outcomes and reassessing goals.
requirements: Educators need funding mechanisms (the grant), tools available to students, and regular meeting time to support all lifecycle stages
constraints: Ten of sixteen club attendees were focal participants with varying attendance frequency
target_learners: 4th and 5th grade students
examples: Students decided which plants to include in the Bird Sanctuary, generated their own field-observation route of about 15 min, and shared campus improvement recommendations at a School District Board meeting

article_title: Novice and expert self-regulated learning phase transitions in medical diagnosis: Implications for adaptive and intelligent systems
citation: Cloude, E. B., Chapman, R., Azevedo, R., Castiglioni, A., LaRochelle, J., Hernandez, C., & Torre, D. (2025). Novice and expert self-regulated learning phase transitions in medical diagnosis: Implications for adaptive and intelligent systems. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09729-4
title: Extending Zimmerman and Moylan's socio-cognitive model of SRL to include metacognitive feelings (uncertainty) as a phase in the clinical-reasoning cycle
description: The article applies Zimmerman and Moylan's socio-cognitive model of SRL, which organizes learning processes into "forethought, performance, and self-reflection" phases, to clinical reasoning in multimedia diagnosis. The authors extend the model by adding metacognitive feelings: they state they "extend the SCT model by including metacognitive feelings as a phase in this cycle", operationalized as a Feelings of Uncertainty code drawn from the Lajoie et al. line of work. The study's sequential pattern mining treats uncertainty as a full phase whose transitions (e.g., UNC→F) cycle back into forethought and performance, framing SRL as non-linear, bidirectional, and cyclical rather than unidirectional.
requirements: Think-aloud verbalizations coded with a scheme covering the three SCT phases plus an uncertainty code
constraints: Findings are from one medical domain (common cough cases) in one multimedia system; the article notes the excluded 20% of the sample has implications including reduced generalizability.
target_learners: medical students
physicians in training and practice
examples: Participants were trained to think-aloud with a 3-min video of a physician thinking aloud during an anemia case in CResME before solving the five cough cases.
key_sources: Cloude, E. B., Chapman, R., Azevedo, R., Castiglioni, A., LaRochelle, J., Hernandez, C., & Torre, D. (2025). article_title: Walking the number line: towards an enactive understanding of integer arithmetic
citation: Jacqueline Anton, Dor Abrahamson. (2025). Walking the number line: towards an enactive understanding of integer arithmetic. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09707-w
title: Scaffold perspective coordination explicitly: give students multiple body-scale sessions and bidirectional switching supports before expecting desk-scale transfer
description: From the pilot's breakdowns, the authors recommend that embodied designs not shift unidirectionally from enactive to normative media. They state that "students must be given scaffolded opportunities to coordinate between perspectives when learning curricular content in an experiential situation" and that "Merely shifting unidirectionally from the BNL to a figurine on the SNL was often not enough." For the next design iteration they specify multiple body-scale sessions before advancing, a longer number line, and switching back and forth between the two lines or teaching a peer how to walk the body-scale line.
requirements: Time for multiple sessions on the body-scale number line before advancing to the desk-scale line
constraints: The pilot's limited time within a typical school day restricted participants' opportunities to train adequately with the new resources
target_learners: middle-school students learning integer arithmetic, including students with disabilities
target_learning_goals: coordinating embodied and symbolic understandings of integer operations
examples: In the pilot, students who spontaneously returned to the body-scale line when stuck used it to validate desk-scale answers; the authors propose building in such switching deliberately

article_title: Discovery learning: zombie, phoenix, or elephant?
citation: Arthur Bakker. (2018). Discovery learning: zombie, phoenix, or elephant? Instructional Science, 46, 169–183. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9450-8
title: Scaffolding as a dialectic teacher-student system rather than one-directional support
description: The article argues that a source of problems in the discovery learning debate is conceptualizing teachers and students as separate systems with a one-way causal relationship. Drawing on Wood et al.'s characterization of scaffolding as "an interactive system of exchange" and Roth and Lee's subject|object ensemble, it holds that students are both subjects and objects of the pedagogical process, and teachers may be guided by their students. Within this systems view, guidance and discovery form a coordinated whole, and questions become what needs to be told, discovered, or practiced.
requirements: Researchers must stick to the original sense of scaffolding with a dynamical systems lens to avoid a one-directional view of scaffolds working on students as objects.
constraints: Answering what to tell, discover, or repeat requires professional judgment there and then, not a general rule.
target_learners: School students working with teachers in zones of proximal development
target_learning_goals: Coordinated teacher-student interaction supporting discovery of what cannot simply be told
examples: The article frames the question as what lies in the region of sensitivity to instruction or the zone of proximal development, requiring in-the-moment professional judgment.
key_sources: Arthur Bakker. (2018). Discovery learning: zombie, phoenix, or elephant? Instructional Science, 46, 169–183. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9450-8

article_title: The learning effects of first, second, and third order interventions in a rule-based and open simulation game
citation: Marieke de Wijse-van Heeswijk, Etienne A. J. A. Rouwette, Sander V. Meijerink. (2025). The learning effects of first, second, and third order interventions in a rule-based and open simulation game. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09715-w
title: Scope and distance as new design dimensions explaining learning in simulation games
description: The article introduces scope and distance as concepts new to game science, derived from Achterbergh and Vriens' work on organizations and applied to SG design. The scope dimension "concerns the number of variables in the game on which player can make decisions (the handling space)", and includes both designed and experienced scope. The distance dimension refers to the translation of the real-world challenge to the SG and how each player perceives that distance. Together they constitute the learning environment and influence experienced cognitive load; both must be balanced, since too narrow a scope restricts autonomy while too wide a scope causes alienation, and too much or too little distance respectively alienates players or creates an unsafe learning environment.
requirements: Scope and distance need to be balanced to generate the envisioned learning environment
constraints: A too narrow scope can reduce the ability to deal with gameplay challenges, while a too wide scope can cause alienation; too much distance makes translation of learning outcomes to the real world more difficult, and too small a distance can create an unsafe learning environment
target_learners: professionals in organizational change contexts
participants in analogue simulation games
target_learning_goals: adaptivity to changes in the organization or its context
meaningful connection of game experiences to learning goals
examples: Case study 1 was a rule-based SG with narrow scope and high distance; case study 2 was an open SG with wide scope and low distance
key_sources: Marieke de Wijse-van Heeswijk, Etienne A. J. A. Rouwette, Sander V. Meijerink. (2025). The learning effects of first, second, and third order interventions in a rule-based and open simulation game. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09715-w

article_title: The effects of representational format on learning combinatorics from an interactive computer simulation
citation: Bas Kolloffel, Tessa H. S. Eysink, Ton de Jong, Pascal Wilhelm. (2009). The effects of representational format on learning combinatorics from an interactive computer simulation. Instr Sci 37:503–517. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9056-7
title: Three-pillar schema theory with format-specific emphases and multiple-representation functions
description: The article holds that a complete schema for a domain "rests on three pillars: conceptual knowledge, procedural knowledge, and situational knowledge", acquired through selecting, organizing, and integrating information. It proposes that representational format influences which pillar is emphasized: diagrams were expected to stress conceptual knowledge, arithmetical representations procedural knowledge, and text situational knowledge. Combining formats into multiple representations is assumed to have three additional effects: formats can complement each other, one representation can constrain the interpretation of another, and integrating information from different representations supports deeper understanding.
requirements: Requires that representational formats be informationally equivalent when their effects on schema construction are compared
constraints: The study's results indicate these expected format-to-emphasis mappings are not as straightforward as expected; the data did not allow interpretation in terms of complementing, constraining, and integrating
target_learners: secondary school pupils learning combinatorics and probability theory
target_learning_goals: schema construction spanning conceptual, procedural, and situational knowledge
examples: Five SIMQUEST-built inquiry environments presented informationally equivalent representations of the same combinatorics domain in diagram, arithmetic, text, or combined formats
key_sources: Bas Kolloffel, Tessa H. S. Eysink, Ton de Jong, Pascal Wilhelm. (2009). The effects of representational format on learning combinatorics from an interactive computer simulation. Instr Sci 37:503–517. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9056-7

article_title: Scrum methodology in context-based secondary chemistry classes: effects on students’ achievement and on students’ perceptions of affective and metacognitive dimensions of their learning
citation: Vogelzang, J., Admiraal, W. F., van Driel, J. H. (2021). Scrum methodology in context-based secondary chemistry classes: effects on students' achievement and on students' perceptions of affective and metacognitive dimensions of their learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09554-5
title: Scrum methodology as an educational scaffold: a project-management framework with ceremonies, roles and artefacts that structures planning, monitoring and reflection in complex context-based learning environments
description: Scrum methodology is "a project management framework" from business and industry, restyled for education. It rests on three pillars: "transparency, inspection and adaptation", enacted through ceremonies (stand-up, sprint review, retrospective), roles (product owner, scrum master) and artefacts (product backlog, scrum board with burndown chart, intermediate products). The article describes how its features scaffold three challenges of student-centred learning: sense making, process management and reflection, and it structures a thirteen-step implementation in a context-based chemistry module (Table 1).
requirements: Teachers need professional development to become familiar with the ceremonies, roles and artefacts; experimental teachers attended five sessions of 4 hours explaining, practising, and sharing experiences with Scrum.
constraints: The article notes implementation is challenging for teachers: some reported a straightforward implementation whereas others experienced it as challenging, including organizational issues and some resistance against Scrum methodology.
target_learners: secondary school chemistry students (grade 11)
examples: In the study, teachers acted as product owners providing product backlogs; student teams formulated their own definitions of done and fun, valued tasks in points, planned on Scrum boards, ran stand-ups each lesson, and released intermediate products with formative-assessment reviews each sprint.
key_sources: Vogelzang, J., Admiraal, W. F., van Driel, J. H. (2021). Scrum methodology in context-based secondary chemistry classes: effects on students' achievement and on students' perceptions of affective and metacognitive dimensions of their learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09554-5

article_title: Effects of a literary intervention on teachers’ monologic and dialogic practices and the quality of students’ contributions
citation: Dammert, Y., Gasser, L., & Murphy, P. K. (2026). Effects of a literary intervention on teachers' monologic and dialogic practices and the quality of students' contributions. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09809-z
title: Scaffold dialogic discussions with talk moves and progressively fade teacher control so students assume interpretive authority
description: The article argues that simply limiting instructional control is insufficient; scaffolding—targeted, adaptive, temporary support—is crucial, and "teacher support must not only be responsive to learners' reasoning and argumentation but also be gradually withdrawn as their competence and autonomy develop". Whole-class mini-lessons model dialogic skills that are then applied and refined in small-group discussions, during which control gradually shifts from teachers to students, who increasingly manage turn-taking and assume interpretive authority over the text. This principle underpins the practice shifts the intervention produced.
requirements: Initial explicit instruction and modeling of dialogic skills before independent small-group application
Ongoing teacher scaffolding via talk moves while control is progressively faded
constraints: Even with dialogic elements present, teachers may retain underlying control through turn management and evaluation (overfacilitation), which the study's monologic codes were designed to detect
target_learners: Primary school students in language-arts/literary discussions
examples: Students demonstrated ownership by allocating speaker turns themselves and independently posing questions and introducing new topics.
key_sources: Dammert, Y., Gasser, L., & Murphy, P. K. (2026). Effects of a literary intervention on teachers' monologic and dialogic practices and the quality of students' contributions. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09809-z

article_title: Instruction in creative and argumentative writing: transfer and crossover effects on writing process and text quality
citation: Anouk ten Peze, Tanja Janssen, Gert Rijlaarsdam, Daphne van Weijen. (2024). Instruction in creative and argumentative writing: transfer and crossover effects on writing process and text quality. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09647-3
title: Balance choice with structure and support through scaffolding with fading and transfer of responsibility in creative writing lessons
description: The article recommends balancing freedom and structure when teaching creative writing: tasks should be authentic, novel and exciting, and students choose between parallel open-ended assignments, while "The scaffolding principle was applied to assert the required balance between structure and freedom". Fading — the gradual withdrawal of scaffolding — provided ample idea-generation support early and removed it in later lessons until students worked independently, so that students' responsibility for task performance gradually increased. This operationalizes Van de Pol et al.'s key scaffolding characteristics cited by the article.
requirements: Open target tasks with multiple possible responses and multiple stimuli (models, examples) for compare-and-contrast discovery
Support must actually fade across the lesson series, not remain constant
constraints: The article grounds this in cited prior work (Lasky & Yoon; Liu et al.; Van de Pol et al.); the present study did not independently test the scaffolding component in isolation
target_learners: Upper secondary students with little prior creative writing experience
examples: In the Writing Lab, students could choose between parallel open-ended creative assignments and among story options (e.g., three photos from nine in lesson 6), while support faded from lesson 1 to independent final drafting
key_sources: Anouk ten Peze, Tanja Janssen, Gert Rijlaarsdam, Daphne van Weijen. (2024). Instruction in creative and argumentative writing: transfer and crossover effects on writing process and text quality. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09647-3

article_title: Scanpath analysis of expertise and culture in teacher gaze in real-world classrooms
citation: Nora A. McIntyre & Tom Foulsham. (2018). Scanpath analysis of expertise and culture in teacher gaze in real-world classrooms. Instructional Science 46, 435-455. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-017-9445-x
title: Scanpath theory of gaze as read-out of a cognitive model applied to real-world teacher gaze
description: Scanpath theory holds that a scanpath is "a 'repetitive sequence of saccades and ﬁxations, idiosyncratic to a particular subject [person] and to a particular target pattern'" and that scanpaths reflect "the read-out of the internal representation of pictures, the so-called 'cognitive model'". The article applies this framework to real-world teaching: if expertise and culture shape teachers' cognitive models, expert and same-culture teachers should show more similar gaze sequences. Its string-edit-distance method represents gaze sequences as letter strings over coded gaze targets, preserving order information that aggregated looking-time measures discard, and the study's intra-individual similarity finding is presented as evidence that top-down cognitive models drive real-world classroom gaze.
requirements: Gaze sequences must be coded into discrete, comparable gaze targets so that sequences can be represented as strings and compared via string edit distance
constraints: Scanpaths are event- rather than duration-based, so a duration-based approach could yield a different picture
The study was limited to teacher-centred lesson segments and to attentional and communicative didactic events only
target_learners: secondary school teachers across expertise levels
target_learning_goals: understanding and improving teachers' classroom gaze behaviour and professional expertise
examples: Forty UK and Hong Kong teachers were eye-tracked with Tobii glasses during 10-minute teacher-centred lesson segments, and scanpaths of the first ten coded gaze behaviours within questioning and lecturing episodes were compared using string edit distance similarity scores
key_sources: Nora A. McIntyre & Tom Foulsham. (2018). Scanpath analysis of expertise and culture in teacher gaze in real-world classrooms. Instructional Science 46, 435-455. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-017-9445-x

article_title: Development of legal expertise
citation: Glöckner, A., Towfigh, E., & Traxler, C. (2013). Development of legal expertise. Instructional Science, 41, 989–1007. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-013-9266-5
title: Students should schedule extended breaks at roughly 8-week intervals to counteract motivational drops
description: Based on the finding of a significant motivational drop at week 8, the authors recommend that "Students might therefore consider scheduling time for somewhat more extended breaks in roughly 8-week intervals." This directly addresses the cyclic motivation decrease observed in the data, where performance drops substantially and recovers thereafter.
requirements: Students must be engaged in sustained exam practice over multiple weeks
constraints: The drop was observed in a specific German legal education context with 5-hour mock exams
target_learners: advanced law students preparing for state exams
target_learning_goals: maintaining performance during sustained practice phases
examples: The authors' recommendation follows directly from the regression estimate of a 0.24 grading-point drop at week 8
key_sources: Glöckner, A., Towfigh, E., & Traxler, C. (2013). Development of legal expertise. Instructional Science, 41, 989–1007. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-013-9266-5

article_title: Relations between undergraduates’ self-regulated learning skill mastery during digital training and biology performance
citation: Matthew L. Bernacki, Megan Claire Cogliano, Shelbi L. Kuhlmann, Jenifer Utz, Christy Strong, Jonathan C. Hilpert, Jeffrey A. Greene. (2023). Relations between undergraduates’ self-regulated learning skill mastery during digital training and biology performance. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09356-9
title: Science of Learning to Learn: a three-module digital SRL skill training embedded in undergraduate biology courses
description: A brief digital training program delivered within high-enrollment STEM courses. "Students completed three modules that trained students on enacting cognitive strategies (e.g., self-testing, spacing, self-explanation), improving self-regulated learning (e.g., defining the task, identifying resources, setting goals, monitoring progress), and engaging in behavioral and environmental regulation." Modules were completed at students' own pace over weeks 2–4, took roughly 90–120 minutes, and earned credit amounting to less than 1% of the course grade. Embedded activities doubled as assessments of skill mastery.
requirements: Completion of all three modules and activities for full-fidelity exposure
Delivery within the course's learning management system with completion indicators
constraints: In the original text-based edition, completion rates were low, which the authors cite as motivation for the multimedia redesign
target_learners: Undergraduate biology students, largely first-generation, at a Minority-Serving Institution
target_learning_goals: Task definition, goal setting, planning, and monitoring
Behavioral and environmental regulation including implementation intentions, mental contrasting, and distraction management
examples: In Study 1 the text-and-static-image edition was administered in weeks 2–4 of an anatomy and physiology course; in Study 2 a video-based multimedia edition replaced textual content to improve learning efficiency
key_sources: Matthew L. Bernacki, Megan Claire Cogliano, Shelbi L. Kuhlmann, Jenifer Utz, Christy Strong, Jonathan C. Hilpert, Jeffrey A. Greene. (2023). Relations between undergraduates’ self-regulated learning skill mastery during digital training and biology performance. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09356-9

article_title: How School Racial Climate Creates Opportunity Structures for Belonging: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis
citation: Christy M. Byrd, Alisa Sas, Renata Halls-Gordon, Jacqueline Cerda-Smith, Stella Jackman-Ryan, Jaylene Patterson. (2026). How School Racial Climate Creates Opportunity Structures for Belonging: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10078-4
title: Multidimensional framework of school racial climate: intergroup interactions and ethnic-racial socialization domains
description: The article conceptualizes school racial climate as a multidimensional construct organized in two domains: "Intergroup interactions, which covers dimensions relating to interactions and relationships; and ethnic-racial socialization, which includes dimensions relating to norms, values, policies, and practices." The intergroup interactions domain includes discrimination (personally experienced and general), equal status, and frequency of interactions. The ethnic-racial socialization domain comprises seven content areas: cultural, intercultural competence, critical consciousness, mainstream, color-evasive, and positive interaction socialization, plus commitment to diversity/diversity messaging. The framework centers racialization and systems of oppression rather than treating climate as unidimensionally positive or negative.
requirements: Measurement at the level of student perceptions of school climate rather than objective institutional features
constraints: The dimensions are based on existing literature on student perceptions; scholars note other salient perceptions such as monocentric identity enforcement, silence about race, ethnic-racial composition, and historical context are not covered
target_learners: students in primary, secondary, and postsecondary settings
target_learning_goals: understanding how racialized school environments shape belonging
examples: Figure 1 illustrates how the two domains are hypothesized to relate to belonging through interpersonal, instructional, and institutional opportunity structures
key_sources: Christy M. Byrd, Alisa Sas, Renata Halls-Gordon, Jacqueline Cerda-Smith, Stella Jackman-Ryan, Jaylene Patterson. (2026). How School Racial Climate Creates Opportunity Structures for Belonging: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10078-4

article_title: How School Racial Climate Creates Opportunity Structures for Belonging: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis
citation: Christy M. Byrd, Alisa Sas, Renata Halls-Gordon, Jacqueline Cerda-Smith, Stella Jackman-Ryan, Jaylene Patterson. (2026). How School Racial Climate Creates Opportunity Structures for Belonging: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10078-4
title: School diversity models: clustering climate dimensions into multicultural/pluralist versus colorblind/assimilationist approaches
description: The article groups racial climate dimensions into clusters characterizing how schools approach cultural difference, called school diversity models (SDMs) or diversity approaches. "More multicultural or pluralist approaches characterize schools that celebrate diversity, actively incorporate different cultural groups into the curriculum, and encourage positive interactions across groups," while colorblind or assimilationist approaches de-emphasize, ignore, or punish cultural differences. Culturally relevant pedagogy is treated as another diversity model emphasizing cultural competence, equal status, and critical understanding of power differences. Figure 2 shows a hypothetical clustering of dimensions for three example SDMs.
requirements: SDMs are inferred from patterns across multiple climate dimensions, particularly in policies
constraints: The clustering shown is explicitly hypothetical, illustrating how average dimension values might vary across school types
target_learners: whole school communities including students, teachers, and staff
target_learning_goals: revealing the ideologies that inform a school's policies, practices, and interactions around cultural difference
examples: An assimilationist school might ban ethnic studies courses or prevent students from speaking a non-dominant language; a culturally relevant school would value ethnic studies, home languages, and engagement in cultural communities
key_sources: Christy M. Byrd, Alisa Sas, Renata Halls-Gordon, Jacqueline Cerda-Smith, Stella Jackman-Ryan, Jaylene Patterson. (2026). How School Racial Climate Creates Opportunity Structures for Belonging: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10078-4

article_title: Contemplative Education: A Systematic, Evidence-Based Review of the effect of Meditation Interventions in Schools
citation: Lea Waters, Adam Barsky, Amanda Ridd, Kelly Allen. (2015). Contemplative Education: A Systematic, Evidence-Based Review of the effect of Meditation Interventions in Schools. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-014-9258-2
title: School-Based Meditation Model
description: The School-Based Meditation Model is the review's conceptual framework linking school meditation programmes to three student success outcomes (well-being, social competence, academic achievement) through two mediating mechanisms: improved cognitive functioning and improved emotional regulation. It was built from three research strands: education research linking cognitive function and emotional regulation to outcomes, adult neuroscience linking meditation to relevant brain areas, and contemplative education studies showing students gain these functions. The authors state "The pathways in the School-Based Meditation Model are hypothetical", and it gives rise to two propositions about meditation increasing cognitive functioning and emotional regulation.
requirements: Future youth meditation research including neuroscience measures to test whether meditation affects students' brains as shown in adults
constraints: The pathways are hypothetical; no neuroscience research has been conducted in youth meditation samples, so the adult neuroscience link is described as an educated guess
target_learners: school students across junior, middle and senior schools
examples: Fig. 1 depicts school meditation programs influencing well-being, social competence and academic achievement via improved cognitive functioning and improved emotional regulation
key_sources: Lea Waters, Adam Barsky, Amanda Ridd, Kelly Allen. (2015). Contemplative Education: A Systematic, Evidence-Based Review of the effect of Meditation Interventions in Schools. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-014-9258-2

article_title: Relocating the Locus of Generation: The AI-GLM Framework for Generative Learning in AI-Mediated Mathematics Education
citation: Hoyun Cho. (2026). Relocating the Locus of Generation: The AI-GLM Framework for Generative Learning in AI-Mediated Mathematics Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10210-y
title: Scaffolding–substitution continuum as the principal analytical axis of AI-mediated generative activity
description: The continuum locates any AI use that supports or replaces an existing generative activity between two poles: "AI use falls along a continuum from scaffolding (supporting the learner's own generative activity) to substitution (performing that activity in place of the learner)". Where a use falls is not a fixed property of the tool but a function of task design, instructional context, and teacher guidance, placing the teacher's pedagogical reasoning at the center of whether AI enhances or undermines generative learning. The continuum defines the Partner and Substitute roles but does not encompass the Catalyst role.
requirements: Position on the continuum should be analyzed as a continuous variable, with any descriptive cut point preregistered and accompanied by a sensitivity analysis
constraints: Does not encompass the Catalyst role, which is distinguished by a functional criterion rather than position on the continuum
target_learners: mathematics learners and teachers designing AI-integrated instruction
examples: Role assignment is coded from the task specification and interaction record: a prior learner attempt plus a high learner share of submitted work places an episode near the Partner pole; absence of both places it near the Substitute pole
key_sources: Hoyun Cho. (2026). Relocating the Locus of Generation: The AI-GLM Framework for Generative Learning in AI-Mediated Mathematics Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10210-y

article_title: A Bayesian Network Meta-Analysis to Synthesize the Influence of                     Contexts of Scaffolding Use on Cognitive Outcomes in STEM                     Education
citation: Belland Brian R., Walker Andrew E., Kim Nam Ju. (2017). A Bayesian Network Meta-Analysis to Synthesize the Influence of Contexts of Scaffolding Use on Cognitive Outcomes in STEM Education. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654317723009
title: Scaffolding as contingent support characterized by contingency, intersubjectivity, and transfer of responsibility
description: The article defines scaffolding as "contingent support that structures and highlights the complexity inherent in problem solving, thereby supporting current performance and promoting skill gain." Three key attributes characterize it: contingency, intersubjectivity, and transfer of responsibility. Scaffolding is contingent on dynamic assessment indicating students' current abilities, so support can be faded or added as skill changes; students must recognize successful performance; and scaffolding must engender independent task completion. The review uses this definition to frame its synthesis of scaffolding across problem-centered instructional models in STEM.
requirements: Scaffolding must be contingent on dynamic assessment of students' current abilities
Students need to recognize successful performance on the scaffolded task
Scaffolding needs to engender independent task completion
target_learners: K–12 through adult learners in STEM education
key_sources: Belland Brian R., Walker Andrew E., Kim Nam Ju. (2017). A Bayesian Network Meta-Analysis to Synthesize the Influence of Contexts of Scaffolding Use on Cognitive Outcomes in STEM Education. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654317723009

article_title: Reviewing the Intellectual Structure of the Knowledge Base on Principal Instructional Leadership: An Integrated Bibliometric and Thematic Analysis, 1941–2024
citation: Gurr, David; Karakose, Turgut; Tulubas, Tijen; Polat, Hakan. (2025). Reviewing the Intellectual Structure of the Knowledge Base on Principal Instructional Leadership: An Integrated Bibliometric and Thematic Analysis, 1941-2024. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251403507
title: SciMAT-based integrated bibliometric and thematic analysis of 695 PIL articles from Scopus and Web of Science, 1941-2024
description: A research artifact and method: the study "combines bibliometric performance and thematic analysis of the principal instructional leadership (PIL) research field using SciMAT." The analysis "included 695 articles indexed on two reputable databases, Scopus and Web of Science (WoSCC)" and covered "three periods of analysis between 1941 and 2024," offering a comparative understanding of the thematic evolution of the field.
requirements: Articles indexed in Scopus and Web of Science (WoSCC); SciMAT as the analysis tool
constraints: Coverage limited to articles indexed on the two databases used
target_learners: educational leadership researchers
target_learning_goals: mapping the intellectual structure and thematic evolution of the PIL research field
examples: Three periods of analysis spanning 1941 to 2024 were compared

article_title: The Association Between School Discipline and Self-Control From Preschoolers to High School Students: A Three-Level Meta-Analysis
citation: Li, J. B., Bi, S. S., Willems, Y. E., & Finkenauer, C. (2021). The Association Between School Discipline and Self-Control From Preschoolers to High School Students: A Three-Level Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research, 91(1), 73-111. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654320979160
title: Three-component taxonomy of school discipline: structure, support, and teacher-student relationship
description: The meta-analysis organizes school discipline into three components: "structure, support, and teacher-student relationship". This taxonomy frames how facets of the school environment are hypothesized to relate to individual differences in students' self-control, and it served as the organizing moderator dimension across the 68 synthesized studies, with effect sizes found similar across the three components.
requirements: Studies must operationalize school discipline through one of the three components to be synthesized under the taxonomy
constraints: The taxonomy concerns school discipline as an environmental factor, not disciplinary techniques such as authoritarian or authoritative styles the keywords mention
target_learners: students from preschool to high school
key_sources: Li, J. B., Bi, S. S., Willems, Y. E., & Finkenauer, C. (2021). The Association Between School Discipline and Self-Control From Preschoolers to High School Students: A Three-Level Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research, 91(1), 73-111. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654320979160

article_title: The Association Between School Discipline and Self-Control From Preschoolers to High School Students: A Three-Level Meta-Analysis
citation: Li, J. B., Bi, S. S., Willems, Y. E., & Finkenauer, C. (2021). The Association Between School Discipline and Self-Control From Preschoolers to High School Students: A Three-Level Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research, 91(1), 73-111. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654320979160
title: Attend to school discipline — structure, support, and teacher-student relationships — when aiming to develop students' self-control
description: Because school discipline is consistently associated with self-control across ages and measures, schools seeking to develop students' self-control should treat discipline practices — structure, support, and teacher-student relationships — as a relevant design lever. The article concludes these "findings point to the importance of school discipline associated with individual differences in self-control in students from preschool to high school".
requirements: Discipline practices must be measurable across the three components for schools to monitor their association with self-control
constraints: The evidence is correlational; the article does not establish that changing discipline causally develops self-control
target_learners: students from preschool to high school
examples: The meta-analysis synthesized 68 studies of school discipline and self-control spanning preschool to high school students
key_sources: Li, J. B., Bi, S. S., Willems, Y. E., & Finkenauer, C. (2021). The Association Between School Discipline and Self-Control From Preschoolers to High School Students: A Three-Level Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research, 91(1), 73-111. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654320979160

article_title: Five Educational-Psychology Lenses for Training and Evaluating AI Models
citation: Peng Wang, Fred Paas. (2026). Five Educational-Psychology Lenses for Training and Evaluating AI Models. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10195-8
title: Test prompting supports with fading and perturbation checks before attributing a performance gain to stable model competence
description: The article recommends treating prompting supports such as chain-of-thought and few-shot exemplars as scaffolds whose gains must be validated against scaffold removal. It states: "A useful validity check is the educational analogue of scaffold fading: evaluate performance when intermediate steps are no longer requested, and when prompts are modified to prevent simple template completion." If accuracy collapses under fading, the gain reflects dependence on external structure rather than stable competence.
requirements: Paired evaluation in which a gain attributed to chain-of-thought, retrieval, or tool use is reported alongside a matched run with the support removed
constraints: The article notes it is an open question whether AI models internalize the benefits of scaffolding or merely exploit the temporary crutch
target_learners: AI developers evaluating training interventions
educational psychologists reviewing AI capability claims
target_learning_goals: Distinguishing support-independent competence from scaffold dependence in model performance
examples: The article proposes evaluating chain-of-thought gains with prompts modified to prevent simple template completion, and interpreting persistence under perturbation as evidence of more general solution procedures
key_sources: Peng Wang, Fred Paas. (2026). Five Educational-Psychology Lenses for Training and Evaluating AI Models. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10195-8

article_title: Validity of Early-Grade Screening Tools in the Three Tier (RTI/MTSS) Model: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Literacy, Language, and Mathematics
citation: Keles, S., ten Braak, D., Hagen, Å. M., & Melby-Lervåg, M. (2025). Validity of Early-Grade Screening Tools in the Three Tier (RTI/MTSS) Model: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Literacy, Language, and Mathematics. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10077-5
title: Treat screening as one input in a dynamic, data-informed tier placement process rather than a single gatekeeping assessment
description: The article argues that within the Three Tier model, screening functions as an initial step to flag potential risk, while tier placement is refined over time through teacher judgment, contextual information, and students' responses to intervention. Contemporary models, the authors note, emphasize "the integration of multiple data sources—including universal screening, progress monitoring, and teacher judgment—to guide instructional decisions and tier placement in a dynamic, iterative manner". This framing treats screening as part of a responsive, evidence-based process rather than a static gatekeeping tool.
requirements: Progress monitoring and additional diagnostic assessments to guide movement into more intensive tiers
Teacher judgment and contextual information alongside screening scores
constraints: Screening occurs about three times per year and progress monitoring even monthly, so assessments must be brief and fit for purpose; resource limitations may prevent schools from serving all students who might benefit
target_learners: Children in ECEC through grade 2 in tiered support systems
target_learning_goals: Accurate identification of students at risk and responsive allocation of tiered interventions
examples: The review included studies where screening data informed—but did not necessarily solely determine—tier placement within broader tiered support systems
key_sources: Keles, S., ten Braak, D., Hagen, Å. M., & Melby-Lervåg, M. (2025). Validity of Early-Grade Screening Tools in the Three Tier (RTI/MTSS) Model: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Literacy, Language, and Mathematics. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10077-5

article_title: Facilitating Diagnostic Competences in Higher Education—a Meta-Analysis in Medical and Teacher Education
citation: Olga Chernikova, Nicole Heitzmann, Maximilian Christian Fink, Venance Timothy, Tina Seidel, Frank Fischer, DFG Research group COSIMA. (2020). Facilitating Diagnostic Competences in Higher Education—a Meta-Analysis in Medical and Teacher Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09492-2
title: Scaffolding types arranged on a continuum of self-regulation of problem-solving
description: The article proposes ordering scaffolding techniques by the degrees of freedom they leave the learner: "we suggest locating the scaffolding types on different positions on a scale of self-regulation of problem-solving, with examples located from a rather low level followed by role assignments and prompts with increasing levels of self-regulation potential." Reflection phases and unscaffolded problem-solving sit at the high end. The continuum builds on scaffolding as a temporary shift of control from learner to teacher or advanced peer, and it underpins the meta-analysis's moderator analysis of which scaffolding type fits which knowledge level.
requirements: Classifying a scaffolding intervention requires coding which techniques it realizes (examples, prompts, roles, reflection phases) and the guidance level provided
constraints: The article states that a convincing framework to integrate the different types of scaffolding does not yet exist and offers this classification heuristically
target_learners: higher education learners in medical and teacher education with varying prior professional knowledge
examples: The meta-analysis coded examples, prompts, roles, and reflection phases as distinct instructional support categories and located them on the self-regulation scale.
key_sources: Olga Chernikova, Nicole Heitzmann, Maximilian Christian Fink, Venance Timothy, Tina Seidel, Frank Fischer, DFG Research group COSIMA. (2020). Facilitating Diagnostic Competences in Higher Education—a Meta-Analysis in Medical and Teacher Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09492-2

article_title: Collaboration Scripts – A Conceptual Analysis
citation: Kollar, I., Fischer, F. & Hesse, F.W. (2006). Collaboration Scripts – A Conceptual Analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 18, 159–185. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-006-9007-2
title: Scripted cooperation and structured dyadic learning approaches as prototypical face-to-face collaboration scripts
description: The article's reference base treats scripted cooperation (O'Donnell & Dansereau) and structured dyadic learning environments as prototypical face-to-face collaboration script approaches. These approaches structure dyadic interaction, for example by sequencing cooperative activities and assigning roles, and have been studied for cognitive, social/affective, and metacognitive outcomes of scripted cooperative learning.
requirements: A dyad or small group following the scripted sequence of activities
target_learners: Students learning in dyads or small groups
target_learning_goals: Academic learning, recall, transfer, and metacognitive outcomes

article_title: Scaffolding of learning activities: Aptitude-treatment-interaction effects in math?
citation: Sarah I. Hofer, Frank Reinhold. (2025). Scaffolding of learning activities: Aptitude-treatment-interaction effects in math?. Learning and Instruction 99 (2025) 102177. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102177
title: Expanded scaffolding framework: scaffolds as modifications of learning activities classified by cognitive, motivational, and metacognitive intentions
description: The article proposes an expanded conception of scaffolding that goes beyond providing additional information to include modifications in the implementation of a learning activity itself, such as dynamic instead of static visualizations or performance-adapted task difficulty. It classifies scaffolds by 'scaffolding intentions' — cognitive, motivational, and metacognitive — noting that "these classifications are not supposed to be deterministic" since one scaffold can serve several functions. The framework connects scaffolds to the specific mechanisms underlying established learning activities, guiding which scaffold fits which activity.
requirements: Scaffolds must tap underlying cognitive, motivational, or metacognitive processes required for the learning activity to work as intended
The learning activity and its affordances must first be identified before choosing scaffolds
constraints: Metacognitive scaffolding is defined but was not investigated in the present study
target_learners: 6th-grade secondary school students in mathematics classrooms
target_learning_goals: Conceptual and procedural knowledge of fractions on the number line
examples: Dynamic visualizations as a cognitive information-processing scaffold for learning with analogies; adaptive task difficulty as a motivational scaffold and individualized explanations based on typical mistakes as a cognitive information scaffold during repeated practice
key_sources: Sarah I. Hofer, Frank Reinhold. (2025). Scaffolding of learning activities: Aptitude-treatment-interaction effects in math?. Learning and Instruction 99 (2025) 102177. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102177

article_title: Increasing the use of conceptually-derived strategies in arithmetic: using inversion problems to promote the use of associativity shortcuts
citation: Joanne Eaves, Nina Attridge, Camilla Gilmore. (2018). Increasing the use of conceptually-derived strategies in arithmetic: using inversion problems to promote the use of associativity shortcuts. Learning and Instruction. https://figshare.com/s/230ee9491e0b67d9d3f3
title: SCADS* strategy discovery model attributing shortcut discovery to attentional mechanisms
description: SCADS* (Strategy Change and Discovery Simulation Model) is a computational model "designed to predict when arithmetic strategies are discovered," developed partly from performance patterns on inversion problems. It proposes that on each trial familiar strategies race against alternative strategies; over trials alternatives gain strength and are eventually applied. Attention is "proposed to be the first process required for shortcut discovery": an individual must direct attention to the right-hand side to discover the shortcut. The article applies SCADS* to associativity, suggesting the same attentional mechanisms may be required, and invokes its 'dynamic feature selection' process to explain how salient features become associated with strategy efficiency.
requirements: Attention must be directed to the right-hand side of the problem for shortcut discovery to occur
Alternative strategies must gain strength over repeated trials before application
constraints: The model was developed from inversion problems; its application to associativity is an extension proposed by Robinson & LeFevre (2012), not a direct derivation
target_learners: learners solving multi-term arithmetic problems (children and adults)
target_learning_goals: discovery and use of arithmetic shortcut strategies
examples: The article cites Dubé & Robinson (2010), who primed participants to look left or right at three-term problems and found faster reaction times in the right-prime condition on large inversion problems
key_sources: Joanne Eaves, Nina Attridge, Camilla Gilmore. (2018). Increasing the use of conceptually-derived strategies in arithmetic: using inversion problems to promote the use of associativity shortcuts. Learning and Instruction. https://figshare.com/s/230ee9491e0b67d9d3f3

article_title: The linguistic nature of Children's scientific reasoning
citation: Van de Sande, E., Kleemans, T., Verhoeven, L., & Segers, E. (2019). The linguistic nature of children's scientific reasoning. Learning and Instruction, 62, 20-26. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2019.02.002
title: Scientific Reasoning Inventory (SRI)
description: The SRI is "a paper-and-pencil test that consists of 20 multiple-choice questions with sub-questions (40 items in total)", rooted in five STEM contextual stories with a common question structure covering generating investigable questions, evaluating evidence, designing experiments (CVS), and generating conclusions (syllogistic reasoning). Its structure is based on the Argumentative Sensemaking Measure for middle-school students. The authors present it as an easy-to-administer group assessment that can help teachers tailor enquiry-based education to individual needs.
requirements: 45 minutes administration time; practice items precede CVS items to introduce the line of reasoning
constraints: Measured with paper-and-pencil tasks although the skills also have an active, hands-on nature; conclusion generation was operationalised narrowly as syllogistic reasoning only
target_learners: sixth-grade primary school children
target_learning_goals: scientific reasoning across the enquiry cycle
examples: Administered classroom-wide with a randomly counterbalanced order relative to the academic vocabulary test

article_title: Schema abstraction with productive failure and analogical comparison: Learning designs for far across domain transfer
citation: Jacobson, Michael, Goldwater, Micah, Markauskaite, Lina, Lai, Polly, Kapur, Manu, Roberts, Gareth, & Hilton, Courtney. (2020). Schema abstraction with productive failure and analogical comparison: Learning designs for far across domain transfer. Learning and Instruction, 65, Article number: 101222. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2019.101222
title: Scaffold comparison of two contrasting-domain models during productive failure exploration to foster far across domain transfer
description: When learners explore problems with productive failure, pairing the target-domain model with an analog model from a different domain and explicitly scaffolding learners to write out the models' similarities and differences can foster far across domain transfer without harming domain knowledge. The article grounds this in evidence that "without explicit instruction to write out similarities, learners often will not deeply compare pairs of analog cases", and in its finding that the scaffolded two-model comparison group outperformed the single-model group on far transfer while matching it on knowledge and near transfer.
requirements: Analog models that implement the same underlying principles as the target-domain model
Explicit comparison scaffolds (writing similarities and differences), since unscaffolded comparison is often shallow
Equal instructional time and identical consolidation scripts across conditions
constraints: The far transfer advantage emerged on a posttest-only item; knowledge and near transfer showed no condition differences
The comparison scaffold was tested with ninth-grade students in an all-girls high-achieving school using NetLogo models
target_learners: secondary school science students
target_learning_goals: far across domain transfer of complex systems principles
examples: The Two Models Group used four non-climate NetLogo analog models (Wolf-Sheep Predation, Ants Foraging, Birds Flocking, Forest Fire) alongside the climate models and wrote out model similarities and differences each day

Schema abstraction with productive failure and analogical comparison: Learning designs for far across domain transfer. Learning and Instruction, 65, Article number: 101222. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2019.101222

article_title: 'Bright' and 'slow' pupils in elementary and high school.
citation: Cummins, R. A. (1917). 'Bright' and 'Slow' Pupils in Elementary and High School. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org
title: The Scholastic Quotient (S. Q.), a weighted-mark formula for ranking pupils' scholarship
description: A formula devised by the author to rank pupils from high school record cards, weighting the counts of A, B, C and D marks as 3A+2B+C−D over A+B+C+D to yield a 'Scholastic Quotient'. The article states the quotient "has a range of from minus 1 to plus 3" and that the limits hold whether a pupil has one mark or a thousand and one. It was used to classify the upper quartile as 'Bright' and the lower quartile as 'Slow'.
requirements: Counts of each kind of mark received (A, B, C, D) from pupils' high school record cards
constraints: The formula "assumes an equal weight for all the subjects for which marks are given", which can place a pupil high on the S. Q. while teachers rate the pupil much lower, as in a case where 11 of 15 A's were in physical training
target_learners: elementary and high school pupils at a private college-preparatory school
target_learning_goals: ranking pupils' scholastic standing and predicting success or failure in school subjects
examples: The author ranked 52 early-entering graduates by S. Q. from .75 to 2.49 and split them into quartiles of 13 pupils each
key_sources: Cummins, R. A. (1917). 'Bright' and 'Slow' Pupils in Elementary and High School. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org

article_title: The Binet-Simon Scale and the Yerkes point Scale - A comparative study based on the examination of 100 cases.
citation: Zimmerman, J. (1914). The Binet-Simon Scale and the Yerkes Point Scale: A Comparative Study Based on the Examination of 100 Cases. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu
title: Use divergence between two intelligence scales to trigger supplementary testing before diagnosis
description: The article recommends administering more than one intelligence scale and treating marked divergence between their mental-age results as diagnostic information in itself. Where the scales agree, the examiner may feel considerable certainty; where they diverge, divergence "prevents over hasty conclusions" and "makes clear the need of supplementary tests before a definite diagnosis is made". This turns disagreement between instruments into a safeguard against premature classification.
requirements: Both scales must be administered under favorable, distraction-free conditions with rapport established with the child before testing begins.
constraints: Agreement between scales supports confidence in the mental-age estimate, but the article notes Binet results themselves are not very reliable after age ten.
target_learners: children aged six to sixteen referred for examination of school progress, truancy, or behavior
target_learning_goals: accurate determination of children's mental age for placement and diagnosis decisions
examples: The examiner gave both the Binet-Simon and Point Scale tests at one sitting to 100 children and used the status-difference column to identify cases needing further testing.
key_sources: Zimmerman, J. (1914). The Binet-Simon Scale and the Yerkes Point Scale: A Comparative Study Based on the Examination of 100 Cases. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu

article_title: The worked example effect, the generation effect, and element interactivity.
citation: Chen, Ouhao. (2016). The Worked Example Effect, the Generation Effect, and Element Interactivity. PhD thesis, School of Education, UNSW. https://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/55865
title: Schema theory: schemas as cognitive constructs organising long-term memory
description: The thesis reviews schema theory as the answer to how information is stored in long-term memory. "A schema can be regarded as a cognitive construct which lets us categorize multiple elements of information into a single element based on the way in which the multiple elements are used." Schemas allow similar situations to be treated similarly, are built through assimilation and accommodation, and reduce working memory load by letting many elements be processed as one entity. The thesis traces the theory from Piaget and Bartlett and gives the example of an equation schema for problems like x+5=8.
requirements: Schemas must already exist or be formed through active, constructive acquisition processes for their load-reduction function to operate
target_learners: students learning structured domains such as algebra and geometry
target_learning_goals: schema acquisition that organises knowledge and reduces working memory load
examples: The thesis uses the algebra problem x+5=8: a learner with a schema for it treats all similar problems as one entity and applies the same procedure
key_sources: Chen, Ouhao. (2016). The Worked Example Effect, the Generation Effect, and Element Interactivity. PhD thesis, School of Education, UNSW. https://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/55865

article_title: The contribution of psychology to education.
citation: Thorndike, E. L. (1910). The contribution of psychology to education. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0074512
title: Bidirectional relation: psychology guides education, and school life is a vast laboratory that contributes back to psychology.
description: The article frames the psychology-education relation as two-way. Psychology's laws from simple, specially arranged experiments help interpret and control mental action under schoolroom conditions, while school-room life is a vast laboratory whose thousands of experiments interest pure psychology. Children's arithmetic mistakes, for example, afford material for studies of the action of the laws of association, analysis and selective thinking. The author predicts this journal will report psychological questions answered from educational experience.
requirements: experts in education studying responses to school situations for the sake of practical control, so that results advance knowledge of the mind
constraints: the article states studies of environmental forces on human nature are as yet crude, speculative and often misguided
target_learners: school children
target_learning_goals: understanding mental action and learning under school conditions
examples: The article cites children's arithmetic mistakes as desirable material for studies of association, analysis and selective thinking.
key_sources: Thorndike, E. L. (1910). The contribution of psychology to education. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0070113

article_title: Derivation of a scale to measure abilities in scientific thinking.
citation: Herring, J. P. (1919). Derivation of a scale to measure abilities in scientific thinking. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu
title: Scientific Method Test scale of 33 problems administered to about 500 pupils in each of grades III–VIII
description: The Scientific Method Test is a series of 33 scientific-thinking problems whose scale values are derived in this article. The data came from administering the test to about 500 pupils in each of grades III to VIII, with printed numbers tested of 362, 482, 518, 449, 500 and 498 across grades III to VIII. The final scale (Table X) orders the problems by difficulty, with problem 1 at 1.952 P.E. and problem 32 at 6.415 P.E. above zero, column C carrying values to the nearest tenth of a P.E. multiplied by 10.
requirements: A normal distribution of the abilities studied
Approximately equal variability of large randomly selected groups of pupils
constraints: Per cents near 0% and 100% are distrusted and weighted low in the derivation
Only in the case of an infinite number of randomly selected measures would the curve correspond perfectly to its formula
target_learners: pupils in school grades III to VIII
examples: Table II shows 50 of the 362 third-grade pupils scored 0 and the third-grade median score was 4.362 problems right
231 pupils of the third grade and 381 of the fourth solved problem 1
key_sources: Herring, J. P. (1919). Derivation of a scale to measure abilities in scientific thinking. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu

article_title: The meetings at Mobile, Alabama, February 22-25, 1911.
citation: The Meetings at Mobile, Alabama, February 22-25, 1911. (1911). The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu
title: The school as community center: extending education beyond school age to the entire community
description: The article characterizes the community-center school as a sociological movement in which the school plant serves the whole community that supports it. It reads the movement as "extending education far beyond the limits of school age" and as "sending the entire community to school," a vista of possibilities the reporter finds fascinating yet potentially distracting from routine classroom work.
requirements: A school plant and community that can be put to community service, as in the year-book experiments reported from cities and rural communities.
constraints: The reporter warns the movement can make routine classroom tasks feel prosaic and of minor significance, a danger he says "inheres in much of our reform work in education."
target_learners: entire community members beyond school age
target_learning_goals: community education and civic use of the school plant
examples: The NSSE 1911 year book collected papers on community work in city schools and on the rural school as a community center.

article_title: Understanding instructions.
citation: Marcus, N. (1998). Understanding Instructions. PhD thesis, University of New South Wales. https://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/70247
title: Schema theory as a framework for expert-novice differences in problem solving
description: The thesis adopts schema theory to characterise expert-novice differences: schemas are organised knowledge structures in long-term memory that let solvers chunk information, recognise problem categories, and apply appropriate solution moves. In the problem-solving context, "a schema is defined as a cognitive structure which allows problem solvers to recognise a problem as belonging to a particular category of problems that usually require particular moves to reach a solution." The framework organises the thesis's review of memory, categorisation, and strategy research.
requirements: A large domain-specific knowledge base acquired through extensive experience within the domain
constraints: Expertise is domain-specific; expert problem solvers in one domain are not necessarily good problem solvers in other domains
target_learners: students acquiring domain-specific problem-solving skill
target_learning_goals: schema acquisition and problem categorisation by solution mode
examples: The thesis reviews chess, electronics, algebra, programming, and physics studies showing experts' superior memory for meaningful configurations that disappears with random materials.
key_sources: Marcus, N. (1998). Understanding Instructions. PhD thesis, University of New South Wales. https://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/70247

article_title: Introducing a science interest network model to reveal country differences.
citation: M.S.M. Sachisthal, B.R.J. Jansen, T.T.D. Peetsma, J. Dalege, H.L.J. van der Maas, M.E.J. Raijmakers. (2019). Introducing a Science Interest Network Model to Reveal Country Differences. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000327
title: Science Interest Network Model: interest as a dynamic relational construct
description: The SINM models science interest as a dynamic relational construct rather than a latent score. In it, "affective, behavioral, and cognitive components and related motivational components mutually reinforce one another within the development of interest", and these mutual interactions are hypothesized to underlie interest development. The article operationalizes the model with network analysis over interest-related indicators and applies it to PISA 2015 data from two countries.
requirements: Interest components must be measurable as indicators so their mutual interactions can be estimated in a network
constraints: First empirical test only; the article states future studies are needed to test theoretically important assumptions of the dynamical perspective
target_learners: adolescents
examples: Applied to PISA 2015 data of the Netherlands and Colombia to illuminate the structure of interactions between interest indicators
key_sources: M.S.M. Sachisthal, B.R.J. Jansen, T.T.D. Peetsma, J. Dalege, H.L.J. van der Maas, M.E.J. Raijmakers. (2019). Introducing a Science Interest Network Model to Reveal Country Differences. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000327

article_title: Differences in exam performance between pupils attending selective and non-selective schools mirror the genetic differences between them
citation: Smith-Woolley, E., Pingault, J.-B., Selzam, S., Rimfeld, K., Krapohl, E., von Stumm, S., Asbury, K., Dale, P. S., Young, T., Allen, R., Kovas, Y. & Plomin, R. (2018). Differences in exam performance between pupils attending selective and non-selective schools mirror the genetic differences between them. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0019-8
title: Attend to pupil-selection factors before attributing achievement gaps to school type: schools matter, but the type of school explains under 1% of achievement variance after controls
description: This principle holds that apparent advantages of selective schooling should be attributed to the heritable pupil characteristics used in admission rather than to school value added, since after controls 'the type of school that a child attends explains less than one percent of the individual differences in educational achievement'. The authors caution that 'by finding a small effect of school type, we are not saying schools are unimportant, or that teaching does not work'—schools matter, but school type appears less important.
requirements: Measures of prior achievement, prior ability and family SES, ideally alongside a polygenic score, available before school-type effects are estimated
constraints: The GCSE measure was a composite of only three core subjects (English, mathematics, science); for other subjects school type may have a greater influence
Grammar and private schools are unevenly distributed geographically, which the authors addressed by splitting non-selective schools by area selectivity
target_learners: Secondary-school students in England
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement at the end of compulsory education (GCSE)
examples: The study compared unadjusted GCSE gaps (d = 1.05 vs grammar) with gaps after hierarchical regression controls, showing the advantage fell to betas of 0.03 (grammar) and 0.07 (private)
