article_title: Associations between school enjoyment at age 6 and later educational achievement: evidence from a UK cohort study
citation: Tim T. Morris, Danny Dorling, Neil M. Davies and George Davey Smith. (2021). Associations between school enjoyment at age 6 and later educational achievement: evidence from a UK cohort study. npj Science of Learning 6:18. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00092-w
title: Treat early school enjoyment as a promising, potentially modifiable intervention target and early indicator of pupils needing educational support
description: The article argues that because school enjoyment is "potentially more modi ﬁable than socioeconomic factors" it "potentially represents a promising intervention target for improving educational outcomes". It suggests a simple measure of school enjoyment at an early age may have long-term predictive value for identifying children who may need greater educational support, and that early schooling may be the most effective period for interventions since positive emotional factors decline from childhood to adolescence.
requirements: School-based interventions capable of promoting positive emotions such as enjoyment, which previous studies have demonstrated
constraints: The article explicitly states these findings should not be taken as evidence that improving school enjoyment will improve educational outcomes; replication in other settings and at other ages is required

Observational data do not allow causal evidence; lack of enjoyment may arise from health problems or social, emotional and behavioural difficulties, where upstream interventions may be more beneficial
target_learners: Primary school children (around age 6)
target_learning_goals: Educational achievement at the end of compulsory schooling
examples: The study measured school enjoyment with two questionnaires at ages 6 and 6.5 in the ALSPAC cohort and linked responses to GCSE results in the UK National Pupil Database
key_sources: Tim T. Morris, Danny Dorling, Neil M. Davies and George Davey Smith. (2021). Associations between school enjoyment at age 6 and later educational achievement: evidence from a UK cohort study. npj Science of Learning 6:18. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00092-w

article_title: Statistical learning occurs during practice while high-order rule learning during rest period
citation: Romain Quentin, Lison Fanuel, Mariann Kiss, Marine Vernet, Teodóra Vékony, Karolina Janacsek, Leonardo G. Cohen and Dezso Nemeth. (2021). Statistical learning occurs during practice while high-order rule learning during rest period. npj Science of Learning 6:14. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00093-9
title: Design training so that rest periods follow practice when high-order rule consolidation is the goal, since different learning subcomponents develop at different times
description: The article's findings motivate training and rehabilitation designs that exploit short rest periods: because high-order rule learning increased during rest while statistical learning developed during practice, schedules alternating practice and rest engage different learning mechanisms than continuous practice. The authors frame the work as relevant "for developing new training and neurorehabilitation strategies in healthy and patient populations" and state that "statistical learning occurs only during practice and high-order rule learning occurs only during breaks."
requirements: Alternating practice blocks with short rest periods, as in the experiments where participants could take a short break after each block
constraints: The general skill offline gain could not be firmly separated from fatigue release; high-order rule learning required many trials or sessions to become visible
target_learners: healthy and patient populations in skill training and neurorehabilitation
target_learning_goals: procedural and sequence skill acquisition, including statistical and high-order rule learning
examples: In the experiments, after each block participants saw speed and accuracy feedback and could take a short break before starting the next block by pressing a button
key_sources: Romain Quentin, Lison Fanuel, Mariann Kiss, Marine Vernet, Teodóra Vékony, Karolina Janacsek, Leonardo G. Cohen and Dezso Nemeth. (2021). article_title: A rodent obstacle course procedure controls delivery of enrichment and enhances complex cognitive functions
citation: Gattas, S., Collett, H. A., Huff, A. E., Creighton, S. D., Weber, S. E., Buckhalter, S. S., Manning, S. A., Ryait, H. S., McNaughton, B. L., & Winters, B. D. (2022). A rodent obstacle course procedure controls delivery of enrichment and enhances complex cognition. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00134-x
title: Improved schema formation as an explanatory account of OC-mediated memory enhancements
description: The authors propose that enrichment benefits, and OC effects in particular, "could be explained at least partly by improved schema formation". Schema formation is described as "a process reliant on semanticization and abstraction of experiences and generation of internal representations which are categorically organized", which could allow items consistent with existing memories to be integrated into long-term memory more rapidly. The OC experience requires rich interactions with a wide variety of object-based obstacles, which the authors suggest may facilitate the establishment of object schemas, giving OC animals more highly diversified internal representations of the world.
requirements: further testing is needed: the authors state this possibility, as well as alternatives involving boosting of neuroplasticity mechanisms, warrants subsequent studies
constraints: The mechanisms by which OC training achieves superior effects cannot be delineated from the present study
target_learners: rodent models (mice) in enrichment research; proposed relevance to behavioral mapping between rodents and humans
target_learning_goals: rapid encoding and consolidation of new information into long-term memory; categorization and generalization
examples: OC mice performed object category recognition at a 1-h delay without the exemplar preexposure period previously reported as necessary, which the authors read as consistent with improved schema formation

A rodent obstacle course procedure controls delivery of enrichment and enhances complex cognition. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00134-x

article_title: Math items about real-world content lower test-scores of students from families with low socioeconomic status
citation: Marjolein Muskens, Willem E. Frankenhuiss & Lex Borghans. (2024). Math items about real-world content lower test-scores of students from families with low socioeconomic status. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00228-8
title: Scarcity mindset and attention capture as an explanatory account of content-induced performance bias
description: The article adopts a scarcity-mindset account, in which "poverty capturing attention and/or generating intrusive and distracting thoughts, reducing an individual 'sc o g n i t i v e resources", with financially salient content in particular causing "attention capture" that interferes with immediate and later performance. The authors apply this account to their finding that money, food, and social-relationship content hinders low-SES performance, assuming attention capture extends to content associated with negative thoughts and feelings. The account is presented as an interpretation aligned with prior monetary-salience findings, not as tested in this study.
requirements: The account is invoked as an interpretation of observational patterns; the article states experimental research is needed to test the mechanisms.
constraints: The article notes its data are observational, so attention capture is a proposed, not demonstrated, mechanism; spill-over evidence is attributed to a prior study by Duquennois.
target_learners: low-SES students in grades 4 and 8 taking standardized math tests
target_learning_goals: fair and unbiased measurement of mathematics achievement
examples: The authors reference a prior study using TIMSS and other datasets showing low-SES students perform worse on money-content items, with spill-over effects on subsequent non-financial items attributed to attention capture.
key_sources: Marjolein Muskens, Willem E. Frankenhuiss & Lex Borghans. (2024). Math items about real-world content lower test-scores of students from families with low socioeconomic status. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00228-8

article_title: Interplay of socioeconomic status, cognition, and school performance in the ABCD sample
citation: Langensee, L., Rumetshofer, T. & Mårtensson, J. (2024). Interplay of socioeconomic status, cognition, and school performance in the ABCD sample. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00233-x
title: Educators and policy makers should work to ensure that academic success chances are not determined by parental wealth and education, and should provide learning resources outside the home where home stimulation is limited
description: The article closes with a design recommendation for learning environments: teachers, policy makers, and educational researchers are called upon "to continue to strive towards creating school environments in which a child's chances at distinguishing themselves academically are controlled entirely by them." Because the study shows SES gradients in self-reported grades that persist over time and across levels of cognitive capacity, it recommends that anyone involved in children's schooling be mindful of possible systematic socioeconomic disadvantage and create optimal learning conditions suited to each child's situation.
requirements: Awareness of possible systematic socioeconomic disadvantage among those involved in children's schooling
constraints: The supporting evidence is observational, from self-reported grades, in a sample skewed toward higher-SES families, limiting conclusions about disadvantaged children.
target_learners: Children and adolescents in primary and secondary school, particularly those from socioeconomically disadvantaged backgrounds
target_learning_goals: Equitable academic achievement regardless of socioeconomic background
examples: The authors recommend that "resources need to be readily available outside children's homes and children should actively be encouraged to take advantage of them" where home intellectual stimulation may be limited.

The study used SCCT to motivate hypotheses that self-efficacy and interest would independently predict STEM career choice; results partially contradicted it, since self-efficacy did not predict independently.

article_title: The Future of Adaptive Learning: Does the Crowd Hold the Key?
citation: Heffernan, N. T., Ostrow, K. S., Kelly, K., Selent, D., Van Inwegen, E. G., Xiong, X., & Williams, J. J. (2016). The Future of Adaptive Learning: Does the Crowd Hold the Key? Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:615–644. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0094-z

description: Because learners are 'experts-in-training', the article argues learnersourcing is acceptable only if the requested task is simplified: "By scaling down the task requested of each learner, the process of learnersourcing becomes much more viable." ASSISTments does this by "relabeling feedback creation as 'self-explanation'" and diluting content creation into elements common to traditional mathematics homework, such as showing work on nightly problems.

constraints: Complexity of self-explanations varies drastically with content, e.g., perimeter problems versus logarithmic functions

target_learning_goals: Self-explanation and producing worked examples that benefit future students

article_title: Integrating Generative AI into Programming Education: Student Perceptions and the Challenge of Correcting AI Errors
citation: Kohen-Vacs, D., Usher, M., & Jansen, M. (2025). Integrating Generative AI into Programming Education: Student Perceptions and the Challenge of Correcting AI Errors. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00496-4
title: Pair instructor-designed programming tasks with LLM-generated debugging challenges in a scaffolded curriculum
description: This principle holds that programming education should combine AI-augmented learning with traditional instruction so students build both fluency and error-correction skill. The article states that "pairing instructor-designed tasks with LLM-generated debugging challenges can help students gradually build their analytical and error-correction abilities," alongside reflective exercises and critical evaluation of AI outputs. It arises directly from the finding that students underperformed on LLM-generated debugging tasks in high-stakes exams without prior training.
requirements: Programming curricula must include both traditional instructor-designed coding exercises and LLM-generated debugging tasks so that core skills such as debugging, logic development, and algorithmic thinking are preserved alongside AI-augmented practice.
constraints: Study 2 was conducted in high-stakes summative exams without prior instruction or training; the article notes task origin was confounded with distinct cognitive demands (debugging versus algorithmic development).
target_learners: Undergraduate students in programming-related courses
target_learning_goals: Debugging and error correction of AI-generated code
Algorithmic thinking and foundational programming competencies
examples: The Study 2 exams included flawed Java code generated by an LLM, such as an RSA implementation with intentionally embedded errors, alongside instructor-designed tasks like implementing a modular inverse method and a Feistel network.

description: Scholar is presented as one of the first AI-based teaching systems in a field the article dates as some 50 years old. It was "based on symbolic AI rather than machine learning, and had the rudimentary pedagogy of asking and answering questions about geographical facts and relationships" (Carbonell, 1970). The article uses Scholar as the baseline against which progress along its seven dimensions is traced.

citation: Uçar, S.-Ş., Aldabe, I., Aranberri, N., & Arruarte, A. (2024). Exploring Automatic Readability Assessment for Science Documents within a Multilingual Educational Context. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00393-2
title: Scientific discourse differs cognitively and linguistically from general-domain text, complicating generic readability assessment
description: The article draws on prior characterizations of scientific texts to argue that generic ARA approaches, developed mostly on general-domain corpora, may not transfer to science textbooks. Scientific texts are said to have 'a more rigid structure, a higher presence of terminology' and be 'consistently formal', and their informative-argumentative core is harder to understand than narrative text despite simpler syntax, because they relate complex events requiring higher abstraction and linguistic competence. This motivates testing domain-specific corpora and models.
requirements: Readability assessment for science classrooms should account for genre, type and topic rather than relying on generic approaches
constraints: Most readability studies of science textbooks have assumed the accuracy of existing approaches with little investigation of performance in this distinct scenario

target_learning_goals: selecting science texts of appropriate difficulty for disciplinary learning
examples: The article notes Ehara (2022) found 10%-30% of scientific texts are not readable to intermediate ESL learners

title: ScratchJr-based CAL curriculum with a four-hour teacher professional development session
description: The CAL-ScratchJr curriculum is a free, screen-based early-childhood coding curriculum of 24 sessions of 45 minutes each, built on the ScratchJr block platform, which "enables the creation of interactive animated stories using basic and more sophisticated programming commands" without depending on formal literacy. title: SCY pedagogical scenarios: reusable blueprints assembled from activity-ELO-tool triplets, LASs, and scenario templates
description: Pedagogical scenarios are the SCY project's formalized instructional design method for building technology-enhanced learning environments. Four services occupy the screen corners: an awareness service reporting on peer presence, an ePortfolio service for saving ELOs and requesting teacher assessment, a repository service for saving, searching, and sharing ELOs, and a mission map for navigation. title: SCY design approach relative to ADDIE: collapsed phases with scenario selection early and infrastructure-driven implementation
description: The article positions the SCY instructional design approach against traditional sequential ISD models labeled ADDIE (Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, Evaluation). It states that "All components of the ADDIE model are incorporated in the SCY approach, with defining learning goals in the beginning and implementation at the end," but with different emphases and collapsed steps: an existing pedagogical scenario is chosen quickly, learning goals are completed early partly from what the scenario offers, parts of design, development, and implementation are done together, the infrastructure takes care of implementation, and evaluation is realized formatively through rapid prototyping and summatively through ongoing experimental and field studies. The approach is characterized as providing templates or blueprints that designers adapt and fill with content, resembling ADAPT IT and the SimQuest authoring approach at a more detailed level.

title: Super Cyber Kids framework: a 30-field matrix crossing adapted NIST dimensions with six child cybersecurity categories
description: The framework organizes children's cybersecurity skills in a matrix whose X-axis holds the five adapted NIST dimensions (Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover) and whose Y-axis holds six categories extracted from the literature: malicious code, frauds, abusive content, preventing technologies, data privacy and awareness, and safety. The article states: "The final result is a matrix-shaped framework with 30 fields comprising the NIST dimensions (X-axis) and the categories extracted from the literature (Y-axis)." Each field contains actionable skills formulated as 'Children can…' statements, extracted from 39 studies, five games, and three platforms, and validated by professionals. It is intended to give practitioners, parents, and curriculum designers a foundation for comprehensive protection of children aged 8–13.

constraints: The adapted NIST dimensions are treated as approximate taxonomies, not exact mappings

target_learning_goals: Cybersecurity awareness and protective online behavior across threats such as malicious code, fraud, abusive content, and privacy risks

description: The study's instructional element was a two-week computational thinking module in a science teaching methods course in which participants learned block-based programming in Scratch, created and tested a water filter, and coded science simulations analogous to the water filter. Tasks followed the computational thinking subskills: participants "decomposed the problem by coding the outcomes of using different purification media, applied abstraction skills by connecting code blocks to science concepts", designed algorithmic steps, applied patterns, and debugged code errors. citation: Automatic Summary Assessment for Intelligent Tutoring Systems. (2009). Preprint submitted to Elsevier February 26, 2009
title: Scaffolding-based pedagogical model with adaptive feedback grounded in Zone of Proximal Development
description: The article's pedagogical model is "a 'scaffolding' model which is able to give students adaptive feedbacks based on their previous learning experience". It draws on Vygotsky's socio-cultural theory and the Zone of Proximal Development, where scaffolding provides "individualized support based on the learner's ZPD". A dynamically updated student model stores knowledge skill levels and learning records, and the system adapts its interactivity based on performance in practice exercises. The authors argue that combining adaptive feedback with the scaffolding teaching strategy provides a better learning experience.

description: The script theory of guidance (SToG) for CSCL, built upon dynamic memory theory, distinguishes between internal and external collaboration scripts. constraints: the effect of the additional structure diminishes over time after multiple practice occasions
target_learners: first-year higher education students
examples: The study assigned 125 first-year students across control, request, content, and combination conditions over three wiki abstract-writing cycles.

article_title: FLoRA: An advanced AI-powered engine to facilitate hybrid human-AI regulated learning
citation: Li, X., Li, T., Yan, L., Li, Y., Zhao, L., Raković, M., Molenaar, I., Gašević, D., & Fan, Y. (2025). FLoRA: An Advanced AI-Powered Engine to Facilitate Hybrid Human-AI Regulated Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.07362
title: Design scaffolding that incorporates both real-time SRL processes and evolving learning conditions
description: The article recommends incorporating both learners' real-time SRL processes and evolving conditions in scaffold design. Learning analytics detect dynamic conditions (e.g., time awareness via trace data) and static conditions (e.g., domain knowledge via pre-task surveys), which are converted into predefined statements added to the GenAI prompt. This allows scaffolds to adapt not only to learners' real-time SRL processes but also to dynamic learning conditions that shift throughout the task.
requirements: Real-time trace data collection
Pre-task surveys or assessments to establish static learning conditions
target_learners: university students
K-12 students

article_title: Student perceptions of technology-enhanced simulation resources in laparoscopic training: a scoping review and implications for surgical instrumentation.

The 11 studies span Asia, Europe, Latin America, the Caribbean and the Middle East, with experimental, quasi-experimental, cross-sectional, observational, mixed-methods and review designs, covering VR, VR simulators, portable endo-trainers, low-cost trainers, online surgical curricula, training systems, laparoscopic simulation and robotic surgery learning.

examples: Included studies include a randomized controlled trial of home-based portable endo-trainer training in Switzerland, a systematic review of online surgical curricula for medical students, and the single direct quasi-experimental VR study with Colombian Surgical Instrumentation students.

article_title: Diabetes knowledge of nurses in sub-Saharan Africa: a scoping review.
citation: Nyalapa McDonald William; Gombachika Belinda Thandizo. (2025). Diabetes knowledge of nurses in sub-Saharan Africa: a scoping review. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2025-106689
title: Scoping review framework mapping nurses' diabetes knowledge, care knowledge, and knowledge-acquisition factors in SSA hospitals
description: The review organises the literature around three review questions: nurses' knowledge of diabetes, nurses' knowledge of diabetes management or care, and factors hindering or promoting knowledge acquisition. It applied the Arksey and O'Malley scoping methodological framework, which "included the following steps: identifying the research question; searching for relevant studies; selecting studies; charting data; and collating, summarising and reporting the results." Primary outcomes covered knowledge of diabetes types, pathophysiology, diagnostics, medications and management; secondary outcomes covered personal, organisational and support-system barriers and facilitators.
requirements: Studies addressing nurses involved in care for adults with diabetes in hospital settings in SSA, published in English from 2000 to 2024.
constraints: The protocol was not pre-registered; studies were not formally assessed for quality; only English-language studies were included, possibly missing Francophone Africa.
target_learners: Nurses in hospital settings in sub-Saharan Africa
target_learning_goals: Diabetes knowledge for care and patient education
examples: The review screened 2974 retrieved records and included 20 studies conducted across twelve SSA countries.

article_title: Comparing the seminar-case learning and lecture-based learning models in medical education: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
citation: Lou Jicheng, Guo Feng. (2025). Comparing the seminar-case learning and lecture-based learning models in medical education: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07041-w
title: The seminar-case learning (SCL) model as a combination of seminar learning and case-based learning
description: The SCL model is a teaching approach that "is a combination of seminar and case-based learning." It integrates "the efficient communication of seminar learning and the clinical thinking of case-based learning." In practice, a teacher selects a typical authentic case and distributes anonymized patient information to students before class. Students independently prepare responses, then during class the teacher gives a brief lecture, introduces the case, and facilitates group analysis and open seminar discussion.
requirements: Teachers require extensive medical knowledge, strong teaching skills, and experience to facilitate discussions and manage classroom interactions.
constraints: Double-blinding is not possible because teachers must implement different teaching methods across conditions.
target_learners: Undergraduate medical students
Postgraduate medical students
examples: Teachers send anonymized patient information to students via a chat software group prior to class, and students independently prepare responses to teacher-posed questions.

article_title: Influences of school climate on emotional health and academic achievement of school-going adolescents in India: a systematic review.
citation: Podiya Jayalaxmi Kaniyagundi, Navaneetham Janardhana, Bhola Poornima. (2025). Influences of school climate on emotional health and academic achievement of school-going adolescents in India: a systematic review. BMC Public Health 25, 54. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-024-21268-0
title: School climate as a multidimensional collective experience shaping adolescent emotional health and academic achievement
description: The review adopts the National School Climate Center definition of school climate as "a collective experience of students, parents, teachers, and other staff, shaped by rules, goals, ethics, interaction patterns, methods of teaching and learning, and institutional structures" guaranteeing social, emotional, and physical safety. It organizes the eleven included studies around climate components—safety, relationships, peer support, teaching methodology, and institutional environment—and maps their interconnected influence on emotional health and academic outcomes (Fig. 2).
requirements: Understanding the perspectives of all stakeholders—teachers, students, parents, administrators, and staff—is essential, since climate aspects can be determined by the perceptions of school teachers and administrators
constraints: The review notes the concept includes cultural aspects, values, available resources, and social networks, and that few Indian studies have examined both outcome domains together
target_learners: school-going adolescents aged 13–16 in Indian secondary schools (grades 8–10)

article_title: Nurse Competency in Providing Spiritual Care and Associated Influencing Factors: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

title: Spiritual Care Competence Scale (SCCS) and its Chinese version
description: The SCCS, translated and revised by Van Leeuwen et al. (2009) from the Dutch version, evaluates the spiritual care competence of clinical nurses. The original has "six dimensions" — assessment and implementation, professional development and quality improvement, support, referral, spiritual attitude towards patients, and communication — with 27 items scored on a five-level Likert method (total 27–110). The Chinese version (Wei et al. 2017) has 22 items, total 22–110, Cronbach's α 0.974.
requirements: Included studies must explicitly use the SCCS scale, per the review's inclusion criteria
constraints: Cronbach's alpha of the original scale's dimensions ranged from 0.56 to 0.82, per the article
target_learners: working nurses

The review reports that "a questionnaire with twenty questions was created and designed to be completed by a twenty-minute telephone interview", and that after a pilot project the final survey contained twenty-three questions taking about fifteen minutes. Respondents were asked whether the course resulted in increased teaching of EBM concepts and about methods used on returning to their institutions.

article_title: A scoping review of medical education research in family medicine.
citation: Webster F, Krueger P, MacDonald H, Archibald D, Telner D, Bytautas J, Whitehead C. (2015). A scoping review of medical education research in family medicine. BMC Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4407512/
title: Scoping review methodology (Arksey and O'Malley framework, advanced by Levac et al.)
description: The review employed a scoping review approach designed to 'map' literature in a particular area, illuminating key concepts and main sources and types of evidence. The authors used "the methodologically rigorous scoping review approach proposed by Arksey and O'Malley and advanced by Levac, Colquhoun, and O'Brien", involving five stages: identifying research questions, identifying relevant studies, study selection, charting the data, and collating, summarizing and reporting results. Unlike systematic reviews, it does not explicitly aim to assess study quality but can identify research gaps.
requirements: Five-stage process: research questions, relevant studies, study selection, data charting, and collating/summarizing/reporting
constraints: Does not explicitly aim to assess the quality of studies; suited to complex topics not extensively reviewed with many study designs
target_learners: education researchers conducting literature reviews
target_learning_goals: mapping the state of a research field and identifying gaps
examples: Applied here to 817 full-text articles screened from 2002 to 2012, yielding 624 included articles from 40 countries

article_title: Science Learning Cycle Method to Enhance the Conceptual Understanding and the Learning Independence on Physics Learning
citation: Dwi Sulisworo, Novitasari Sutadi. (2017). Science Learning Cycle Method to Enhance the Conceptual Understanding and the Learning Independence on Physics Learning. International Journal of Evaluation and Research in Education (IJERE), 6(1). http://iaesjournal.com/online/index.php/IJERE
title: Science Learning Cycle (SLC) model with seven stages of investigation
description: SLC is a learning approach that "use science literature including reflection journals, class notes, the inquiry data, and other artifacts of learning that reflect the stages of a scientific investigation", represented through discussion between group roles. It consists of three interconnected components — organizing the science record, role on literacy cycles, and student-made artifacts — and proceeds through seven stages: questions, prediction, planning, observation, conclusions, new questions or ideas, and conclusion journal. The article applies it in grade-11 physics on Direct Current Electricity.

Learning instruments including syllabus, lesson plan, and student worksheet aligned to national competency standards
constraints: The article notes responsibilities of each role should be adjusted to the ability development of each student, since not all students have the same ability
target_learners: secondary vocational school students, grade 11

examples: In the study, treatment-group students moved through question, prediction, planning, observation, conclusion, new idea, and journal-writing stages, including preparing simple electric circuits and presenting discussion results

citation: Jitendra, A. K., Harwell, M. R., Dupuis, D. N., & Karl, S. R. (2017). title: Schema-based instruction (SBI) for proportional reasoning
description: SBI is an instructional approach rooted in schema theory and cognitive models of mathematical problem solving, aimed at improving learning of ratios and proportional relationships. Its components are "activation of the mathematical structure of problems," representation of information using diagrams, development of procedural flexibility through selection of appropriate solution strategies, and problem solving and metacognitive strategy instruction. It integrates features such as explicit and systematic instruction, scaffolding with guided questions, corrective feedback, and frequent cumulative review, and was delivered here as two replacement units on Ratio/Proportion and Percent.

constraints: In this study the intervention ran six weeks of daily instruction, below the 12-week criterion recommended in best evidence syntheses, and percent effects were not sustained at delayed posttest

target_learning_goals: Proportional problem solving across ratio, proportion, and percent topics
examples: Teachers implemented two replacement units embedding SBI components in seventh-grade ratio, proportion, and percent instruction after an intensive 2-day (16 hr) professional development training

article_title: Examining the Effectiveness of Pre-Reading Strategies on Saudi EFL College Students' Reading Comprehension
citation: Hana S. S. Al Rasheed. (2014). Examining the Effectiveness of Pre-reading Strategies on Saudi EFL College Students' Reading Comprehension. English Language Teaching, 7(11). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n11p79
title: Schema theory: comprehension as an interaction between the reader's background knowledge and the text
description: Schema theory holds that comprehending a text is "an interactive process between the reader's background knowledge and the text": readers combine pre-existent knowledge organized in long-term memory with the information in the text. The article uses it as the theoretical framework for pre-reading strategies, which aim both at activating prior knowledge and constructing relevant schemata. It distinguishes formal schemata (knowledge of discourse-level forms) from content schemata (the substance conveyed in the text).
requirements: A message is easily comprehended only if the reader can activate or construct a schema that gives a good account of the objects and events described
constraints: For nonnative readers, some content schema does not exist, and the same concepts may carry other interpretations in the native language, which can lead to misunderstanding
target_learners: EFL college students
examples: The article's pre-questioning and vocabulary pre-teaching treatments were designed to activate students' prior knowledge before reading four English passages

article_title: Expediency of Study of the Scientists' Biographies in Physics Course

description: The article defines a "scientist's image" as a three-component construct used to structure biographic material for physics teaching. As printed, "Biographical data, scientific achievements and character traits are the components of “scientist's image”" (Figure 1). Scientific achievements are further broken into reasons prompting the study, the method of solving the problem, and difficulties of scientific research. The framework guides teachers in selecting and presenting biography content, illustrated by a full example of Maria Skłodowska-Curie.

constraints: Not every scientist can be covered in the physics course; edification of opinions and life facts is the main criterion for selection

examples: The article presents Maria Skłodowska-Curie's biography organised by the three components: biographical data, scientific achievements (double Nobel laureate), and character traits (refusing to patent radium)

article_title: Implementation of Research-Based ESL Strategies with Lower Grade Middle School ELLs in the Science Classroom: Findings from an Experimental Study
citation: Irby, B. J., Lara-Alecio, R., Tong, F., Guerrero, C., Sutton-Jones, K. L., & Abdelrahman, N. (2018). article_title: Moderators of School Intervention Outcomes for Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder
citation: Lopata, C., Donnelly, J. P., Thomeer, M. L., Rodgers, J. D., Lodi-Smith, J., Booth, A. J., & Volker, M. A. (2020). Moderators of School Intervention Outcomes for Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder. Journal of Abnormal Child Psychology, 48, 1105-1114. https://link.springer.com/journal/10802
title: schoolMAX comprehensive school intervention
description: schoolMAX is a manualized, school-staff delivered intervention for elementary children with ASD without ID consisting of "social skills groups (SSGs), emotion recognition instruction, therapeutic activities (TAs), a behavioral reinforcement system (Individual Daily Note [IDN]), and parent training (PT)". It uses cognitive and behavioral strategies to teach and reinforce social-cognitive understanding and social skills. Components were delivered by different educational team members, with SSGs 2-3 times weekly, computer-based emotion recognition instruction using Mind Reading software, cooperative therapeutic activities with peers, a daily point-based reinforcement system with home rewards, and monthly parent training. Overall implementation fidelity was high (M=96.0%).

constraints: Delivered and tested with children with ASD without intellectual disability, ages 6-12, in public elementary schools

examples: In the cluster RCT, 17 schools (52 children) received schoolMAX and 18 schools (51 children) received services-as-usual, with fidelity M=96.0% (range 93.4%-98.8%) versus M=2.6% intervention elements in SAU schools

citation: Li-Ying Liu, Meng-Tzu Cheng. (2015). Interactive Projector as an Interactive Teaching Tool in the Classroom: Evaluating Teaching Efficiency and Interactivity. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 14(2). http://www.tojet.net/

citation: Lina S. Calucag. (2016). Divergence of Scientific Heuristic Method and Direct Algebraic Instruction. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.3. https://www.iiste.org
title: Scientific heuristic method as controlled-discovery teaching
description: The scientific heuristic method is a mathematics teaching approach the article contrasts with direct instruction, in which mathematics appears as a finished body of knowledge. It is described as "concerned with those of controlled discoveries", where learning arises from students' reactions to situations and assumptions are scrutinized as further realities are revealed. The teacher acts as facilitator and participant-guide, creating an environment where students inquire and discuss freely, and students proceed at their own pace.
requirements: A teacher who facilitates rather than acts as the authority, creating situations where free discussion takes place among students
Practice tasks given after the lesson so students apply what they learned
constraints: The study applied it only to selected college algebra topics (real numbers, sets, linear equations, factoring, inequalities, rational expressions) with AMA International University-Bahrain freshmen
target_learners: freshmen college algebra students
examples: Over twelve sessions the experimental class was taught real numbers, sets, linear equations in one variable, factoring of quadratic polynomials, inequalities, and operations with rational algebraic expressions via controlled discovery techniques
key_sources: Lina S. Calucag. (2016). Divergence of Scientific Heuristic Method and Direct Algebraic Instruction. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.3. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1089794

article_title: The Effect of In-Service Training of Computer Science Teachers on Scratch Programming Language Skills Using an Electronic Learning Platform on Programming Skills and the Attitudes towards Teaching Programming
citation: Ahmed Alkaria, Riyadh Alhassan. (2017). The Effect of In-service Training of Computer Science Teachers on Scratch Programming Language Skills Using an Electronic Learning Platform on Programming Skills and the Attitudes towards Teaching Programming. Journal of Education and Training Studies, 5(11). https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v5i11.2608
title: Scratch as a beginner-friendly block-based programming environment for teacher training
description: Scratch is described as "a simple programming environment designed primarily for beginners" developed by the Lifelong Kindergarten group at MIT's Media Lab, using "graphical objects instead of the complex codes" of other languages. The article presents it as suited to training teachers who lack prior programming preparation, letting users create games and interactive stories while learning concepts such as loops, conditionals, coordinates, and variables.
requirements: Teachers need training on modern programming languages not covered in their preparation programs
constraints: The article notes complexity of general programming languages has hindered integration at lower school levels, which Scratch addresses
target_learners: beginners including children and adults inexperienced in programming
middle school computer science teachers
examples: The study trained in-service teachers on a Scratch unit from the third intermediate grade computer curriculum

The Effect of In-service Training of Computer Science Teachers on Scratch Programming Language Skills Using an Electronic Learning Platform on Programming Skills and the Attitudes towards Teaching Programming. article_title: The Effects of Arts-Integrated Instruction on Students' Memory for Science Content: Results from a Randomized Control Trial Study
citation: Mariale M. Hardiman, Ranjini Mahinda JohnBull, Deborah Carran. (2017). The Effects of Arts-Integrated Instruction on Students' Memory for Science Content: Results from a Randomized Control Trial Study. Paper presented at the annual meeting of the American Educational Research Association. https://www.aera.net
title: Scripted matched science unit pairs with curriculum-based assessments for arts-integrated and conventional instruction
description: The research team developed four pairs of matched science units (Astronomy, Life Science, Chemistry, Environmental Science), each covering 15 days of instruction aligned to Next Generation Science Standards and Common Core, following the 5E Learning Cycle model. Units included scripted teacher presentation language, student workbooks, PowerPoint presentations, and lesson materials, with pre, post, and delayed 30-item multiple-choice curriculum-based assessments. Scripting was added, based on a preliminary study, to control implementation fidelity.
requirements: Teachers received ten hours of formal training plus one-on-one coaching, and lesson plan guide books, workbooks, and all activity materials
constraints: Fidelity observers were present for 40% to 60% of instructional time; teachers implemented lessons to fidelity at least 90% of the time during observed lessons
target_learners: fifth-grade students in an urban mid-Atlantic school district
target_learning_goals: science content knowledge and its long-term retention
examples: Items scoring below 10% correct at posttest were dropped from the test pool: seven from Life Sciences, one from Chemistry, four from Environmental Science, none from Astronomy
key_sources: Mariale M. Hardiman, Ranjini Mahinda JohnBull, Deborah Carran. (2017). The Effects of Arts-Integrated Instruction on Students' Memory for Science Content: Results from a Randomized Control Trial Study. Paper presented at the annual meeting of the American Educational Research Association. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED576190

article_title: The Effectiveness of Educational Games on Scientific Concepts Acquisition in First Grade Students in Science
citation: Mohammad Hasan Al-Tarawneh. (2016). The Effectiveness of Educational Games on Scientific Concepts Acquisition in the First Grade Students in Science. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.3. https://www.iiste.org
title: Scientific concepts acquisition test (23 items, KR-21 = 0.85)
description: A researcher-built test measuring first graders' acquisition of five-senses concepts, consisting of 23 items covering knowledge, comprehension and application. Item formats are matching (5 items), multiple choice (11 items) and true/false (7 items), with a maximum score of 23. Validity was checked by a jury of six reviewers, after which one item was deleted; reliability via a pilot on 25 students in a third first-grade section gave KR-21 = 0.85, considered acceptable.
requirements: Administered as pre-test and post-test around the instructional period
constraints: Designed specifically for the five-senses unit and first grade
target_learners: first grade students
key_sources: Mohammad Hasan Al-Tarawneh. (2016). The Effectiveness of Educational Games on Scientific Concepts Acquisition in the First Grade Students in Science. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.3. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1089788

article_title: Sustainability of Professional Development to Enhance Student Achievement: A Shift in the Professional Development Paradigm
citation: Wendi Mizer Stachler, R. Brent Young, Mari Borr. (2013). Sustainability of professional development to enhance student achievement: A shift in the professional development paradigm. Journal of Agricultural Education, 54(4), 13-30. https://www.jae-online.org
title: Science-in-CTE seven-element pedagogical model and science-enhanced agricultural education lessons
description: The Science-in-CTE intervention consists of a seven-element pedagogical model and 15 science-enhanced agricultural education lesson plans developed by agricultural education/science teacher partners during seven days of intensive professional development. Lessons were "developed by the agricultural education/science teacher partners and evaluated by their peers," and each experimental teacher had the opportunity to teach all 15 lessons. The model was adapted from the Math-in-CTE study's seven-element pedagogical model, and the follow-up study assessed whether teachers continued using both the model and the lessons after the pilot ended.
requirements: Development through paired collaboration between CTE and science teachers, peer review of lessons, and intensive extended professional development
constraints: Evaluated only within the Science-in-CTE pilot and follow-up studies in North Dakota
target_learners: secondary agricultural education students
secondary science students
target_learning_goals: science content knowledge within agricultural education
integration of core academics into CTE curricula
examples: Experimental teachers were paired with science teacher partners, developed and peer-reviewed 15 science-enhanced lessons, and taught them during the 2009-2010 pilot study
key_sources: Wendi Mizer Stachler, R. Brent Young, Mari Borr. (2013). Sustainability of professional development to enhance student achievement: A shift in the professional development paradigm. Journal of Agricultural Education, 54(4), 13-30. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1122391

article_title: Efficacy, Intent to Teach, and Implementation of Nutrition Education Increases after Training for Health Educators
citation: Fahlman M, McCaughtry N, Martin J, Shen B. (2011). School health educators' self-efficacy, intentions to teach, and implementation of nutrition education increases after in-service training. Am J Health Educ. 2011;42(3):181-190. https://doi.org/10.1080/19325037.2011.10599191
title: Social Cognitive Theory and the Theory of Planned Behavior as a framework for teacher nutrition-education training
description: The study is guided by Bandura's Social Cognitive Theory, whose "three essential components" are self-efficacy, outcome expectations, and outcome value, combined with the intention component of Ajzen's Theory of Planned Behavior, under which "people who have strong intentions to do something are more likely to carry out those actions." The article uses this combined framework to select the four teacher psychosocial variables measured before and after the in-service intervention, treating them as precursors to curricular implementation and student outcomes.
requirements: Measuring self-efficacy, outcome expectations, outcome value, and intentions to teach as distinct constructs with validated subscales
constraints: The article notes a paucity of research regarding teachers' intentions to teach health education broadly and nutrition education more specifically
target_learners: Grade 6-12 health education teachers
target_learning_goals: Increasing teachers' psychosocial readiness to teach nutrition education
examples: The framework operationalized as a 42-item survey with subscales for self-efficacy (16 items), outcome expectations (11 items), intentions to teach (8 items), and a single outcome-value item
key_sources: Fahlman M, McCaughtry N, Martin J, Shen B. (2011). School health educators' self-efficacy, intentions to teach, and implementation of nutrition education increases after in-service training. Am J Health Educ. 2011;42(3):181-190. https://doi.org/10.1080/19325037.2011.10599191

article_title: The Effect of Scaffolded Think-Group-Share Learning on Indonesian Elementary Schooler Satisfaction and Learning Achievement in English Classes
citation: Octavia Mantik, Hee Jun Choi. (2017). The Effect of Scaffolded Think-Group-Share Learning on Indonesian Elementary Schooler Satisfaction and Learning Achievement in English Classes. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education. https://doi.org/10.26822/iejee.2017236113
title: Scaffolded Think-Group-Share learning: a three-step cooperative method with an individual hard-scaffolding worksheet before group work
description: Scaffolded Think-Group-Share is a cooperative learning method developed by the authors from Lyman's Think-Pair-Share, with three components: an individual 'Scaffolded Think' step on a paper-based worksheet, a 'Group' step completing the group task, and a 'Share' step presenting answers to the class. The worksheet contains 'cues and questions that can prompt students to think about certain concepts' relevant to the group task, embodying hard scaffolding devised in advance. It was designed to resolve passive participation and task difficulty and to minimize the free-rider effect by promoting individual accountability.
requirements: Students work on the scaffolding worksheet individually before group activity begins
Small learning groups of three or four students with assigned roles
constraints: The study sample came only from students at an elementary school near Jakarta, Indonesia, which the authors state limits generalization
Findings were drawn from only quantitative data, which the authors say provides limited information
target_learners: Elementary school students learning English as a foreign language
target_learning_goals: Active participation and cognitive engagement in group work
examples: In the six-week study, the experimental group completed the scaffolding worksheet individually, then worked in groups on the task related to the prior week's lecture, then shared answers with the class
key_sources: Octavia Mantik, Hee Jun Choi. (2017). The Effect of Scaffolded Think-Group-Share Learning on Indonesian Elementary Schooler Satisfaction and Learning Achievement in English Classes. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education. https://doi.org/10.26822/iejee.2017236113

article_title: The Effect of Flipped Classroom Model on Students' Classroom Engagement in Teaching English
citation: Ayçiçek, B., & Yanpar Yelken, T. (2018). The Effect of Flipped Classroom Model on Students’ Classroom Engagement in Teaching English. International Journal of Instruction, 11(2), 385-398. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.11226a
title: Screencast-o-matic video lectures with embedded Edpuzzle questions used as pre-class materials
description: The experimental intervention's out-of-class component consisted of video lectures the instructor produced with Screencast-o-matic software, which records the user's screen and voice and supports edits such as "adding emphasis, adding and saving sounds, making videos interactive by adding questions and easy sharing". The videos lasted approximately 18-20 minutes, a duration the authors say was shortened based on literature recommending short videos, and each contained the curriculum content. The videos were uploaded to Edpuzzle, an educational platform where lectures are made available via class code and password, with multiple and open-ended questions embedded; Edpuzzle reports to the instructor whether students watched, their answers, and the number of viewings. Access was restricted to the experimental group.
requirements: Students must access and watch the videos before class; the platform provides the instructor watch and answer reports
constraints: If students have problems accessing internet, the authors suggest providing contents via CD, DVD or portable memory
target_learners: seventh-grade secondary school English students
target_learning_goals: preparation for in-class interactive English learning and classroom engagement
examples: Figure 1 shows an Edpuzzle sample question screenshot from the study's video lectures
key_sources: Ayçiçek, B., & Yanpar Yelken, T. (2018). The Effect of Flipped Classroom Model on Students’ Classroom Engagement in Teaching English. International Journal of Instruction, 11(2), 385-398. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.11226a

article_title: Learning Effectiveness and Students' Perceptions in a Flexible Learning Course
citation: Claude Müller, Michael Stahl, Mark Alder, Maximilian Müller. (2018). Learning Effectiveness and Students' Perceptions in a Flexible Learning Course. European Journal of Open, Distance and e-Learning, 21(2). https://www.eurodl.org/
title: Scripting workshops with a didactic visualization language for redesigning courses into blended formats
description: To move courses into the flexible format, lecturers redesign them in "scripting workshops" using a specially developed didactic visualization language adapted from other systems. The visualization shows how virtual self-study phases are embedded in face-to-face phases, with different shapes marking information delivery, activation and interaction, and learning assessment, giving an overview of the didactic design. The pilot course IBA was redesigned this way.
requirements: Lecturers participate in scripting workshops following a defined process
Online phases combine information delivery with elaboration through exercises, case studies and other tasks
target_learners: University lecturers transitioning courses to blended formats
target_learning_goals: Didactic course design for blended learning
examples: Figure 1 shows the scripting result for the pilot course Introduction to Business Administration, with yellow self-study phases embedded in blue classroom phases
key_sources: Claude Müller, Michael Stahl, Mark Alder, Maximilian Müller. (2018). Learning Effectiveness and Students' Perceptions in a Flexible Learning Course. European Journal of Open, Distance and e-Learning, 21(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1208426

article_title: Improving 7th Grade Students' Epistemological Beliefs by Epistemologically Enriched Argumentation Model
citation: Kızkapan, O., & Bektaş, O. (2021). Improving 7th Grade Students’ Epistemological Beliefs by Epistemologically Enriched Argumentation Model. Pedagogical Research, 6(3), em0095. https://doi.org/10.29333/pr/10949
title: Schommer's multidimensional model of epistemological beliefs
description: The article adopts Schommer's (1990) account in which epistemological beliefs are "a system of thought that consists of several independent dimensions" rather than one progressive developmental stages. It names five dimensions — simple knowledge, certain knowledge, omniscient authority, innate ability and quick learning — each ranging from naive to sophisticated views (e.g., knowledge is compartmentalized versus highly integrated). The study's intervention and its epistemological belief scale are organized around these dimensions.
requirements: Beliefs treated as context-dependent, subject-specific dimensions rather than a single stable trait
constraints: The article notes many studies support that epistemological beliefs are more or less independent dimensions and dependent on subject context
target_learners: Middle school science students
target_learning_goals: Developing more sophisticated epistemological beliefs about scientific knowledge and learning
examples: The EETAM intervention scheduled specific Schommer dimensions per week, e.g., certain knowledge, source of knowledge and innate ability in week two
key_sources: Kızkapan, O., & Bektaş, O. (2021). Improving 7th Grade Students’ Epistemological Beliefs by Epistemologically Enriched Argumentation Model. Pedagogical Research, 6(3), em0095. https://doi.org/10.29333/pr/10949

article_title: Exploring the Moderating Effects of Cognitive Abilities on Social Competence Intervention Outcomes
citation: Janine P. Stichter, Melissa J. Herzog, Stephen P. Kilgus, and Alexander M. Schoemann. (2018). Exploring the Moderating Effects of Cognitive Abilities on Social Competence Intervention Outcomes. Behavior Modification. https://doi.org/10.1177/0145445517698654
title: SCI-A: a scaffolded, group-based cognitive-behavioral social competence curriculum for early adolescents
description: SCI-A is a school-delivered social competence intervention for early adolescents (age 11-14) with high functioning ASD or similar social challenges who have scholastic aptitude. It is "based in principals of cognitive behavioral intervention" and addresses deficits in social perspective taking, emotion recognition, and executive functioning. It comprises five curricular units — recognizing facial expressions, sharing ideas, turn taking in conversations, recognizing feelings and emotions, and problem solving — delivered in a scaffolded fashion with modeling, role-playing, and performance feedback, in 32 lessons to groups of 4-6 students.
requirements: Delivered by a specifically trained implementer (special educators or speech language pathologists) in a group format of 4-6 students at consistent scheduled times
Students must meet inclusion criteria: absence of intellectual disabilities, access to general education, and school-identified social needs
constraints: Requires minimum cognitive and verbal capacities, per the authors
Purposeful group-based design required students to consistently attend the group together, which some schools found challenging
target_learners: Middle school students (age 11-14) with high functioning autism spectrum disorder, emotional/behavioral disorders, or similar social competence deficits without intellectual impairment
examples: In the CRT, trained school personnel delivered SCI-A in 32 lessons (e.g., 45-min lessons, always during the same period on specific days) during the spring semester
key_sources: Janine P. Stichter, Melissa J. Herzog, Stephen P. Kilgus, and Alexander M. Schoemann. (2018). Exploring the Moderating Effects of Cognitive Abilities on Social Competence Intervention Outcomes. Behavior Modification. https://doi.org/10.1177/0145445517698654

article_title: The Effect of the Science-Fiction Books on Arousing Curiosity about Science in Secondary School Students
citation: Karadeniz, E. & Degirmencay, Ş. A. (2020). The Effect of the Science-Fiction Books on Arousing Curiosity about Science in Secondary School Students. Journal of Turkish Science Education, 17(2), 225-241. https://doi.org/10.36681/tused.2020.23
title: Use science-fiction books as a supplement to the science curriculum to enhance students' interest and curiosity about science
description: This principle holds that science-fiction books can be added to the standard science curriculum to enhance students' interest and curiosity about science. The article's experimental study found that students who read 12 science-fiction books alongside the regular curriculum showed a significant increase in science curiosity scores, while the control group did not. The authors state that "Science-fiction books can be used in order to enhance the students’ interest and curiosity about science lessons."
requirements: Access to age-appropriate science-fiction books selected for scientific content and readability
constraints: The article's evidence comes from 5th and 6th grade students in a single Turkish secondary school; the article notes the groups were not homogenous at pre-test
target_learners: secondary school students in 5th and 6th grades
examples: In the study, the experimental group read 12 science-fiction books added to the exact same 2013 Science Curriculum followed by the control group
key_sources: Karadeniz, E. & Degirmencay, Ş. A. (2020). The Effect of the Science-Fiction Books on Arousing Curiosity about Science in Secondary School Students. Journal of Turkish Science Education, 17(2), 225-241. https://doi.org/10.36681/tused.2020.23

article_title: The Effect of the Science-Fiction Books on Arousing Curiosity about Science in Secondary School Students
citation: Karadeniz, E. & Degirmencay, Ş. A. (2020). The Effect of the Science-Fiction Books on Arousing Curiosity about Science in Secondary School Students. Journal of Turkish Science Education, 17(2), 225-241. https://doi.org/10.36681/tused.2020.23
title: Science Curiosity Scale (Harty & Beall, 1984; Turkish translation by Serin, 2010)
description: The Science Curiosity Scale is the quantitative instrument used to measure students' science curiosity before and after the experiment. It is a 5-point Likert scale consisting of 30 items, 8 of which are negative, based on four factors: novelty, lack of clarity, complexity of stimuli, and surprise/bafflement. The article reports the Cronbach's α reliability coefficient as 0.85 for the English version, 0.87 for the Turkish version, and 0.81 in this study's sample of 100 students. Scores range from 30 (lowest) to 150 (highest possible).
requirements: Administration to students able to respond to a 5-point Likert format
constraints: The article notes uncertainty about whether students answer the scale questions with full comprehension, which motivated the supplementary diaries
target_learners: secondary school students in 5th and 6th grades
examples: In this study the scale was administered as pre-test and post-test to both experimental and control groups
key_sources: Karadeniz, E. & Degirmencay, Ş. A. (2020). The Effect of the Science-Fiction Books on Arousing Curiosity about Science in Secondary School Students. Journal of Turkish Science Education, 17(2), 225-241. https://doi.org/10.36681/tused.2020.23

article_title: Philosophy for Children: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Stephen Gorard, Nadia Siddiqui and Beng Huat See. (2015). Philosophy for Children: Evaluation report and Executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: Schedule philosophical enquiry sessions into the timetable on a regular basis to protect them from being crowded out
description: The evaluation found that implementation success depended on giving P4C a protected, regular slot: teachers reported that "the overall success of the intervention depended on incorporating P4C into the timetable on a regular basis". Without such a slot there was a risk the programme would be crowded out by activities that appear to more directly address the national curriculum. The principle applies to whole-class dialogic enquiry programmes delivered alongside a standard curriculum.
requirements: A regular, protected timetable slot for the enquiry sessions, agreed at school level
constraints: Without regular timetabling there was a risk the programme would be crowded out by curriculum-focused activities
target_learners: Primary school pupils (Key Stage 2)
examples: In the trial, pupils received on average one period of P4C per week, although this varied across schools, and each school appointed a P4C lead staff member to ensure regular implementation.
key_sources: Stephen Gorard, Nadia Siddiqui and Beng Huat See. (2015). Philosophy for Children: Evaluation report and Executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED581147

article_title: Scaffolding Fidelity and Adaptation in Educational Program Implementation: Experimental Evidence from a Literacy Intervention
citation: David M. Quinn, James S. Kim. (2017). Scaffolding Fidelity and Adaptation in Educational Program Implementation: Experimental Evidence From a Literacy Intervention. American Educational Research Journal. https://doi.org/10.3102/0002831217717692
title: The scaffolded sequence of program implementation: fidelity-focused phase followed by a structured adaptive phase
description: A conceptual model in which schools first implement an evidence-based program with fidelity so teachers internalize the program theory and achieve proficiency, then transition to a structured adaptive phase in which teachers collaboratively tailor the program to their context. The article describes it as "a structure for chronologically organizing the fidelity-focused and adaptive approaches," grounded in a Vygotskyan scaffolding perspective and Frank et al.'s focus, fiddle, friends progression. The present study tests it by interacting condition with teachers' prior Core READS experience.
requirements: Teachers must first master the program as designed through fidelity-focused implementation before entering the adaptive phase
The adaptive phase requires program management structures, such as classifying components as core versus noncore and collaborative working groups
constraints: The article notes no experimental studies had directly tested this approach prior to this trial
Adaptation introduces the possibility that teachers alter practices in ways that make them less effective
target_learners: elementary school students in high-poverty schools
elementary school teachers implementing literacy programs
examples: In the trial, a subset of teachers implemented Core READS in year 1 and Adaptive READS in year 2, enacting the full scaffolded sequence
key_sources: David M. Quinn, James S. Kim. (2017). Scaffolding Fidelity and Adaptation in Educational Program Implementation: Experimental Evidence From a Literacy Intervention. American Educational Research Journal. https://doi.org/10.3102/0002831217717692

article_title: Scaffolding Middle School Students' Comprehension and Response to Short Stories
citation: Liang, L. A. (2011). Scaffolding Middle School Students' Comprehension and Response to Short Stories. RMLE Online, 34(8). ISSN 1940-4476.
title: Scaffolded Reading Experience (SRE) framework
description: The SRE framework is "designed to assist students in comprehending individual texts", enabling a teacher to provide scaffolding that increases the likelihood students complete the reading task successfully. It rests on four instructional concepts: scaffolding, the gradual release of responsibility, the zone of proximal development, and the notion of success. It has two major phases: a planning phase, in which teachers consider the text, the purposes for reading, and students' strengths and needs, and an implementation phase of pre-, during-, and post-reading activities. In this study it served as the common instructional container that allowed fair comparison of the two teaching approaches.
requirements: Teachers select pre-, during-, and post-reading activities based on consideration of the text, the reading purpose, and the students' strengths and needs
constraints: In this study the SRE was operationalized with approach-specific purposes, so its comparison value depends on holding text and students constant
target_learners: middle school students reading individual narrative texts
examples: Two SREs were written for each experimental story: cognitive-oriented SREs targeting defending answers with textual evidence, and reader-response SREs targeting responses in four response modes
key_sources: Liang, L. A. (2011). Scaffolding Middle School Students' Comprehension and Response to Short Stories. RMLE Online, 34(8). ISSN 1940-4476. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ925248

article_title: Revisions of Physical Geology Laboratory Courses to Increase the Level of Inquiry: Implications for Teaching and Learning
citation: Grissom, A. N., Czajka, C. D., and McConnell, D. A. (2015). Revisions of Physical Geology Laboratory Courses to Increase the Level of Inquiry: Implications for Teaching and Learning. Journal of Geoscience Education 63, 285–296. https://doi.org/10.5408/14-050.1
title: Scaffold laboratory assignments with a mixture of high- and low-level inquiry activities
description: The article holds that lower-level inquiry activities retain value for introducing basic information, and that instructors "should always strive to scaffold their assignments with a mixture of both high- and low-level inquiry activities in order to maximize student learning." Inquiry level should be matched to class time available, the concepts to be learned, and student ability level, rather than maximizing inquiry uniformly across all activities.
requirements: Instructors must judge the appropriate mix based on class time, concepts to be learned, and student ability level
constraints: Lower-level inquiry activities remain appropriate for introducing basic information
target_learners: introductory undergraduate science students
examples: The revised geologic time laboratory retained structured relative- and absolute-dating activities while raising the Earth history portion to guided inquiry
key_sources: Grissom, A. N., Czajka, C. D., and McConnell, D. A. (2015). Revisions of Physical Geology Laboratory Courses to Increase the Level of Inquiry: Implications for Teaching and Learning. Journal of Geoscience Education 63, 285–296. https://doi.org/10.5408/14-050.1

article_title: Examining the Impact of Using the Science Writing Heuristic Approach in Learning Science: A Cluster Randomized Study
citation: Brian Hand, William Therrien, Mack Shelley. (2013). Examining the impact of using the Science Writing Heuristic approach in learning science: A cluster randomized study. SREE Fall 2013 Conference abstract.
title: Science Writing Heuristic (SWH) approach: argumentation-centered science pedagogy
description: The SWH approach, developed by Hand and Keys (1999), "shifts teaching from memorizing facts about science to focusing on argumentation as a means of learning the big ideas and theories of topics studied." It centers on students' ability to construct and critique ideas by negotiating questioning, claims and evidence, and "consists of a framework to guide activities as well as metacognitive support to prompt student reasoning about data." In the study it was introduced as the central pedagogical approach for teaching science in treatment schools.
requirements: Teacher training in the SWH technique, delivered here as a 2-year workshop and implementation program including three-day summer workshops and in-year training days
constraints: In this study it was implemented with elementary students in grades 3-5 in Iowa elementary schools
target_learners: 3rd-6th grade elementary students
examples: Treatment teachers were trained to foster cooperative and individual learning by requiring student groups to examine science problems and think of solutions through intergroup and intragroup discourse, write down discussion ideas, and formulate and test their own hypotheses
key_sources: Brian Hand, William Therrien, Mack Shelley. (2013). Examining the impact of using the Science Writing Heuristic approach in learning science: A cluster randomized study. SREE Fall 2013 Conference abstract. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED563211

article_title: Comparative Effect of Memory and Cognitive Strategies Training on EFL Intermediate Learners' Vocabulary Learning
citation: Maryam Banisaeid. (2013). Comparative Effect of Memory and Cognitive Strategies Training on EFL Intermediate Learners' Vocabulary Learning. English Language Teaching, 6(8). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n8p108
title: Schmitt's taxonomy of vocabulary learning strategies: discovery versus consolidation of a word's meaning
description: The article presents Schmitt's (1997) taxonomy, which it calls the most comprehensive vocabulary learning strategy classification, as a two-branch framework: "strategies for the discovery of a new word's meaning and strategies for consolidating a word once it has been encountered". Discovery strategies include determination (dictionary use, guessing from context, analyzing affixes) and social strategies; consolidation strategies overlap Oxford's direct categories of memory, cognitive, and metacognitive strategies. The article uses this taxonomy to situate its memory (keyword, semantic map) and cognitive (repetition, flashcards) training conditions.
requirements: A pedagogical framework grounded in Oxford's (1990) language learning strategy classification, as the article describes
constraints: Schmitt found it difficult to clearly distinguish cognitive from memory strategies because both assist recall through language manipulation; he adopted Purpura's division of less obviously mental-manipulative strategies as cognitive
target_learners: L2 vocabulary learners
examples: Table 2 lists discovery strategies such as bilingual dictionary use and consolidation strategies such as the keyword method, semantic maps, verbal and written repetition, and flash cards
key_sources: Maryam Banisaeid. (2013). Comparative Effect of Memory and Cognitive Strategies Training on EFL Intermediate Learners' Vocabulary Learning. English Language Teaching, 6(8). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n8p108

article_title: Investigating the Efficiency of Scenario Based Learning and Reflective Learning Approaches in Teacher Education
citation: Hursen, C., & Gezer Fasli, F. (2017). Investigating the Efficiency of Scenario Based Learning and Reflective Learning Approaches in Teacher Education. European Journal of Contemporary Education, 6(2). https://doi.org/10.13187/ejced.2017.2.264
title: Scenario based learning as a situated-learning approach bridging theory and practice in teacher education
description: Within situated learning theory, scenario based learning is described as "one of the current approaches that reinforces gaining meaningful learning within the authentic context". Learners act like players who solve the problems presented in scenarios, becoming more active and improving real-life skills; scenarios must connect with the real world and the future profession, and mistakes should be allowed during learning. In this study, skill-based scenarios were prepared by the researchers from classroom problems observed by previous interns and presented with only the present situation, requiring participants to research details, discuss, and produce group solution reports.
requirements: Scenarios should have a connection with the real world
Scenarios prepared with expert knowledge and matched to the target group's level
Learners' mistakes should be allowed during the learning process
constraints: Preparing scenarios requires expert knowledge, so the researchers prepared all scenarios themselves

The games taught parts of speech from the 6th grade Turkish Teaching Program over a 12-week plan, two course hours per week, played on a smart board and on students' tablets, individually and in groups of 5 or 6. title: Science process skills taxonomy: 14 skills in basic, experimental, and causative sub-dimensions
description: The article organizes science process skills as "14 science process skills in 3 sub-dimensions": basic processes (observation, quantification, classification, saving data, establishing a connection between number and space), experimental processes (estimation, defining variables, interpreting data, reaching a conclusion), and causative processes (creating a hypothesis, using data and creating value, experimenting, changing and controlling the variables, reaching a decision), citing Çepni, Ayas, Johnson & Turgut (1996). It states basic skills may be learned from pre-school while more complex experimental and causative skills may be learned from secondary school.

constraints: The article states more complex skills (experimental and causative) may be learned starting from secondary school

examples: The taxonomy underlies the outcome measure used to evaluate the place-based General Geography course

higher order thinking skills in mathematics

title: Shadish, Cook, and Campbell validity framework for describing implications of design complications
description: The paper uses the Shadish, Cook, and Campbell (2002) validity framework to organize how design and analysis complications threaten research conclusions. It distinguishes internal, external, construct, and statistical conclusion validity, applying each to decisions such as network-identified treatment schools, within-pair analysis, IPTW weighting, and missing-data weights. The framework is used "to describe the implications of different complications and decisions during the data collection and analysis phases of the study."
requirements: Application to a specific study's design decisions and complications
constraints: Framework as applied in this paper addresses quasi-experimental matching studies in complex field settings
target_learners: education researchers conducting quasi-experimental studies
target_learning_goals: understanding validity trade-offs in matched quasi-experimental designs
examples: Table 3 maps each complication, study decision, and validity implication across sample selection, data collection, missing data, and communication phases.
