article_title: Developing Computational Fluency with the Help of Science: A Turkish Middle and High School Grades Study
citation: Corlu, M. S., Capraro, R. M., & Corlu, M. A. (2011). Developing computational fluency with the help of science: A Turkish middle and high school grades study. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 10(2), 72-81. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ932560
title: Use science-contextualized problems as non-traditional drill exercises to develop computational fluency alongside conceptual understanding
description: The article recommends replacing context-free repeated algorithmic drills with homework problems embedded in science contexts (e.g., Richter scale energy comparisons requiring scientific notation division). The study showed "science-contextualized drill exercises produced higher gains for both middle and high school students' computational fluencies than the traditional drill exercises". This allows computational practice to reinforce science learning while freeing mathematics class time for conceptual understanding and problem-solving strategies.
requirements: Problems must present the same algorithmic computation as traditional drills but within contexts drawn from the science curriculum, with solutions and correct answers provided with subsequent homework
Students must show their work and calculators should not be permitted during the practice
constraints: The benefit was larger for middle school students (ES=0.82) than high school students (ES=0.17), possibly because high school students were already comfortable with the exponentials unit
The intervention targeted one mathematics topic (exponentials) chosen because it is explicitly covered in Turkish middle and high school science curricula
target_learners: middle school students (grades 7-8)
high school students (grades 9-10)
target_learning_goals: computational fluency with exponentials and scientific notation
examples: Homework assignments gave the control group a question like 'Find the solution in scientific notation (4.2 × 10^18) / (150 × 10^14) = ?' while the experiment group answered a Richter magnitude scale question requiring the same division, with the answer written in scientific notation

citation: Majid Haghverdi and Lynda R. Wiest. (2016). The Effect of Contextual and Conceptual Rewording on Mathematical Problem-Solving Performance. The Mathematics Educator, 25(1), 56–73. https://matheducator
title: Scaffold word problems with greater and clearer detail for younger and struggling students, gradually reducing the support over time
description: The article recommends matching problem wording to student need: "This suggests scaffolding problems by providing greater and clearer detail for younger and struggling students and for all students when solving more challenging problems." The additional structure "can be gradually reduced over time" as students' problem-solving abilities and experience improve. The authors caution this should not lock students into prescriptive problems without increasing challenge, and that better performance on reworded problems does not equate with improved problem-solving ability.

constraints: Better performance on reworded problems does not equate with improved problem-solving ability, per the authors

struggling or lower-achieving students

description: A program of thematic immersion realized at the Taganrog institute of A. Chekhov within the historical and patriotic direction of educational work, in which 68 students of the experimental group took part. Its purpose is drawing attention of students to the Russian history and a role of Russia in world historical process and formation of creative civil activity of youth. Three thematic days included a training on acquaintance, self-determination and identification of leaders, reconstruction of a family tree, the game «That? Where? When?» on stories of Russia, game elections, a master class of bases of civil self-defense, a film society meeting and a patriotic flashmob.

article_title: The Effectiveness of Scaffolding Design in Training Writing Skills Physics Teaching Materials
citation: Sinaga, P., Suhandi, A., & Liliasari. (2015). The Effectiveness of Scaffolding Design in Training Writing Skills Physics Teaching Materials. International Journal of Instruction, 8(1). https://www.e-iji.net
title: Five-stage scaffolding design between planning and translating in the Hayes and Flower writing model
description: The article designs a scaffolding sequence inserted between the planning and translating-plans-into-text stages of the Hayes and Flower writing model. It comprises five stages: "Concept mapping, modes of concept representation, translation among different modes of representation, multiple representations, and multimodal representation." Concept mapping trains hierarchical content arrangement; mode identification introduces text, picture, diagram, graph, equation, table and photo modes; translation and multiple-representation stages build flexibility across modes; multimodal representation integrates modes into cohesive writing reviewed by peers or experts.
requirements: Students first produce a planning outline of an assigned sub-topic before entering the scaffolding stages
Writing is reviewed individually by peer review or expert review at the multimodal stage
constraints: Tested only with pre-service physics teachers on the topics of electromagnetism and waves and optics in small classes of about 17 students
target_learners: pre-service physics teachers
examples: Each student wrote teaching materials for one randomly assigned sub-topic; topics were divided into 17 sub-topics matching the number of students enrolling in the course

title: Science Writing Heuristic (SWH): argument-based science inquiry built on questions, claims, and evidence
description: The Science Writing Heuristic (Hand & Keys, 1999) is a guided, argument-based approach to classroom science inquiry designed to involve students in inquiry, argumentation, and experimentation as a means of learning science and improving critical thinking. It rests on writing-to-learn strategies, science literacy, and inquiry-based instruction, and "requires students to use 'questions, claims, and evidence' to display their understanding of science content and concepts". citation: Duane E. Wallace & Alec M. Bodzin. (2017). Developing Scientific Citizenship Identity Using Mobile Learning and Authentic Practice. Electronic Journal of Science Education, 21(6). http://ejse.southwestern.edu
title: SCI-ML Survey: Scientific Citizenship, STEM Interest and Mobile Learning instrument
description: The SCI-ML Survey is a 41-item quantitative Likert-type scale (1 strongly disagree to 5 strongly agree; possible scores 41-205) developed by the authors to measure citizen science identity formation, perceptions of mobile learning, and interest in STEM fields. It has four subscales: Ideas about Learning Science and Technology (10 items), Ideas about Careers (8 items), Ideas about Citizen Science (13 items), and Ideas about Mobile Learning (10 items). Two subscales were adapted from the SITS Survey, and the instrument was expert-reviewed and pilot-tested. The article reports "a Cronbach’s alpha of 0.850 for both the pre-survey and post-survey for the entire SCI-ML instrument."

citation: Junaidi Mistar, Alfan Zuhairi & Nofita Yanti. (2016). Strategies Training in the Teaching of Reading Comprehension for EFL Learners in Indonesia. English Language Teaching, 9(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n2p49
title: Schema-theory account of why predicting, text mapping, and summarizing training aids EFL reading comprehension
description: The authors explain their finding through schema theory, which distinguishes content schemata (background knowledge of the topic) from formal schemata (knowledge of rhetorical organizational structures). Predicting trains students to activate content schemata, while text mapping and summarizing enrich formal schemata by tracing the text's organizational structure. The article states that "A reader's failure to activate appropriate schemata, content or formal, during reading results in various degrees of non-comprehension." This is the authors' interpretation of their result, not a separately tested mechanism.
requirements: Readers must possess relevant prior knowledge of the topic and of text organizational structures to activate
constraints: Offered as a post-hoc theoretical explanation for the observed group differences, not tested directly in the study
target_learners: EFL learners in secondary reading classes
examples: The discussion links the prediction step to content schemata and the text-mapping/summarizing steps to formal schemata of descriptive, procedure, and report texts

article_title: Distributed Pair Programming Using Collaboration Scripts: An Educational System and Initial Results
citation: Despina TSOMPANOUDI, Maya SATRATZEMI, Stelios XINOGALOS. (2015). Distributed Pair Programming Using Collaboration Scripts: An Educational System and Initial Results. Informatics in Education. https://doi.org/10.15388/infedu.2015.17
title: SCEPPSys: an educational distributed pair programming system built on an Eclipse plugin with collaboration script authoring
description: SCEPPSys (Scripted Collaboration in an Educational Pair Programming System) is an educational DPP system based on the XecliP Eclipse plugin with a client-server architecture of server, database, and plugin. It supports standard DPP features (shared editor, floor control, chat, remote code highlighting, awareness) plus synchronic program execution, a collaboration script authoring tool for teachers, an administration panel with contribution statistics, and enhanced logging of user interactions. The article states "SCEPPSys extends existing plugins by combining collaboration scripts and DPP".

constraints: The system captures only the work of the driver and not the contributions of the navigator; content analysis is not supported

title: Scripted distributed pair programming: structuring DPP with collaboration scripts to balance participation
description: The article's framework combines distributed pair programming with collaboration scripts: a script defines participants, groups, activities, roles, and policies for group formation and task distribution. Programming assignments are decomposed into smaller problem-solving tasks categorized by learning goals, and task-role distribution policies ("rotating role switching" and "balanced knowledge") guide pairs through problem solving. The approach "aims to address the most important drawback of PP, namely unbalanced student participation".
requirements: A teacher defines script components and mechanisms via the authoring tool; assignments must be decomposable into tasks with learning goals
constraints: Role assignment is not mandatory; students may request individual role switches at any time

target_learning_goals: symmetric skill acquisition across learning goals

article_title: Distributed Pair Programming Using Collaboration Scripts: An Educational System and Initial Results
citation: Despina TSOMPANOUDI, Maya SATRATZEMI, Stelios XINOGALOS. (2015). Distributed Pair Programming Using Collaboration Scripts: An Educational System and Initial Results. Informatics in Education. https://doi.org/10.15388/infedu.2015.17
title: Structure pair programming with collaboration scripts that decompose assignments into learning-goal tasks and rotate roles
description: The article recommends structuring DPP through collaboration scripts that decompose assignments into smaller problem-solving tasks categorized by learning goals, distribute tasks via rotating or balanced-knowledge policies, and trigger role switches. Students indicated that "solving consecutive tasks facilitated the problem-solving process". This addresses uneven workload and infrequent role switches that available DPP systems could not address.

constraints: Students may not understand the purpose of system-driven role switches; the system captures only driver contributions

article_title: Exploring the Technical Expression of Academic Knowledge: The Science-in-CTE Pilot Study
citation: Pearson, D., Young, R. B., & Richardson, G. B. (2013). Exploring the Technical Expression of Academic Knowledge: The Science-in-CTE Pilot Study. Journal of Agricultural Education, 54(4), 162-179. https://doi.org/10.5032/jae.2013.04162
title: Seven-element pedagogic framework for science-enhanced CTE lessons
description: The Science-in-CTE pilot adopted the Math-in-CTE pedagogic framework, a seven-element instructional sequence used to guide teachers' development of integrated lessons and their subsequent instruction. The elements move from introducing the CTE lesson and assessing students' science awareness, through working through the science embedded in the CTE lesson and related contextual and explicit science examples, to students demonstrating understanding and formal assessment. Elements 3-5 embody transfer of learning: solving a real, relevant problem, practicing several similar examples, and then applying the concept to a more abstract problem.
requirements: CTE teachers paired with science teacher partners who develop integrated lessons together during extended professional development
constraints: In post-study focus groups, some teachers reported challenges in moving from Element 4 to Element 5, suggesting the transfer of knowledge steps may not have been fully articulated in some lessons
target_learners: secondary agricultural education students
target_learning_goals: science knowledge and skills embedded in CTE curricula
examples: Each CTE-science teacher team created one science-enhanced lesson for a total of 15 for the group; fourteen of the fifteen agricultural teachers taught all 15 lessons, and 97% (219 of 225) of the scheduled lessons were implemented as scheduled.

article_title: The Effect of Scientific Inquiry Learning Model Based on Conceptual Change on Physics Cognitive Competence and Science Process Skill (SPS) of Students at Senior High School
citation: Sahhyar & Nst, F. H. (2017). The Effect of Scientific Inquiry Learning Model Based on Conceptual Change on Physics Cognitive Competence and Science Process Skill (SPS) of Students at Senior High School. Journal of Education and Practice, 8(5), 120-126. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1140975
title: Scientific inquiry learning model based on conceptual change as a four-phase instructional framework
description: The scientific inquiry learning model based on conceptual change is a learning model that focuses on changing students' concepts by involving them in genuine problems of inquiry. It guides students through four phases: first, an area of investigation is posed to students (elicit and confirm current ideas); second, students structure the problem (exposure to conflicting evidence); third, students identify the problem in the investigation (construct new explanations); fourth, students speculate on ways to clear up the difficulty (apply and evaluate new explanations and review change in ideas and explanations). The model aims to help students discard naive concepts in favor of scientifically accurate explanations by explicitly recognizing discrepancies between current beliefs and scientific ones.
requirements: Students must be engaged in genuine problems of inquiry that can be investigated
Learning must include eliciting and confirming students' current ideas before exposing them to conflicting evidence
Teachers guide students to propose explanations based on evidence derived from their investigations
constraints: The model was tested in physics learning at senior high school level in Indonesia
The study compared it against conventional learning, not against other inquiry-based or conceptual change approaches
target_learners: Senior high school students (Class XI) studying physics
target_learning_goals: Conceptual change toward scientifically accepted explanations
examples: In the study, the experimental class used this four-phase model while the control class used conventional learning with lecture, discussion, investigation, and concept mapping methods not conducted as the phases of each model.
key_sources: Sahhyar & Nst, F. H. (2017). The Effect of Scientific Inquiry Learning Model Based on Conceptual Change on Physics Cognitive Competence and Science Process Skill (SPS) of Students at Senior High School. It provides "audio and visual activities, educational games and test online", along with e-books, problem-solving exercises, and practical tests. Teachers can assign homework through the program, monitor student progress, and check results online. Students may take tests eight times a year, and various educational games are offered per subject to increase motivation.

From week 4 of a 10-week practice period, students received "1 scenario a week, totaling to 8 scenarios", submitted solutions online, and discussed scenarios and solutions at biweekly face-to-face meetings. Each scenario solution was rated by four examiners using a performance assessment scale (rubric) developed by the examiners.

problem solving from distinct points of view

title: Scenario-based learning model
description: The article defines scenario-based learning as "a learning model, based on having the student put him/herself into an actor/actress, and display the goals and behaviors for solving the problems they come across, by plotting the expected goals and behaviors within the framework of a scenario". By bringing true or likewise real-life stories into the classroom, it enables students to think about real events, transfer knowledge to them, and research solutions, so that "students come to structuring their knowledge" (Veznedaroğlu, 2005). In this study it is implemented through weekly online scenarios tied to students' school practice experiences.

title: Scripted small-group strategy instruction program for Grade 3 word problems
description: The intervention comprised "20scriptedlessons administeredover 8 weeks," each 30 minutes, three times a week, in small groups of two to four children, delivered by six tutors. Each lesson had four phases: warm-up, instruction, guided practice, and independent practice. Treatment fidelity was high, with tutors following strategy steps at a mean of 98% across observed sequences, and interrater agreement exceeding 90% across all observed categories.

constraints: The article notes concerns can be raised about the Level 2 sample size of 18 classrooms for HLM standard error estimates, addressed with robust standard errors

article_title: Adult Hispanic ESL Students and Graded Readers
citation: Liza E. Martinez. (2017). Adult Hispanic ESL Students and Graded Readers. The CATESOL Journal, 29(2). https://www.catesol.org
title: Scaffolded silent reading with graded readers: teacher-guided book selection, accountability conferences, reading logs, and journals in a set silent-reading block
description: The pattern adapts Reutzel et al.'s scaffolded silent reading for adult ESL: unlike sustained silent reading, "The teacher plays a more active role." In this study the teacher "assisted the participants in selecting graded readers, monitored their progress, and provided them with feedback," while participants kept a reading log and wrote three journal entries for accountability. Students read graded readers in a 20-minute class block with the goal of finishing and selecting a new book weekly, while the teacher conferenced individually and modeled silent reading himself.
requirements: A supply of graded readers at students' independent reading levels across varied topics and genres
A set block of class time for silent reading with individual teacher-student conferences
Accountability structures such as a reading log and journal entries
constraints: ScSR had mainly been used with native-English-speaking elementary students before this study; adult ESL response was the present study's question
target_learners: adult intermediate-level ESL students at a community college
examples: Treatment participants selected and read graded readers, met individually with the instructor, kept a journal and reading log, and read for 20 minutes per class over 14 weeks

article_title: The Impact of an Interdisciplinary Learning Community Course on Pseudoscientific Reasoning in First-Year Science Students
citation: Franz, T. M., & Green, K. H. (2013). The impact of an interdisciplinary learning community course on pseudoscientific reasoning in first-year science students. Journal of the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning, 13(5), 90–105.
title: Science Scholars Learning Community: a two-course, writing-intensive, team-taught interdisciplinary cluster comparing scientific and pseudoscientific thinking
description: A six-semester-hour learning community in which two newly created courses, neither counting toward any major, explored the nature of science by comparing scientific fields and thinking with pseudoscience and science fiction. Students received "the same grade for both courses", both instructors read all major papers, and a substantial grade component came from writing assignments and "a group research project that culminated in a large team-run debate". Faculty met regularly to connect each class period to the previous and subsequent ones.

Regular faculty meetings to maintain integration across class periods
constraints: Designed for selected scholarship students with strong high school science and mathematics backgrounds
Neither course counts for credit in any major

article_title: Linking Task-Based Language Teaching and Sociocultural Theory: Private Speech and Scaffolding in Reading Comprehension
citation: Soheila Tahmasebi, Morteza Yamini. (2011). Linking Task-based Language Teaching and Sociocultural Theory: Private Speech and Scaffolding in Reading Comprehension. https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.2n.1p.41
title: Sociocultural Theory mediation through scaffolding, private speech, and artifacts
description: The article draws on Sociocultural Theory (SCT), in which mediation of human behavior happens through tools, sign systems, and social interaction. It identifies three types of mediation: by others, by self, and by artifacts. Scaffolding (collaborative learning) and private speech are the two components operationalized in the study's task-based framework. The article states "in SCT language development emerges out of talks in two distinct ways: (1) through some forms of scaffolding when the learner is interacting with others; and (2) through private talk when the learner tries to regulate his/her thoughts."
requirements: Learners must be engaged in tasks within their zone of proximal development, with access to peers, teachers, or self-directed talk as mediators.
constraints: The article notes that the effects of different SCT components were not separated in the study design, so the relative contributions of scaffolding versus private speech cannot be disentangled.
target_learners: Iranian EFL freshmen in a reading comprehension course
examples: The study asked students to paraphrase and summarize paragraphs alternately through collaboration and private speech across eight 90-minute sessions.
key_sources: Soheila Tahmasebi, Morteza Yamini. (2011). Linking Task-based Language Teaching and Sociocultural Theory: Private Speech and Scaffolding in Reading Comprehension. https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.2n.1p.41

title: Use SCT-based collaborative and private speech instruction to foster learner autonomy and reduce error anxiety
description: The article recommends that EFL teachers use sociocultural components (scaffolding and private speech) within task-based frameworks to develop autonomous learners. The authors suggest this approach can "benefit from natural classroom interactions that lead to autonomous learners" and note that the collaborative climate encouraged students to participate voluntarily without fear of mistakes.

Alternating opportunities for collaboration and self-directed work
A classroom climate that tolerates errors as learning opportunities
constraints: The article notes the study did not separate the effects of private speech from collaborative learning, so the relative contribution of each component is unknown.
target_learners: EFL freshmen
Intermediate-level language learners
examples: The article suggests the effects of SCT through a TBLT method be used for other language courses like conversation and writing.

article_title: Beyond Behavioral Modification: Benefits of Socio-Emotional/Self-Regulation Training for Preschoolers with Behavior Problems
citation: Graziano, P. A., & Hart, K. (2016). Beyond behavior modification: Benefits of social–emotional/self-regulation training for preschoolers with behavior problems. Journal of School Psychology, 58, 91–111. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.jsp.2016.07.004

description: The SRPP is an 8-week weekly group parent training program (1.5–2 h sessions) described as "the first and most cost effective intervention package." The first half covers behavioral parent training content based on PCIT and COPE-style modeling; the second half covers school readiness topics including dialogic reading, homework behavior management, and home-school communication via daily report cards. It was provided alone to one group and alongside the summer programs to the other two groups.
requirements: Weekly group sessions of 90–120 min for 8 weeks, delivered by trained therapists with fidelity monitoring
constraints: The article notes PT programs tend to have low participation rates and high attrition rates and do not directly address multiple aspects of school readiness, most notably academic impairment
target_learners: parents of preschool children with externalizing behavior problems entering kindergarten
examples: Parents practiced dialogic reading and received feedback, and learned to implement a home-school communication plan with kindergarten teachers via daily report cards

"The SET consists of 29 items organized into the following seven subscales that represent the seven key features of SW-PBIS," including Expectations Defined, Behavioral Expectations Taught, and District-Level Support. In Minnesota, an independent SET evaluator completed the SET during a two and one half hour site visit, and full implementation is defined as a score of 80 or better overall and 80 or better in Behavioral Expectations Taught.

constraints: In this quasi-experimental design it was not possible to track retrospectively the SET scores of the two cohort groups

article_title: An Examination of an Online Tutoring Program's Impact on Low-Achieving Middle School Students' Mathematics Achievement
citation: Chappell, S., Arnold, P., Nunnery, J., & Grant, M. (2015). An Examination of an Online Tutoring Program's Impact on Low-Achieving Middle School Students' Mathematics Achievement. Online Learning, 19(5). https://jolt.merlot.org/2015/vol11no2.htm
title: Schema theory account of explicit instruction for students with mathematics difficulties
description: The article draws on schema theory to explain why individualized tutoring benefits students with mathematics deficits. Learners develop recognition of mathematical problems across numerous experiences to abstract problem-solving strategies that may be generalized, forming categories of similar problem types. While typically developing students do this more inductively, students with math deficits benefit from explicit instruction facilitated by an expert providing clearly articulated schema-broadening instruction with guided opportunities to recognize underlying mathematical structure.

constraints: The account is offered as theoretical grounding, not tested directly in this study
target_learners: students who have accrued math deficits
students struggling with mathematics
examples: The article grounds the Focus EduVation tutoring program's focus on expert instructional explication in schema theory and the literature on analogical transfer.

article_title: Effects of Scaffolds and Scientific Reasoning Ability on Web-Based Scientific Inquiry
citation: Wu, H.-L., Weng, H.-L., & She, H.-C. (2016). Effects of scaffolds and scientific reasoning ability on web-based scientific inquiry. International Journal of Contemporary Educational Research, 3(1), 12-24. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1102367
title: Scientific reasoning ability as an internal cognitive factor shaping inquiry learning outcomes
description: The study frames scientific reasoning ability as an internal cognitive attribute that, together with external instructional scaffolding, determines success in web-based scientific inquiry. Reasoning is defined as the "ability to think and to make logical and rational decisions" and encompasses hypothetical-deductive cycles that drive hypothesis testing and evidence evaluation. The article positions prior reasoning skill as a learner characteristic that educators should assess and consider when designing inquiry supports.
requirements: Assessment of prior scientific reasoning ability (e.g., Lawson's Classroom Test of Scientific Reasoning) before assigning inquiry supports
constraints: The extent to which reasoning ability influences scientific inquiry was noted as remaining unclear in prior literature
target_learners: middle school and junior high school students
target_learning_goals: scientific inquiry, hypothesis generation, evidence-based reasoning
examples: The study used the revised Lawson Classroom Test of Scientific Reasoning, a two-tier instrument covering conservation of weight, proportional thinking, identification and control of variables, probabilistic thinking, and hypothetico-deductive reasoning

description: The Style of Categorisation Test (SCT) in this study is Oltman, Raskin, and Witkin's (1982) Group Embedded Figures Test (GEFT), a non-verbal instrument requiring participants to trace simple figures embedded within complex designs. It was chosen for its minimal language demands, cross-cultural psychometric validation, and prior adaptation for Nigerian use. article_title: Scaffolding EFL Students' Writing through the Writing Process Approach
citation: Faraj, A. K. A. (2015). Scaffolding EFL Students’ Writing through the Writing Process Approach. Journal of Education and Practice, 6(13), 131-141. https://www.iiste.org/Journals/index.php/JEP/article/view/23823
title: Scaffolding as gradual transfer of responsibility from teacher assistance to independent learner performance.
description: The article draws on Bodrova & Leong's account of scaffolding, in which "teachers step by step provides the students with en ough guidance till the students can learn the process, then teachers gradually give up the students’ support in order to transfer the responsibility to learners for completing the task." Scaffolding is presented as a tool of instructors to help learners transition from assisted tasks to independent performances. In this study, scaffolding is operationalized as teacher guidance, feedback, and questioning across all five stages of the writing process, with support withdrawn as students become more capable of revising and editing independently.
requirements: Teacher provides step-by-step guidance until students can learn the process
Teacher gradually withdraws support to transfer responsibility to learners
target_learners: EFL college students
examples: The teacher provided guidance across prewriting through publishing, then gradually reduced support so students could correct mistakes independently before the publishing stage.
key_sources: Faraj, A. K. A. (2015). Scaffolding EFL Students’ Writing through the Writing Process Approach. Journal of Education and Practice, 6(13), 131-141. https://www.iiste.org/Journals/index.php/JEP/article/view/23823

article_title: The role of problem-solving and decision-making skills in linking critical thinking dispositions to perceptions of success.
citation: Akçay Ahmet Oğuz, Karahan Engin, Kara Ahmet. (2026). The role of problem-solving and decision-making skills in linking critical thinking dispositions to perceptions of success. BMC Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-026-04918-3
title: Social Cognitive Theory as the framework for the mediation model
description: The article interprets its parallel mediation model through Bandura's Social Cognitive Theory, in which "personal, behavioral, and environmental factors continuously interact (triadic reciprocal determinism)". Critical thinking dispositions are treated as personal-cognitive characteristics, problem-solving and decision-making as self-regulatory behaviors, and perception of success as the environmental and motivational outcome. The theory provides the rationale for a parallel mediation model in which one dispositional factor can activate multiple regulatory responses simultaneously.
requirements: The model assumes a single dispositional factor can activate multiple regulatory responses simultaneously

description: The SCORS is a survey tool designed by Leighton et al. to assist organisations in evaluating institutional and programme readiness for simulation integration. citation: Vieira Douglas; Barros Cinthia Rodrigues; Thuany Mabliny; Gomes Thayse Natacha. (2026). The British Journal of Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjdp.70035
title: School achievement as a complex system analyzed through the Process-Person-Context-Time (PPCT) model and network analysis
description: The article frames school achievement as a complex system of interacting, interdependent individual and environmental factors whose combined behaviour cannot be predicted from components alone, grounded in Bronfenbrenner's "Process-Person-Context-Time (PPCT) model". It operationalizes this framework using Gaussian graphical model network analysis with graphical LASSO regularization and EBIC optimization, estimating partial correlations among age, attention, physical activity, motor coordination, physical fitness, and residence variables across subgroups defined by achievement level and residence distance.

constraints: The cross-sectional design prevents causal inference
Small subgroup sample sizes mean centrality indices should be interpreted as relative importance within each group, not definitive absolute rankings
The findings are structural and not intended for broad generalization outside the defined model
The use of METs values to estimate physical activity is a limitation

target_learning_goals: Understanding how individual, environmental, cognitive and motor factors interact to influence school achievement
examples: The study analysed four subgroups defined by school achievement (good/insufficient) and place of residence (village/distant village) using GGM networks with four centrality measures

title: Extended Social Cognitive Theory framework integrating thoughtless GenAI use into triadic reciprocal determinism
description: The study adopts Social Cognitive Theory, which "conceptualizes human functioning as the dynamic interaction among three core dimensions: personal factors, behavior, and environment", as its core analytical framework. It extends SCT by incorporating TUGA as a behavior within the triadic system, so that thoughtless use, personal factors such as SE and MOV, and the GenAI-constituted environment jointly shape SDL. The article argues classical SCT’s static conception of environment lags behind GenAI’s "dynamic, autonomous, and interactive characteristics". Multi-group analysis operationalises SCT’s emphasis on individual differences for gender.
requirements: TUGA conceptualized as a behavioral pattern within the triadic reciprocal system alongside personal factors and the technological environment
constraints: The article states SCT’s traditional framework conceptualizes environment statically and lacks systematic theoretical support for gender-differentiated pathways in GenAI contexts

examples: The study surveyed 487 undergraduates and tested the hypothesized SCT-based model (Fig. 1) with PLS-SEM and multi-group analysis

title: Social-cognitive-theory-based moderated mediation framework linking critical thinking, engagement, self-efficacy, and competence
description: The article proposes and tests a moderated mediation framework grounded in social cognitive theory, in which "academic competence is shaped through the dynamic interplay of three interconnected factors: personal factors, behavioral factors, and environmental factors". Critical thinking (a personal cognitive resource) predicts engagement and competence; academic engagement serves as "a proximal mediator linking critical thinking to academic competence"; and academic self-efficacy, a domain-specific confidence belief, sets the boundary condition under which critical thinking translates into engagement. All six hypotheses were supported in the three-wave data, and the authors present the framework as a new explanatory account of how cognitive resources become academic competence in higher education.

description: The study organizes its analysis of learner agency through Bandura's Social Cognitive Theory, which "conceptualizes human functioning through triadic reciprocal causation where personal factors, behaviors, and environmental conditions influence one another." constraints: The article applies the framework within preclinical PBL in a single dental program; dimensions were examined through student perceptions rather than direct behavioral measures

The corpus supports trend, country, journal, author, keyword and thematic analyses, and the extended data are released in a Zenodo repository with R source code on GitHub.
requirements: Publications must be Scopus-indexed, English-language journal or proceedings documents discussing critical thinking in English language teaching
constraints: The article states that relying only on Scopus data limits the range of publications covered, and that manual screening and inconsistent author-name and institution data may affect conclusions
target_learners: Researchers and curriculum developers in English language teaching and higher education
target_learning_goals: Mapping research trends on critical thinking development in English language teaching
examples: Screening removed 21 papers for language and document type and 123 for relevance, leaving 129 publications collected on December 8, 2024

article_title: Modeling information literacy in Chinese physical education: the roles of technology integration, teaching practices, self-efficacy, and academic performance.
citation: Zhang Xiangle, Tian Hongxia. (2025). Modeling information literacy in Chinese physical education: the roles of technology integration, teaching practices, self-efficacy, and academic performance. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-26990-2
title: Integrated Social Cognitive Theory and Technology Acceptance Model framework for PE information literacy
description: The article proposes an integrated SCT-TAM framework in which personal, environmental, and technological factors jointly explain information literacy in physical education. SCT contributes self-efficacy as a psychological mechanism; TAM contributes perceived usefulness and ease of use of technology. As the authors put it, "TAM explains how technology affects information literacy, whereas SCT supports self-efficacy as a mitigating psychological aspect," with the learning environment linking the two models.
requirements: The learning environment must link the two models, allowing students to turn self-confidence and perceived utility into performance outcomes
constraints: The framework was examined in a cross-sectional survey of first-year PE undergraduates in five Chinese provinces and is presented as associations, not causal effects
target_learners: Undergraduate physical education students in Chinese colleges
target_learning_goals: Information literacy: locating, evaluating, and using information about physical activity and health
examples: The study operationalized the framework with seven Likert-scale constructs, including the Digital Competency Scale for information literacy and the TTIBUS scale for technology integration

citation: Bayram Hilal Çelik, Ergün Sibel. (2025). Effect of screen-based simulation on pediatric drug administration among nursing students: a randomized controlled trial. Revista da Escola de Enfermagem da USP. https://doi.org/10.1590/1980-220X-REEUSP-2025-0249en

"A total of four scenarios were created for the screen-based simulation": matching interacting drug groups in a fictional Family Health Center, weight-based dose calculation for home health patients, dry powder volume calculation, and listing the steps of drug administration in children. Students completed scenarios individually in a computer laboratory, each lasting approximately 10–15 minutes.

description: In resource preparation, the article recommends pointing trainees to key resources while withholding solutions. It states: "Prepare or indicate key learning resources for trainees, such as the latest version of the NCCN/CSCO lymphoma diagnosis and treatment guidelines, core textbook chapters, key review literature, and authoritative databases (such as UpToDate). article_title: PROMPTa-A multifaceted assessment approach to develop writing skills.
citation: Puro Vezolu, Nittala Noel Anurag Prashanth, A Hariharasudan. (2025). PROMPTa—A multifaceted assessment approach to develop writing skills. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0337342
title: Integrated SCT–constructivist–constructionist framework for ICT-mediated writing assessment
description: The study builds a unified conceptual framework drawing on Social Cognitive Theory, the Social Cognitive Model of Writing, Constructivism, and Constructionism. Its central premise is that "writing proficiency develops most effectively when learners are actively engaged in constructing meaning, regulating their progress, and receiving scaffolded feedback". ICT expands the space for meaningful engagement by letting students collaborate, share feedback, and monitor progress, operationalizing self-efficacy, collaborative meaning-making, and learner agency. The framework informed PROMPTa's design and the inclusion of peer, mentor, and expert feedback.
requirements: Iterative feedback loops and guided practice through which learners' self-efficacy beliefs develop
constraints: The article notes the outcomes are context-specific to the Nagaland undergraduate setting
target_learners: Undergraduate learners
target_learning_goals: Writing development through self-regulated, socially scaffolded practice
examples: The framework guided the design of PROMPTa's peer, mentor, and expert assessment rounds and process-based writing assessment

description: The article concludes that "simulated clinical scenarios, when used as a repetition tool in Dentistry, represent an effective pedagogical strategy". Repeating the same scenarios six months later, in a Gerodontology course that "shares content and instructors", coincided with significantly higher checklist scores, which the authors interpret as long-term improvement in clinical performance and retention.
requirements: The same scenarios repeated and re-evaluated with the same checklists in a later course sharing content and instructors
constraints: Students participated in clinical practice with real patients during the six-month interval, making it difficult to isolate the effect of simulation alone
No control group was used

target_learning_goals: long-term retention of clinical performance in dental emergencies and special care dentistry
examples: All students participated in 1 or 2 scenarios in the Special Needs Dentistry course and repeated them six months later in the Gerodontology course

article_title: A reflective learning conversation debriefing model for interprofessional simulation based education.
citation: Almomani Emad, Tobin John, Fernandes Sonia, Sullivan Jacqueline, Saadeh Omar, Mustafa Emad, Pattison Natalie, Alinier Guillaume. (2025). description: The authors recommend structured debriefing models such as RLC as a scaffolded route to higher reflective capacity for less experienced learners. They state: "Structured debriefing models like RLC may be especially valuable for junior or less experienced staff, who require scaffolded opportunities to build higher reflective capacity and advanced cognitive process." This is grounded in their finding that junior control-group participants, without a gradual and constructive framework, may struggle to sustain reflective practice independently.
requirements: Debriefers competent in applying the structured model flexibly rather than rigidly
constraints: Outcomes may reflect combined effects of the model, facilitator competence, and learner characteristics; the study did not isolate these

description: The article recommends that schools serving refugee children routinely assess cognitive skills and embed cognitive activity training within occupational therapy programs. The conclusion states that "cognitive skills should be assessed in schools for refugee children and cognitive activity training to be applied within the scope of rehabilitation should be included in occupational therapy programs for this population". This rests on the trial's finding that a school-based CAT program improved cognitive, academic, and quality-of-life outcomes in trauma-exposed refugee adolescents.

constraints: The authors note the study was conducted at a single center in Istanbul, which may restrict applicability, and that further research is needed on feasibility, scalability, and long-term sustainability of school-based implementation

examples: The trial screened 82 children at a single public secondary school in Istanbul and delivered CAT twice weekly for 10 weeks within the school setting

"At each stage, in case of mistakes, feedback is given to him on what things he did not consider and what would have been a better path for the examination." Correct choices receive a green card and mistakes a red card, making correctness visible at every decision point.

description: Each training unit pairs a short immersive simulation with a longer instructor-facilitated debriefing: "20 min of live simulation followed by 25 min of video-assisted debriefing". Instructors adjusted the simulated patient's condition during the scenario based on participant performance, then consolidated knowledge in the debrief.

Video documentation of scenarios for use in debriefing
Predefined core debriefing elements to keep debriefing standardized

nursing staff

description: Each simulation scene was standardized to include "a goal, the required non-technical skills, and the concrete operations needed to achieve that goal". title: Scientific Competence and Activity Scale (SCAS) for medical faculty research assistants
description: A 29-item, 5-point Likert self-report instrument measuring the scientific competence and activity of medical faculty research assistants, organized into four subdimensions: Competence (14 items), Literacy (8 items), Opportunities (4 items), and Barriers (3 items). Scores range from 29 to 145 with no reverse-scored items, and a cut-off of 92 separates those considered "competent and active" from those who are not. requirements: Respondents are research assistants in medical faculties; the authors advise re-testing the theoretical structure in different sample groups to generalize validity and reliability
constraints: The sample consisted solely of research assistants from a single medical faculty; known-groups validity analyses and test-retest analyses were not performed
target_learners: medical faculty research assistants (specialty and subspecialty trainees)
target_learning_goals: scientific research competence and activity, including research methodology knowledge, scientific literacy, and engagement in publications and projects
examples: Administered via Google Forms with a 15-item sociodemographic survey to 299 research assistants distributed proportionally across departments at Ankara University Faculty of Medicine between October 2023 and May 2024

constraints: Implementation processes and educational efficacy remain insufficiently investigated within nursing education contexts, per the article

citation: Zhou LongYuan, Cai Chang, Wu RuiLan, Qi Yong. (2025). Effectiveness of scaffolded case-based learning in anesthesiology residency training: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07236-1

In this study STM was integrated with case-based discussion to teach complex HOCM anesthesia management, progressing from intensive guidance to autonomous practice.

citation: Jia Xiaoshi, Guo Jiawen, Wu Maodan, Wang Xiaodong, Fan Le, Yao Yichen, Deng Xiaoyi, Yang Ling. (2025). Study on the effect of simulation-based case teaching method on the preclinical teaching of tooth defects restoration. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07010-3

description: The article's SCT course is a situational teaching pattern in which "teachers provide background information of typical cases and students solve problems and propose different solutions through discussion and analysis". Students query a teacher role-playing the patient, discuss feasible restoration plans in groups of 8, perform the chosen preparation or restoration on a head model, report, defend their plan under teacher questioning, and handle simulated post-treatment problems. Group work is scored across operating process (20), teeth preparation (30), oral presentation (35) and defense (15), totalling 100 points.

Two cases are needed: one for classroom teaching and one for before-and-after effect evaluation

title: A 12-week scenario-based simulation course pattern: three themed units, each following a four-step weekly sequence from introduction to role-play with simulated patients to tested counseling with debriefing
description: The course pattern organizes clinical communication training into three four-week units — nutrition assessment of diabetes, diabetes education, and nutrition education for hyperlipidemia — each with a two-hour weekly session. Weeks progress from introduction via narration and Q&A, through video simulation observation with small-group discussion, to hands-on role-play with trained simulated patients who give immediate feedback, ending with a tested counseling encounter and a debriefing led by a senior dietitian. The design used Jeffries et al.'s simulation framework with "a gradual increase in complexity to facilitate deep learning".

Instructional materials developed with senior dietitians and reviewed by experts for content validity
Examiners with OSCE accreditation and consensus/scoring training for SPs and examiners
constraints: The intervention was conducted at a single institution, which the authors state limits generalizability
The 12-week duration aligned with academic schedules but may have constrained long-term skill development
target_learners: third-year undergraduate dietetic students
target_learning_goals: clinical communication competence in nutrition assessment and education
examples: Week 3 of each unit used hands-on role-play with simulated patients — fourth-year students trained on structured scripts — observed by a researcher and a senior dietitian
Week 4 randomly selected one student per group to counsel a simulated patient, followed by a senior-dietitian-led debriefing

description: This article applies a co-created framework of best practices for physical activity counseling with adults with spinal cord injury, developed by an international multidisciplinary expert panel. It is organized into two branches: "best practices on how to have a conversation and best practices on what to discuss about PA", covering building rapport, a client-centered approach in the spirit of motivational interviewing, and tailoring support. description: The SCT is described as "a validated tool for evaluating diagnostic reasoning and adaptability in high-fidelity, real-world context situations" that assesses how certainty in a diagnostic hypothesis evolves as new clinical information is introduced. In this study it was administered as pre-tests and post-tests of 30 questions each, with students randomly assigned to one of two test sets to minimize familiarity, covering the 10 clinical symptoms of the TBL course on a 30-point scale. It assesses ten dimensions: somatization, obsessive–compulsive symptoms, interpersonal sensitivity, depression, anxiety, hostility, phobic anxiety, paranoid ideation, psychoticism, and additional sleep/diet items. In this study it was used to screen 6,923 undergraduates and classify positivity against national norms.

citation: Gu Xiaoxia, Hassan Norlizah Che, Sulaiman Tajularipin, Wei Zhixia, Dong Jingyi. (2024). The impact of video game playing on Chinese adolescents’ academic achievement: Evidence from a moderated multi-mediation model. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0313405
title: A social cognitive theory-based moderated multi-mediation model of video game playing and academic achievement
description: The article proposes and tests a moderated mediation model grounded in Bandura's social cognitive theory, in which video game playing affects academic achievement directly and indirectly through two parallel individual-level self-processes, self-educational expectation and learning attitude, with parent-child relationship as a family-level moderator of the direct path and the expectation path. The authors argue that "most external influences work through intermediary self-processing rather than directly affecting human functioning", so gaming operates on internal cognitions rather than only on behavior. The model was supported for the direct path and both mediation paths, with moderation confirmed for two of three moderated paths.
requirements: Measures of video game playing, self-educational expectation, learning attitude, parent-child relationship, and academic achievement within one dataset
Control of individual, family, and school covariates when estimating paths
constraints: Cross-sectional design constrains causal inference, as the authors state
Sample limited to Chinese junior high students who visit net bars or video arcades
target_learners: Chinese junior high school adolescents
examples: Tested on 824 CEPS Grade 8 students using PROCESS macro parallel and moderated mediation models with 5,000 bootstrap samples

title: Scaffold and govern ultrasound training continuously across medical school and internship, starting early with gradually increasing complexity
description: The article recommends organizing ultrasound education as a scaffolded, governed continuum rather than isolated courses: "Starting early – possibly in medical school – with a scaffolded educational plan continuously offering support while gradually increasing complexity fosters skill development". Training governance and scaffolding continuous learning are presented as responses to interns' independently pursued training and prevalent barriers. The recommendation rests on the survey's findings that structured components and tests associated with perceived competence.
requirements: Requires structured educational components including practical training on patients, required scan numbers, and competence tests, which the article found associated with perceived competence.
Requires continuous exposure to ultrasound, since the article states scanning competence develops over time and requires practice.
constraints: Traditional lectures cannot stand alone, and restricting teaching to short practical sessions is insufficient according to the article.
Implementation has previously been challenged by lack of qualified faculty teachers and ultrasound equipment, though the article says the importance of these factors may be transient.
Filled curricula in medical school and internship pose dilemmas for prioritization.

Medical interns in their postgraduate internship year
examples: The survey found 68.5% of interns had to pursue ultrasound training independently during internship, which the authors cite as evidence that organizational scaffolding may be needed.

title: Social Cognitive Theory (SCT) chain mediation model of social support, self-efficacy, learning engagement and academic performance
description: The article operationalizes Bandura's Social Cognitive Theory as a chain mediation model in which "human behavior is influenced by three variables: personal factors (e.g., self-efficacy), behavioral factors (e.g., learning engagement and achievement), and environmental factors (e.g., social support)." Within this framework, supportive relationships from peers, parents and educators raise adolescents' self-efficacy, which in turn raises learning engagement and thereby academic performance. The theory is used both to derive the study's four hypotheses (H1–H4) and to interpret the finding that social support was the primary source of learning engagement. The results of the structural model are presented as supporting the framework within the Chinese exam-oriented context.
requirements: Measurement of social support, self-efficacy and learning engagement with validated Likert-scale instruments, and standardized academic scores, so the four SCT-identified factors can be modeled
constraints: The authors state the model was tested within China's test-oriented learning environment, which may limit applicability to other educational contexts
target_learners: Chinese middle school adolescents aged 13-15
target_learning_goals: Improving academic performance in Chinese, Math and English
examples: The authors developed a theoretical model (Fig 1) under SCT guidance and tested it with SEM in Amos 24.0 on survey data from four middle schools in Shandong Province

title: Script theory: clinicians organize knowledge as illness scripts built through experience, underpinning script concordance testing
description: Script theory, derived from cognitive psychology, holds that health care providers organize, store, and access knowledge through 'illness scripts' that support pattern recognition and drawing on previous clinical experience during patient care. Scripts form over years of practice and help clinicians recognize diagnoses, choose treatments, and decide efficiently in novel situations. This framework is the stated theoretical basis for script concordance tests, which present ambiguous clinical vignettes scored by concordance with a reference panel.
requirements: Scripts are formed throughout years of practice, so the framework presupposes accumulated clinical experience for expert-level reasoning.
target_learners: first-year Doctor of Physical Therapy students
health professions students
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning in situations of uncertainty and ambiguity
examples: The study's SCT presented clinical vignettes with follow-up questions asking how new information reinforces or weakens clinical judgment, scored against a reference panel's modal answers.

citation: Kojich Lindsey, Miller Stephanie A., Axman Katelyn, Eacret Timothy, Koontz J. Atticus, Smith Caroline. (2024). Evaluating clinical reasoning in first year DPT students using a script concordance test. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05281-w
title: A 77-item script concordance test for first-year DPT clinical reasoning, developed over four phases and scored by aggregate scoring against a reference panel
description: The article describes a script concordance test built from thirty clinical vignettes with three follow-up questions each, mapped to first-year DPT curriculum objectives and CAPTE accreditation standards. It presents new case information and asks test takers how it impacts clinical judgment on a 5-point Likert scale, with no single correct answer. Scoring uses aggregate scoring: answers matching the reference panel's modal answer receive full credit and other answers receive partial credit proportional to panel endorsement. Thirteen items were eliminated in optimization, yielding a 77-item test.
requirements: A reference panel of 15-20 experienced clinicians is desirable for SCT reliability and validity, per literature the authors cite.
constraints: The SCT was developed from the content of one DPT curriculum, and the authors note institutions with differing curricular structure may find it not applicable to their first-year students.
target_learners: first-year Doctor of Physical Therapy students
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning in ambiguous, uncertain clinical situations
examples: Administered via Qualtrics to 44 students proctored in person and to 15 reference panel physical therapists virtually, with a three-minute instructional video preceding the test.

description: The study's training cycle embeds DAS guideline learning inside the same simulation environment where deficits were observed. Debriefing followed the standardized TALK system covering Target, Analysis, Learning points, and Key actions.
requirements: A simulation environment with mannequin, monitor, and a full set of airway tools sufficient for every step of the protocol being taught
Instructors with background in both the clinical domain and simulation teaching
A structured debriefing framework (here, TALK) applied after each scenario
constraints: Skill retention was demonstrated only to six months; one-year retention was not assessed
A single training centre; small sample (24 consented, 19 returned at 6 months) limits power
Simulation of this fidelity "may not be considered a replacement to the real clinical experience, but are viewed here as a way to complement it"

procedural skills such as intubation with bougie/Airtraq and cricothyroidotomy
decision-making including timely call for help and surgical airway initiation
examples: 24 anaesthesiologists completed two scenarios (CI, CICV) with TALK debrief, received DAS protocol learning and hands-on practice (intubation with bougie, Airtraq, cricothyroidotomy with scalpel, bougie, tube technique) on the same SimMom mannequin, then repeated scenarios the next day and six months later.

title: Self-guided e-learning course on SCI physical activity counselling best practices (10 modules plus bonus material)
description: A self-guided e-learning course co-developed by an international expert panel to familiarize health, fitness and lifestyle professionals with the best practices for SCI physical activity counselling. It comprises 10 modules plus two bonus reflection modules, targets the 'remembering' and 'understanding' levels of the revised Bloom's Taxonomy, follows UDL Guidelines, and takes on average about 2.5 hours to complete. The course will be made freely available after the study.
requirements: Designed for professionals who provide guidance or counselling to adults with SCI on starting, changing and/or maintaining a physically active lifestyle
Learning objectives: describe and understand the best practices, understand how to use them in conversations, and use SCI-specific physical activity knowledge
constraints: Some participants experienced technical difficulties, including the system not saving progress between sessions
Participants suggested adding closed captions and more counselling example videos
target_learners: Health, fitness and lifestyle professionals (counsellors, physiotherapists, occupational and recreation therapists, fitness trainers, SCI peer mentors)
target_learning_goals: Knowledge of SCI physical activity counselling best practices
Self-efficacy for using the best practices in conversations with clients with SCI
examples: In the RCT, 21 intervention participants completed the course within one week of the pre-survey; pilot testing showed it takes on average ~ 2.5 h to complete

article_title: Efficiently exploring the causal role of contextual moderators in behavioral science.
citation: Hecht, C. A., Dweck, C. S., Murphy, M. C., Kroeper, K. M., & Yeager, D. S. (2022). Efficiently exploring the causal role of contextual moderators in behavioral science. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America, 120(1). https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2216315120
title: Scenario study approach for efficiently interrogating causal contextual moderators of behavioral interventions
description: A three-part experimental method the article proposes and illustrates: (a) craft scenarios that vividly represent candidate moderating contexts based on available observational, survey, and experimental evidence; (b) measure a short-term behavioral outcome known to relate to typical intervention outcomes; and (c) randomly assign participants to scenario conditions to assess "the causal effect of the moderating context on the link between the psychological variable typically targeted by interventions and this short-term outcome". It is positioned as a bridge between initial identification of measured moderators and large, costly multisite field experiments.
requirements: The scenario must be able to evoke the contextual moderator, causing the participant to vividly and authentically imagine the real-life situations important to the theory
It must be possible to measure a choice at immediate posttest that is a reasonable, unbiased proxy for the intervention outcome of interest
constraints: The method may be less informative when there is only one plausible interpretation of a moderator, as with a form-simplification nudge effective only among people who have not yet filled out the form
target_learners: Adolescent students in secondary school contexts
target_learning_goals: Understanding when contextual conditions causally enable learners to act on targeted motivational beliefs
examples: The method was applied across four experiments manipulating teachers' mindset messages and structural opportunities to test their causal moderating role in the growth mindset–choice link
key_sources: Hecht, C. A., Dweck, C. S., Murphy, M. C., Kroeper, K. M., & Yeager, D. S. (2022). Efficiently exploring the causal role of contextual moderators in behavioral science. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America, 120(1). https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2216315120

article_title: Classroom-Based Physical Activity as a Means to Improve Self-Efficacy and Academic Achievement among Normal-Weight and Overweight Youth.
citation: Latino Francesca, Tafuri Francesco, Saraiello Emma, Tafuri Domenico. (2023). Classroom-Based Physical Activity as a Means to Improve Self-Efficacy and Academic Achievement among Normal-Weight and Overweight Youth. Nutrients 15(9):2061. https://doi.org/10.3390/nu15092061
title: Social-cognitive-theory-based design of physical activity breaks to build self-efficacy
description: The intervention was planned in accordance with the social-cognitive theory, under which "self-efficacy perceptions as feelings based on 4 main lines of evidence: past performances, vicarious experiences, verbal persuasion and physiological state". The program translated these sources into design choices: enjoyable activities calibrated so overweight students could succeed, occasions for students to influence each other as a team, verbal encouragement, and avoidance of competition to reduce exercise anxiety. Sessions moved from flexibility work through moderate-to-vigorous aerobic exercise to a cool-down, with intensity monitored on the OMNI scale.
requirements: Sessions must be enjoyable and calibrated so that overweight students can achieve success
Intensity must be monitored to stay in the MVPA range (5 < RPE < 8)
constraints: The article frames this design for a school science-class setting with certified physical education teachers supervising
target_learners: adolescents aged 14–15, overweight and non-overweight
examples: Each 20-min break used warm-up exercises such as marching in place and high knees, a 15-min moderate-to-vigorous aerobic core, and static cool-down stretches
key_sources: Latino Francesca, Tafuri Francesco, Saraiello Emma, Tafuri Domenico. (2023). Classroom-Based Physical Activity as a Means to Improve Self-Efficacy and Academic Achievement among Normal-Weight and Overweight Youth. Nutrients 15(9):2061. https://doi.org/10.3390/nu15092061

article_title: Scalable Science Education via Online Cooperative Questioning.
citation: Hilton, C. B., Goldwater, M. B., Hancock, D., Clemson, M., Huang, A., & Denyer, G. (2022). Scalable Science Education via Online Cooperative Questioning. CBE—Life Sciences Education, 21(1). https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.19-11-0249
title: Scaffold question authoring with self-explanation, analogical comparison, and misconception confrontation to elicit deep engagement
description: The principle holds that having students author multiple-choice questions benefits learning deeply only when the authoring process is explicitly supported. The article states that "unscaffolded question authoring is potentially not enough to elicit these broad and deep conceptual benefits" and therefore designed exercises that "leverage analogical comparison, self-explanation, and confronting misconceptions," with instructor and peer feedback. Students are prompted to consider how information was discovered, how inhibitors or mutations would produce results, and what common misconceptions could serve as plausible distractors.
requirements: Explicit scaffolding activities and prompts; a peer platform for feedback; instructor evaluation of question quality
constraints: It remains for future research to more systematically test and compare different approaches for encouraging deeper forms of engagement
target_learners: large tertiary undergraduate science classes
target_learning_goals: deep conceptual understanding, question quality, transfer to novel contexts
examples: The step 3 instructions asked students to write at least five statements on an allocated learning outcome, share a draft MCQ with a peer, and embed the question in experimental or problem-solving context.
key_sources: Hilton, C. B., Goldwater, M. B., Hancock, D., Clemson, M., Huang, A., & Denyer, G. (2022). Scalable Science Education via Online Cooperative Questioning. CBE—Life Sciences Education, 21(1). https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.19-11-0249

article_title: Evaluation of a Physical Activity and Multi-Micronutrient Intervention on Cognitive and Academic Performance in South African Primary Schoolchildren.
citation: Beckmann Johanna, Nqweniso Siphesihle, Ludyga Sebastian, du Randt Rosa, Gresse Annelie, Long Kurt Z., Nienaber Madeleine, Seelig Harald, Pühse Uwe, Steinmann Peter, Utzinger Jürg, Walter Cheryl, Gerber Markus, Lang Christin. (2022). Evaluation of a Physical Activity and Multi-Micronutrient Intervention on Cognitive and Academic Performance in South African Primary Schoolchildren. Nutrients. https://doi.org/10.3390/nu14132609
title: School-based PA and nutrition interventions shown to work in high-income countries cannot simply be transferred to disadvantaged South African primary schools without redesign
description: The article concludes that interventions known to benefit inhibitory control elsewhere do not automatically work in marginalized settings, and that "interventions, such as PA programs, which are known to benefit inhibitory control (in Western and high-income countries) cannot easily be transferred to primary school-aged children attending South African quintile 3 public schools". It calls for determining optimal program design for these contexts.
requirements: Future studies must determine the optimal design (type, frequency and intensity) of school-based PA programs and the optimal nutrition programs for older children from marginalized areas.
constraints: Results come from peri-urban quintile-3 schools and might not apply to urban or rural areas, other socioeconomic backgrounds, or other LMICs.
target_learners: Primary schoolchildren (grades 1–4, ages 6–12) in marginalized, peri-urban communities
examples: The 12-week KaziKidz-based PA program (two weekly 45-min lessons) plus daily MMNS chewing tablets showed no benefit over placebo in the cluster-RCT.

article_title: The longitudinal association between objectively-measured school-day physical activity and academic achievement in US elementary school students.
citation: Elish Paul N., Bryan Cassandra S., Boedeker Peter J., Calvert Hannah G., Kay Christi M., Meyer Adria M., Gazmararian Julie A. (2022). The longitudinal association between objectively-measured school-day physical activity and academic achievement in US elementary school students. International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12966-022-01328-7
title: Schools can implement school-based MVPA at recommended levels without meaningfully detracting from academic progress
description: The article's central design recommendation is that concerns about school-day physical activity harming academics are not well founded: even doubling the recommended 30 daily minutes would lower grades only about 2 points on a 100-point scale. It recommends schools "increase MVPA in ways that do not compete with other academic subjects, such as during recess, in enhanced PE classes, and through 'academic accelerators'". Schools should be considered appropriate venues for PA promotion supporting physical, mental, and emotional development.
requirements: School-based MVPA implemented in accordance with the 30-minute in-school recommendation
constraints: Findings are for school-day MVPA only, not full-day MVPA; no Grade 5 standardized tests were conducted because of COVID-related disruptions; results come from one suburban Georgia district
target_learners: Elementary school students (Grade 4)
target_learning_goals: Maintaining academic achievement while increasing school-day physical activity
examples: In this sample, a 10-minute increase in daily school-day MVPA would meet the recommendation for 30 minutes of school-day MVPA; the cluster-randomized Health Empowers You! intervention raised MVPA by 3 to over 5 minutes daily without meaningful academic harm
key_sources: Elish Paul N., Bryan Cassandra S., Boedeker Peter J., Calvert Hannah G., Kay Christi M., Meyer Adria M., Gazmararian Julie A. (2022). article_title: The Associations Between Sluggish Cognitive Tempo, Internalizing Symptoms, and Academic Performance in Children With Reading Disorder: A Longitudinal Cohort Study.
citation: Hossain Bushra, Bent Stephen, Parenteau China, Widjaja Felicia, Davis Matthew, Hendren Robert L. (2022). The Associations Between Sluggish Cognitive Tempo, Internalizing Symptoms, and Academic Performance in Children With Reading Disorder: A Longitudinal Cohort Study. Journal of Attention Disorders. https://doi.org/10.1177/10870547221085493
title: Sluggish cognitive tempo as a clinical construct distinct from ADHD-Inattention
description: The article treats SCT as a constellation of symptoms including "lethargy, daydreaming, drowsiness, mental confusion, and slowed behavior and thinking." It presents SCT as a distinct construct rather than a symptom of ADHD-Inattention, citing a meta-analysis of 73 factor analytic studies in which SCT items consistently loaded on the SCT factor rather than the ADHD factor. In this study's own exploratory factor analysis, the 15 K-SCT items grouped into three factors (Daydreaming, Working Memory Problems, Sleepy/Tired) while ADHD-IN items formed a separate factor. The construct is measured with the Kiddie-SCT Rating Scale.
requirements: Measured with a multi-item rating scale such as the 15-item K-SCT, which has parent and teacher versions and scores 0 to 45.
constraints: The article notes the K-SCT Rating Scale has not been formally validated in an RD population.
target_learners: children and adolescents aged 6–18 with reading disorder
target_learning_goals: identifying SCT symptoms that may exacerbate academic and internalizing difficulties in learners with reading disorder
key_sources: Hossain Bushra, Bent Stephen, Parenteau China, Widjaja Felicia, Davis Matthew, Hendren Robert L. (2022). The Associations Between Sluggish Cognitive Tempo, Internalizing Symptoms, and Academic Performance in Children With Reading Disorder: A Longitudinal Cohort Study. article_title: Change in pre- and in-service early childhood educators' knowledge, self-efficacy, and intentions following an e-learning course in physical activity and sedentary behaviour: a pilot study.
citation: Bruijns BA, Vanderloo LM, Johnson AM, Adamo KB, Burke SM, Carson V, Heydon R, Irwin JD, Naylor P-J, Timmons BW, Tucker P. (2022). Change in pre- and in-service early childhood educators’ knowledge, self-efficacy, and intentions following an e-learning course in physical activity and sedentary behaviour: a pilot study. BMC Public Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-022-12591-5
title: Social Cognitive Theory and Theory of Planned Behaviour constructs as the framework for educator-focused movement-behaviour interventions
description: The article frames educator training effects through Social Cognitive Theory and the Theory of Planned Behaviour, which "highlight the importance of self-efficacy, behavioural intention (i.e., likelihood to perform a behaviour), and perceived behavioural control (i.e., perception of the ease or difficulty to perform a behaviour) for behaviour change". Self-efficacy is described as developed from knowledge acquisition and thus predicted to be influenced by educational interventions, while intention is described as the closest factor to behaviour and often regulated by perceived control. The study measures these constructs as indicators of potential behaviour change in ECEs.
requirements: Educator-based constructs (self-efficacy, behavioural intention, perceived behavioural control) must be measured to index potential behaviour change, which the article notes is infrequently done in childcare intervention studies
constraints: The article notes few studies have explored the direct relationship between educator training and improved physical activity levels among children in childcare
target_learners: pre- and in-service early childhood educators
target_learning_goals: confidence and intention to promote physical activity and minimize sedentary behaviour in childcare
examples: The pilot measured self-efficacy with the ECE-COMPASS tool informed by Bandura's Guide for Creating Self-Efficacy Scales, and intention and perceived control with the ECE-MBIPC questionnaire informed by TPB questionnaire construction recommendations
key_sources: Bruijns BA, Vanderloo LM, Johnson AM, Adamo KB, Burke SM, Carson V, Heydon R, Irwin JD, Naylor P-J, Timmons BW, Tucker P. (2022).
