article_title: The impact of psychopathology on academic performance in school-age children and adolescents.
citation: Pagerols M, Prat R, Rivas C, Español-Martín G, Puigbó J, Pagespetit È, Haro JM, Ramos-Quiroga JA, Casas M, Bosch R. (2022). The impact of psychopathology on academic performance in school-age children and adolescents. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-08242-9
title: Provide school-based mental health assessment and treatment interventions to support students' functioning at school
description: The article concludes that subclinical psychiatric symptoms are independently associated with academic performance, which "emphasize[s] the need for preventive and treatment interventions targeted at students' mental health to improve their psychological well-being and functioning at school". It cites a Canadian early preventive intervention that increased high-school completion rates and a Chilean school-based mental health program linked to better academic progress. It further recommends programs give students resources to manage motivation and cope with stress.
requirements: Programs should target students whose symptoms are not extreme enough to attract a diagnosis as well as diagnosed students, since subclinical symptoms were independently associated with grades.
constraints: The supporting evidence is cross-sectional; the article states the design "hinders the ability to establish conclusions on causal relationships".
target_learners: School-age children and adolescents aged 5–17 in primary and secondary education
target_learning_goals: Improve academic performance and psychological well-being and functioning at school
examples: The article cites early preventive intervention for individuals at risk of antisocial behavior in Canada increasing high-school completion, and the world's largest school-based mental health program in Chile leading to better academic progress among students whose mental health improved.
key_sources: Pagerols M, Prat R, Rivas C, Español-Martín G, Puigbó J, Pagespetit È, Haro JM, Ramos-Quiroga JA, Casas M, Bosch R. (2022). The impact of psychopathology on academic performance in school-age children and adolescents. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-08242-9

article_title: The Role of Academic Achievement in the Relationship between School Ethos and Adolescent Distress and Aggression: A Study of Ninth Grade Students in the Segregated School Landscape of Stockholm.
citation: Granvik Saminathen Maria; Plenty Stephanie; Modin Bitte. (2020). The Role of Academic Achievement in the Relationship between School Ethos and Adolescent Distress and Aggression: A Study of Ninth Grade Students in the Segregated School Landscape of Stockholm. Journal of Youth and Adolescence. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8116286/
title: School ethos as a teacher-level, value-based dimension of school effectiveness distinct from school climate
description: The article defines school ethos as "a fundamental element of the broader theory of school effectiveness", experienced at the teacher level and encompassing "the beliefs, values and norms that shape the way that teachers and students relate, interact, and behave towards each other". It is measured as a unidimensional school-level composite of 12 teacher-reported items covering value-system clarity, teacher expectations and motivation, anti-bullying interventions, student-teacher relationships and staff turnover, aggregated to school means. The construct is treated as distinct from school climate and as potentially compensating for students' family background.
requirements: Requires teacher reports aggregated to school-level means; the index was developed in a previous study and showed Cronbach's alpha of 0.90
constraints: Assessed in lower secondary schools in Stockholm; ethos is an exploratory measure considered distinct from school climate
target_learners: Ninth-grade students aged 15-16 in lower secondary schools
examples: Teachers responded to 12 items such as "At this school we have a value system (värdegrund) which is clear to students" and "Teachers have high expectations of student performance", summed and aggregated to the school mean

article_title: Using working memory performance to predict mathematics performance 2 years on.
citation: Allen, K., Giofrè, D., Higgins, S., & Adams, J. (2020). Using working memory performance to predict mathematics performance 2 years on. Psychological Research. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00426-020-01382-5
title: Screen children for mathematics risk using measures predictive over longer periods of time
description: Because the working memory components predictive of mathematics change with age, screening instruments should prioritise measures whose predictive value persists over years rather than only capturing immediate risk. The article states that "when developing a screening measure, children should be screened on measures that are predictive over longer periods of time", while still including shorter-term predictors to pick up children who fall behind immediately. This follows from the finding that different working memory subcomponents predict mathematics at different ages.
requirements: Knowledge of which elements of working memory are most important for mathematics at different ages.
constraints: Shorter-term predictors should also be included to identify children likely to fall behind immediately.
target_learners: children in the early years of formal schooling
target_learning_goals: early identification of children at risk of mathematics difficulties
examples: The study used working memory measures administered once in year 3 to predict mathematics performance in year 5.

article_title: Reliability and validity study of the Spanish adaptation of the "Student Satisfaction and Self-Confidence in Learning Scale" (SCLS).
citation: Farrés-Tarafa M, Bande D, Roldán-Merino J, Hurtado-Pardos B, Biurrun-Garrido A, Molina-Raya L, Raurell-Torredà M, Casas I, Lorenzo-Seva U. (2021). Reliability and validity study of the Spanish adaptation of the “Student Satisfaction and Self-Confidence in Learning Scale” (SCLS). PLoS ONE 16(7): e0255188. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0255188
title: Spanish adaptation of the 13-item Student Satisfaction and Self-Confidence in Learning Scale (SCLS)
description: The SCLS-Spanish is a translated and validated 13-item questionnaire measuring two dimensions: "Satisfaction with Current Learning" (items 1 to 5, score range 5–25) and "Self-confidence in Learning" (items 6 to 13, range 8–40), each rated on a five-point Likert scale from strongly disagree to strongly agree. It was adapted by independent bilingual translation and back-translation following the Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing, with the expert committee changing "teacher" to "Instructor/facilitator". Administration takes 5–10 minutes and it is administered at the end of every simulation session.
requirements: Requires students to have performed some clinical simulation during the course and to give consent to participate
Translation permission and copyright are held by the National League for Nursing (NLN)
constraints: Validated on a convenience sample from a single university in Barcelona, so results may not generalise to all nursing students, though the sample's characteristics are similar to other Spanish universities
target_learners: undergraduate nursing students
target_learning_goals: assessing student satisfaction with simulation-based instruction
assessing student self-confidence in learning during clinical simulation
examples: Administered at the end of every simulation session to 489 nursing students across second, third and fourth academic years in the 2018–19 academic year

article_title: Remote training in laparoscopy: a randomized trial comparing home-based self-regulated training to centralized instructor-regulated training.
citation: Sloth Sigurd Beier, Jensen Rune Dall, Seyer-Hansen Mikkel, Christensen Mette Krogh, De Win Gunter. (2021). Remote training in laparoscopy: a randomized trial comparing home-based self-regulated training to centralized instructor-regulated training. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-021-08429-7
title: Scaffolding for self-regulated learning: temporary support structures that enable learners to perform beyond their independent capacity
description: The article frames HSRT through self-regulated learning and scaffolding: scaffolding is "a dynamic pedagogical tool based on a flexible, temporary, and ‘teacher-regulated’ structure of support, which is gradually dismantled as the learner progress towards independence". It links scaffolding to Vygotsky's zone of proximal development and to directed self-regulated learning, in which trainees organize their own training within designed educational supports. In the study, the scaffolding for HSRT comprised proficiency-based training with protected training time, instructional videos, process goals, computer-generated feedback, self-evaluation, and written feedback on submitted videos.
requirements: Supportive instructional designs with educational supports such as goal lists, video instructions, video reviews, and computer-generated feedback, which the article says have proven effective for simulation-based training
constraints: The article states SRL should not be framed as an individualistic activity and that extrinsic performance goals can sometimes have unfavorable effects on trainees' performances
target_learners: First-year trainees in abdominal surgery, gynecology, and urology
target_learning_goals: Basic laparoscopic psychomotor skills including hand–eye coordination, bimanual coordination, and suturing with intracorporeal knot-tying
examples: HSRT trainees trained at home with the eoSim box trainer and SurgTrac software, submitted video-recorded performances, and received short written corrective feedback when videos did not meet proficiency criteria

article_title: Effects of a school-based physical activity intervention on academic performance in 14-year old adolescents: a cluster randomized controlled trial - the School in Motion study.
citation: Solberg Runar Barstad, Steene-Johannessen Jostein, Anderssen Sigmund Alfred, Ekelund Ulf, Säfvenbom Reidar, Haugen Tommy, Berntsen Sveinung, Åvitsland Andreas, Lerum Øystein, Resaland Geir Kåre, Kolle Elin. (2021). Effects of a school-based physical activity intervention on academic performance in 14-year old adolescents: a cluster randomized controlled trial – the School in Motion study. BMC Public Health 21, 871. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-021-10901-x
title: School in Motion (ScIM) physically active learning and Don't worry – Be Happy interventions
description: ScIM comprised two multicomponent school-based PA interventions for ninth-grade adolescents, each targeting approximately 120 min/week of additional PA on top of mandatory PE. The PAL intervention "consisted of three components" — 30 min of PA in academic subjects, 60 min of PE, and 30 min of student-chosen activity — grounded in a socio-ecological framework, with an online toolkit of activities. DWBH consisted of two components: a self-organized 'Be happy' activity class chosen by interest-based groups across classes, and a student-led 'Don't worry' PE lesson, anchored in an integrative relational developmental systems approach promoting friendship through PA.
requirements: At least one teacher per intervention school attended a one-day delivery course; all intervention components were mandatory and adherence self-reported weekly on an online platform
constraints: Delivery averaged 78–83% of the 120 min/week target, ranging 67–95% across schools, mainly due to exams, holidays and school trips
target_learners: 14-year-old lower secondary school students (ninth grade) in Norway
target_learning_goals: Increased physical activity during school hours and improved academic performance in numeracy and reading
examples: Thirty schools were cluster-randomized 1:1:1 to PAL, DWBH or control during the 2017/2018 school year; intervention schools received $90 per student to cover increased expenses

(2021). Effects of a school-based physical activity intervention on academic performance in 14-year old adolescents: a cluster randomized controlled trial – the School in Motion study. article_title: Usability of mental illness simulation involving scenarios with patients with schizophrenia via immersive virtual reality: A mixed methods study.
citation: Lee Youngho, Kim Sun Kyung, Eom Mi-Ran. (2020). Usability of mental illness simulation involving scenarios with patients with schizophrenia via immersive virtual reality: A mixed methods study. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0238437
title: 360-degree video VR simulation program for schizophrenia symptoms (five scenarios, ten clips, Oculus Go HMDs)
description: A mental health nursing VR simulation delivering "360-degree videos of five different scenarios reflecting clinical symptoms of schizophrenia patients and related treatment tasks" via Oculus Go head-mounted displays, filmed with Gear 360 cameras and developed in Unity3D. "Five different scenarios were developed that incorporated five different symptoms of schizophrenia—risk of violation, auditory hallucination, visual hallucination, delusion, and risk of suicide," enacted by professional actors in two constructed rooms (a patient room and a day room). Ten clips of 60-90 seconds each are followed by on-screen decision-making questions and scenario-based quizzes with therapeutic-communication tasks.
requirements: Scenario scripts written by a researcher and reviewed by two professors and one mental health nursing professional, with videos validated for realism by psychiatric professionals and a nurse practitioner.
Participants receive phased instructions on HMD and controller use (about 15-20 minutes) before the simulation.
constraints: Participants were instructed not to use the device for more than 20 minutes at a time.
Rooms were open two to three hours per day under research-assistant supervision.
target_learners: Undergraduate nursing students in their last semester who have completed most clinical placements
target_learning_goals: Clinical decision-making in acute psychiatric settings
examples: The intervention delivered ten video clips (two per scenario) on Oculus Go HMDs, with on-screen questions after each clip testing decision-making such as recognizing a threatening situation and choosing appropriate medication.
key_sources: Lee Youngho, Kim Sun Kyung, Eom Mi-Ran. (2020). Usability of mental illness simulation involving scenarios with patients with schizophrenia via immersive virtual reality: A mixed methods study. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0238437

article_title: Dogs' insensitivity to scaffolding behaviour in an A-not-B task provides support for the theory of natural pedagogy.
citation: Neilands P., Kingsley-Smith O., Taylor A. H. (2021). Dogs’ insensitivity to scaffolding behaviour in an A-not-B task provides support for the theory of natural pedagogy. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-020-79557-8
title: Scaffolding effectiveness may depend on learners interpreting ostensive cues as informative rather than merely attending to them
description: The article proposes that scaffolding behaviour works not simply by redirecting attention but because learners expect ostensive-communicative cues to carry relevant, generalizable information. Dogs sensitive to such cues did not benefit from scaffolding, suggesting that effective scaffolding requires the learner to treat the cue as informative about a specific object or location. This distinguishes deep scaffolding effects from mere stimulus enhancement or social facilitation.
requirements: Learners must interpret ostensive-communicative cues as informative rather than as commands or requests
constraints: Demonstrated only as an explanation for the absence of scaffolding effects in dogs; the positive case in children relies on cited prior literature
target_learners: young children
learners of any species sensitive to ostensive cues
examples: In the experiment, experimenter pointing and route demonstration before release produced no improvement in dogs' A-not-B performance

article_title: Actor feedback and rigorous monitoring: Essential quality assurance tools for testing behavioral interventions with simulation.
citation: Abshire Martha A., Li Xintong, Basyal Pragyashree Sharma, Teply Melissa L., Singh Arun L., Hayes Margaret M., Turnbull Alison E. (2020). Actor feedback and rigorous monitoring: Essential quality assurance tools for testing behavioral interventions with simulation. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0233538
title: SCIP trial simulation quality assurance program for standardizing actor performances
description: The quality assurance program built for the SCIP randomized trial combined a two-person QA team of clinical fellows who reviewed every simulation video and transcript, double data entry in REDCap with discrepancy resolution, an operations manual for consistent error coding, and three feedback modes for actors. As the article describes, each simulation was run by a study team member "who provided immediate feedback to the actor based on real-time observation of the simulation," supplemented by written QA error reports and three 60-minute group feedback sessions.
requirements: Actors were hired through auditions testing their ability to receive critical feedback and adapt performances, then trained through repeated video-recorded rehearsal simulations with group feedback sessions until the study team was confident in script adherence
constraints: The article notes many programs "will not be able to support a dedicated, 2-person QA team in addition to immediate feedback from the study or teaching team"
target_learners: Practicing ICU physicians (intensivists) participating in simulated family meetings
Standardized family member actors
target_learning_goals: Consistent, high-fidelity actor performances that preserve valid measurement of physician communication behavior in simulation-based trials
examples: QA reviewers marked errors as minor or major depending on whether they could influence physician behavior, such as an SFM seeking clarification about prognosis when the script forbade it
key_sources: Abshire Martha A., Li Xintong, Basyal Pragyashree Sharma, Teply Melissa L., Singh Arun L., Hayes Margaret M., Turnbull Alison E. (2020). Actor feedback and rigorous monitoring: Essential quality assurance tools for testing behavioral interventions with simulation. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0233538

article_title: Experiential learning for children's dental anxiety: a cluster randomized trial.
citation: Zhu Minmin, Yu Hongbing, Xie Bo, Li Hongwen, He Qian, Li Huimin, Su Jing, Li Xueqi. (2020). Experiential learning for children's dental anxiety: a cluster randomized trial. BMC Oral Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12903-020-01204-5
title: School-based experiential learning intervention: oral health presentation plus simulated dental clinic role play
description: A multi-session school-based intervention in which children first receive "a lively 40-min presentation on oral health given by dentists" using slides, cartoon videos and dental models; one month later they take part in a simulated dental clinic in the classroom, demonstrating dental tools and role-playing patient, dentist, nurse and parent in 4-person groups; a month after that they visit the dental clinic for PFS treatment. The trial compared this with a conventional 5-min Tell-Show-Do session at the time of the visit.
requirements: Class as the unit of delivery with dentists and dental nurses to run the presentation, tool demonstration and role play; a simulated dental clinic setup in the classroom with a dental bed
constraints: Evaluated in 7-8-year-old children in Shenzhen primary schools immediately before planned pit and fissure sealant; the authors note different EL activities might be needed to cover other dental procedures than PFS
target_learners: Children aged 7–8 years in primary school, before their first preventive dental visit
target_learning_goals: Familiarity with dental procedures and tools, dental health knowledge, reduced dental anxiety
examples: Children were organized in 4-person-groups for a five-minute role play around a dental bed, playing a patient, a dentist, a nurse and a parent, while other groups watched oral health cartoon videos
key_sources: Zhu Minmin, Yu Hongbing, Xie Bo, Li Hongwen, He Qian, Li Huimin, Su Jing, Li Xueqi. (2020). Experiential learning for children's dental anxiety: a cluster randomized trial. BMC Oral Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12903-020-01204-5

article_title: Subcutaneous immunoglobulin in primary immunodeficiency - impact of training and infusion characteristics on patient-reported outcomes.
citation: Mallick R., Henderson T., Lahue B. J., Kafal A., Bassett P., Scalchunes C. (2020). Subcutaneous immunoglobulin in primary immunodeficiency – impact of training and infusion characteristics on patient-reported outcomes. BMC Immunology. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7418302/
title: SCIG patient training should ensure high patient confidence by the final training session while keeping overall training duration concise
description: The article proposes that SCIG training for patients with primary immunodeficiency should be designed so that patients feel confident by their final training session, while keeping the overall duration of training concise. The authors state that "while thorough training with a skilled professional would facilitate greater confidence in SCIG use, the overall duration of training should ideally be concise to ensure the benefits outweigh the burden of time-consuming training." This principle is grounded in the finding that higher post-training confidence was associated with better PROs across multiple domains, while longer total training time was associated with lower ease of training.
requirements: Training delivered by a skilled professional to build patient confidence in SCIG self-infusion
constraints: The exact amount of SCIG training, training location, and ease of training will differ at a patient level
target_learners: Patients with primary immunodeficiency transitioning to SCIG self-administration
Parent/caregiver proxy respondents for pediatric patients
target_learning_goals: Developing confidence and competence in SCIG self-infusion technique
Understanding infusion parameters and ancillary supplies
examples: The survey found that requiring ≤3 training sessions was associated with higher TSQM effectiveness and side effects scores, and total SCIG training lasting <4 h was associated with high ease of training
key_sources: Mallick R., Henderson T., Lahue B. J., Kafal A., Bassett P., Scalchunes C. (2020). Subcutaneous immunoglobulin in primary immunodeficiency – impact of training and infusion characteristics on patient-reported outcomes. BMC Immunology. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7418302/

article_title: Subcutaneous immunoglobulin in primary immunodeficiency - impact of training and infusion characteristics on patient-reported outcomes.
citation: Mallick R., Henderson T., Lahue B. J., Kafal A., Bassett P., Scalchunes C. (2020). Subcutaneous immunoglobulin in primary immunodeficiency – impact of training and infusion characteristics on patient-reported outcomes. BMC Immunology. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7418302/
title: Patient education for SCIG should include information on needle length/gauge, number of sites and rotation, and different flow rate tubing sets to optimize infusion set-up
description: The article recommends that patient education as part of SCIG training should cover specific infusion set-up parameters. The authors state that "Patient education, as part of SCIG training, should include information on needle length/gauge, number of sites and rotation, and different flow rate tubing sets." This recommendation is grounded in findings that higher GHP was predicted by fewer infusion sites, and that shorter infusion preparation and actual infusion times were associated with better treatment satisfaction and lower fatigue. Understanding these variables and using the right supplies could lead to reduced infusion times and higher satisfaction.
requirements: Access to appropriate ancillary supplies for SCIG infusion
Training that covers infusion set-up parameters
constraints: As IgG therapy requires individualization, the process from SCIG initiation to a fully independent and optimized self-infusion regimen can take time
target_learners: Patients with primary immunodeficiency self-administering SCIG at home
target_learning_goals: Optimizing infusion set-up and ancillary supply selection
Reducing infusion preparation and administration time
examples: The survey found that respondents with ≥4 infusion sites had lower odds of being in the best GHP tertile (OR = 0.44) compared with those with 1–3 sites
key_sources: Mallick R., Henderson T., Lahue B. J., Kafal A., Bassett P., Scalchunes C. (2020). Subcutaneous immunoglobulin in primary immunodeficiency – impact of training and infusion characteristics on patient-reported outcomes. BMC Immunology. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7418302/

article_title: How to Introduce Scopemanship Into Your Training Program.
citation: Bollipo Steven, Bilal Mohammad, Siau Keith, Charabaty Aline. (2020). How to Introduce Scopemanship Into Your Training Program. Gastroenterology. https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2020.08.013
title: Scopemanship: a six-domain framework of holistic endoscopist attributes beyond technical skill
description: Scopemanship is defined as "the art, professionalism, ethics, and the holistic approach befitting endoscopists that transcends beyond the core technical and nontechnical skills." The article organizes it into six key domains — communication and compassion, teamwork and empowerment, situational awareness, decision making, leadership, and training — with before, during, and after procedure examples in Table 1. Its core concepts include "being ethical, compassionate and attentive to the needs of others, and fostering communication and leadership skills." The framework originated on Twitter under the hashtag #Scopemanship and is offered as a legacy to impart to trainees.
requirements: Trainers and unit staff at all hierarchies commit to embracing the values of scopemanship
constraints: Attributes vary depending on individual personalities, mood, physical or emotional stressors, time pressure, and factors out of one's control
target_learners: Gastroenterology fellows and endoscopy trainees
target_learning_goals: Professionalism, communication, teamwork, leadership, situational awareness, and decision making in endoscopy
examples: Table 1 lists domain-specific behaviors such as walking the patient through what to expect, setting team expectations and roles, and providing structured and constructive feedback after the procedure
key_sources: Bollipo Steven, Bilal Mohammad, Siau Keith, Charabaty Aline. (2020). How to Introduce Scopemanship Into Your Training Program. Gastroenterology. https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2020.08.013

article_title: Course-based research experience of undergraduate medical students through project-based learning.
citation: Si Jihyun. (2020). Course-based research experience of undergraduate medical students through project-based learning. Korean Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.3946/kjme.2020.152
title: Scientific thinking and medical research: a three-credit introductory course-based research experience through PBL
description: An introductory-level CRE developed as "the first point of entry into research for undergraduate medical students," aiming to expose students to research, provide authentic research experiences, and develop basic research skills. It was a three-credit course meeting twice weekly for 120 minutes across a 15-week semester, with nine groups of four to five students each guided by a professor. Grades combined individual components (attendance, contribution, self- and peer-assessment) and group components (presentation, proposal, report).
requirements: Professors assigned to each group from diverse biomedical majors
Protected time within the core curriculum so all students can participate
target_learners: second-year premedical undergraduate students
examples: Weeks 1–5 covered lectures on research ethics, literature search, experimental method, and report writing; weeks 6–15 were devoted to group research, proposals, and final reports
key_sources: Si Jihyun. (2020). Course-based research experience of undergraduate medical students through project-based learning. Korean Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.3946/kjme.2020.152

article_title: The school-subject-specificity hypothesis: Implication in the relationship with grades.
citation: Chanal J, Paumier D. (2020). The school-subject-specificity hypothesis: Implication in the relationship with grades. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0230103
title: The school-subject-specificity hypothesis within the Hierarchical Model of Intrinsic and Extrinsic Motivation
description: The school-subject-specificity hypothesis is an explanatory account within SDT's Hierarchical Model of Intrinsic and Extrinsic Motivation, which postulates global, contextual and situational levels of motivation. The hypothesis states that "autonomous motivation is more differentiated than controlled motivation because it is more related to the situational level (i.e., more school-subject-specific) than controlled motivation". This article tested and confirmed the hypothesis with seven regulation types and linked it to grade correlations.
requirements: Simultaneous assessment of motivation at contextual and situational levels across multiple school subjects
Statistical modeling able to disentangle situational, contextual and item sources of variance (CTCM-1)
constraints: The study's sample was a single public junior high school in Geneva and cannot be considered representative of a larger population
target_learners: junior high school students
target_learning_goals: academic motivation across school subjects and its relation to achievement
examples: 579 students completed questionnaires assessing motivation at the academic level and in French, mathematics, English and physical education simultaneously
key_sources: Chanal J, Paumier D. (2020). The school-subject-specificity hypothesis: Implication in the relationship with grades. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0230103

article_title: Callous-Unemotional Traits and Academic Performance in Secondary School Students: Examining the Moderating Effect of Gender.
citation: Bird E., Chhoa C. Y., Midouhas E., Allen J. L. (2019). Callous-Unemotional Traits and Academic Performance in Secondary School Students: Examining the Moderating Effect of Gender. Journal of Abnormal Child Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10802-019-00545-2
title: Use CU traits and gender together to identify students at risk of poor academic performance and target school resources
description: The article proposes that assessing children's callous-unemotional traits, jointly with gender, can flag students likely to earn poor grades so schools can allocate support. It argues that "Investigating the relationship between CU traits and academic outcomes may assist in identifying children at risk for poor academic performance and help schools to direct resources towards students most in need of support." The Science-specific moderation suggests boys high in CU traits warrant particular attention in Science.
requirements: Child-report CU trait screening (e.g., the ICU) alongside collection of academic grades from school records
constraints: The study is cross-sectional, so the direction of the CU-trait–grade relationship is unknown; the Science interaction needs replication
target_learners: Secondary school students aged 11–14 (Key Stage 3)
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement across English, Math and Science
examples: The study gathered ICU self-reports and school-record grades for 437 students in Years 7–9 at one English state secondary school and fitted multilevel models per subject
key_sources: Bird E., Chhoa C. Y., Midouhas E., Allen J. L. (2019). Callous-Unemotional Traits and Academic Performance in Secondary School Students: Examining the Moderating Effect of Gender. Journal of Abnormal Child Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10802-019-00545-2
